nodes.problem: When retransmission or re-read is impossible or too slow, correction must come from the data itself; redundant encodings trade space for self-healing data. Code-family variants (Hamming, Reed-Solomon, LDPC) stay in the algorithmics zoo.
nodes.named_in: Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes - Hamming (1950)

nodes.name: Hidden Class
nodes.what: The runtime assigns each object a shared internal layout descriptor (map/shape/hidden class) recording its property names and slot offsets, transitioning objects between descriptors as properties are added, so objects created the same way share one layout.
nodes.problem: Prototype- and dictionary-based languages have no static classes, so naive objects carry per-instance property tables; shared layout descriptors recover class-like memory density and give inline caches a cheap identity to guard on.
nodes.named_in: Chambers, Ungar & Lee, 'An Efficient Implementation of SELF, a Dynamically-Typed Object-Oriented Language Based on Prototypes', OOPSLA 1989 (names 'maps'; verified live this session); 'hidden class' is the V8 documentation term

nodes.name: Level of Detail
nodes.what: Maintain multiple representations of an object at different fidelities and select the cheapest one whose error is imperceptible given current importance (typically distance from the viewer).
nodes.problem: Rendering or simulating everything at full fidelity wastes resources on objects that contribute little to the result; graded representations bound cost while preserving perceived quality. Generalizes beyond graphics (audio, AI, simulation LOD).
nodes.named_in: Level of Detail for 3D Graphics - Luebke, Reddy, Cohen, Varshney, Watson, Huebner (2003)
nodes.borderline: Graphics-domain optimization technique rather than a general software mechanism, but it is named, recurring, and implementable inside one component; included per charter.

nodes.name: Multiple Representations
nodes.what: Provide several implementations of an object, each optimized for different size/speed trade-offs, behind one common interface.
nodes.problem: One representation cannot be optimal for all instances (small vs large, read-only vs mutable); switching representations per instance keeps memory minimal without changing clients.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Newtype
nodes.what: Wrap an existing type in a distinct single-field type so the compiler distinguishes semantically different values (Miles vs Kilometers) and the wrapper can carry its own invariants and trait implementations.
nodes.problem: Raw primitives let unrelated quantities be mixed silently and leak representation; the zero-cost wrapper restores type safety and API encapsulation.
nodes.named_in: Rust Design Patterns (rust-unofficial, living); keyword-level origin in Haskell (newtype)

nodes.name: Opaque Pointer
nodes.what: An API exposes only a forward-declared struct pointer whose definition lives in the implementation file, so clients cannot see or touch the representation.
nodes.problem: C has no access control; the incomplete type makes information hiding compiler-enforced and keeps ABI stable across representation changes.
nodes.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996)

nodes.name: Packed Data
nodes.what: Pack data items within a structure (bit-fields, smaller types, eliminated padding) so they occupy minimum space.
nodes.problem: Naturally-aligned, full-width representations waste scarce RAM; packing trades access cost for a smaller memory footprint.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: PAX Page Layout
nodes.what: Within each fixed-size storage page, values are grouped per attribute into minipages instead of being stored row-contiguously, keeping a page's records together on disk while making each attribute cache-line-contiguous in memory.
nodes.problem: Row-oriented (NSM) pages drag all attributes of a record through the cache when a scan touches only a few columns, while full column stores (DSM) pay record-reconstruction joins; PAX gets columnar cache behavior without changing page-level I/O or record placement.
nodes.named_in: Ailamaki, DeWitt, Hill, Skounakis — Weaving Relations for Cache Performance, VLDB 2001

nodes.name: Pointer Swizzling
nodes.what: Converts persistent references (file offsets, object IDs, page-relative addresses) into raw in-memory pointers when data is loaded, and back again on write-out.
nodes.problem: Persisted or memory-mapped object graphs cannot store raw virtual addresses; following offset-based references on every access is slow, so references are rewritten to native pointers while resident.
nodes.named_in: Wilson & Kakkad, 'Pointer Swizzling at Page Fault Time' (1992); Moss, 'Working with Persistent Objects: To Swizzle or Not to Swizzle' (IEEE TSE, 1992)

nodes.name: Pointer Tagging
nodes.what: Encodes type or other metadata in otherwise-unused bits of a pointer-sized word (low alignment bits, high address bits, or unused NaN payload space), so small values carry their own type tag and need no heap allocation.
nodes.problem: Dynamic-language runtimes must represent values of many types uniformly and compactly; boxing every integer or float on the heap costs allocation, indirection, and GC pressure.
nodes.named_in: Gudeman, 'Representing Type Information in Dynamically Typed Languages', Univ. of Arizona TR 93-27, 1993 (canonical survey; verified via live search this session)
nodes.borderline: index's reference-counting entry lists 'ABA Mitigation via Tagged Pointer' as an aka — that is a different mechanism (version bits for ABA), not type tagging; no dedup conflict

nodes.name: Quantity
nodes.what: A value type pairing a number with its unit of measure, with arithmetic and comparisons that respect unit compatibility and conversion.
nodes.problem: Bare numbers lose their units, inviting silent unit-mismatch bugs (feet vs meters, dollars vs euros); carrying the unit in the type makes mismatched arithmetic impossible or explicit.
nodes.named_in: Analysis Patterns: Reusable Object Models - Martin Fowler (1996)
nodes.borderline: Analysis-pattern (domain-modeling) altitude, but a directly implementable value type recurring across codebases.

nodes.name: Range
nodes.what: A value object representing an interval by its start and end (with open/closed ends), answering inclusion, overlap, and abutment queries.
nodes.problem: Pairs of loose start/end fields breed off-by-one and boundary-convention bugs repeated at every comparison; one range type centralizes the boundary logic.
nodes.named_in: Analysis Patterns: Reusable Object Models - Martin Fowler (1996)
nodes.borderline: Analysis-pattern (domain-modeling) altitude, but a directly implementable value type recurring across codebases.

nodes.name: Record Set
nodes.what: An in-memory representation of tabular data that looks and acts like the result of a database query but can be built and manipulated disconnected from the database.
nodes.problem: UI machinery and table-oriented logic want a generic table-shaped data structure independent of any live connection; a disconnected record set lets the same tooling work on queried or synthesized data.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Relationship Object
nodes.what: Reify a relationship between objects as a first-class object that stores the participants plus the relationship's own attributes and behavior, instead of encoding the link as mutual references.
nodes.problem: Relationships with their own state (start date, role, quantity) or lifecycle cannot live naturally inside either participant; direct mutual pointers scatter the relationship's logic and complicate consistency.
nodes.named_in: Noble, 'Basic Relationship Patterns', PLoPD4 (2000); also Boyd, 'Business Patterns of Association Objects', PLoPD3 (1997) (both ToCs loaded live)

nodes.name: Slotted Page Layout
nodes.what: A page format with a slot directory growing from one end and variable-length records growing from the other, so records are addressed by stable slot number rather than byte offset.
nodes.problem: Variable-length records must be inserted, deleted, and relocated within a fixed-size page without invalidating external record identifiers; the indirection slot array permits in-page compaction while record ids stay stable.
nodes.named_in: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

nodes.name: Tagged Union
nodes.what: A data type whose value is exactly one of several named alternatives, carrying a tag that identifies which alternative is present.
nodes.problem: Safely representing 'one of N shapes' data without unchecked casts or sentinel conventions; enables exhaustive case analysis so unhandled alternatives are caught statically.
nodes.named_in: Types and Programming Languages - Benjamin C. Pierce (2002)

nodes.name: Temporal Property
nodes.what: Represent an attribute (or whole object) as a time-indexed collection of values so the model can answer 'what was/is/will be the value at time T' rather than only the current value.
nodes.problem: Domain data changes over time and past states must remain queryable (retroactive corrections, effective dates); overwriting in place destroys history.
nodes.named_in: Carlson, Estepp & Fowler, 'Temporal Patterns', PLoPD4 (2000) (ToC loaded live); living treatment: Fowler's eaaDev temporal patterns (Temporal Property, Temporal Object, Snapshot, Effectivity)

nodes.name: Texture Atlas
nodes.what: Pack many small images into one large texture and remap each user's texture coordinates into its sub-rectangle, so a single bound resource serves many logical images.
nodes.problem: Per-texture bind/state changes break rendering batches and dominate CPU submission cost; consolidating images into one atlas lets unrelated geometry share render state and be submitted together, at the cost of packing, bleeding/padding, and mip-level management.
nodes.named_in: NVIDIA SDK White Paper 'Improve Batching Using Texture Atlases' (WP-01387-001, 2004); Ivan-Assen Ivanov, 'Practical Texture Atlases', Gamasutra/Game Developer, 2006

nodes.name: Type-Safe Enum
nodes.what: Represent an enumerated type as a class with a fixed set of public static final instances and a private constructor, giving type safety, namespacing, and behavior per constant.
nodes.problem: int/#define constants are unchecked, unprintable, and collide; the pattern (since absorbed into Java enum / C++ enum class) makes enumerations real types. Bloch's enum-singleton is a folded application.
nodes.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (1st ed. 2001, Item 21)

nodes.name: Value Object
nodes.what: A small immutable object, such as a date or money amount, whose equality is based on its attribute values rather than on identity.
nodes.problem: Treating conceptually value-like data as identity-bearing objects invites aliasing bugs and wrong equality; value semantics (immutability, whole-value replacement, structural equality) make such data safe to share and compare.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Virtual DOM
nodes.what: Keeps a lightweight in-memory tree describing the desired UI, diffs it against the previous tree on every update, and applies only the minimal set of mutations (reconciliation) to the real, expensive display tree.
nodes.problem: Direct manipulation of a retained display tree (the browser DOM) is slow and hard to reason about; declaring the whole UI and diffing lets code be written as 'render from state' while paying only for what changed. Keyed list reconciliation and the incremental-DOM alternative are variants folded here.
nodes.named_in: Reconciliation - React documentation - Meta

nodes.name: B-tree
nodes.what: Self-balancing wide-fanout search tree whose nodes hold many keys sized to a block/page, keeping the tree shallow; B+ trees keep all values in linked leaves for range scans.
nodes.problem: Binary trees generate one I/O or cache miss per level; matching node size to the storage block minimizes disk/page accesses for ordered indexes, making it the default database and filesystem index.
nodes.named_in: Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes - Bayer & McCreight (1972)

nodes.name: Binary Heap (Priority Queue)
nodes.what: Implicit complete binary tree stored in an array maintaining the heap order property, giving O(log n) insert and extract-min/max with no pointers.
nodes.problem: Schedulers, event queues, Dijkstra-style algorithms, and timer systems repeatedly need the next-highest-priority item without keeping the whole collection sorted.
nodes.named_in: Algorithm 232: Heapsort - J. W. J. Williams (1964)

nodes.name: Binary Search Tree
aka: treap / splay tree (research variants, sibling corpus)
nodes.what: Binary tree maintaining the search-order invariant (left < node < right); self-balancing variants (red-black, AVL) guarantee O(log n) ordered operations.
nodes.problem: Ordered maps/sets needing sorted iteration, predecessor/successor, and range queries - which hash tables cannot provide - with logarithmic worst-case bounds (std::map, kernel schedulers).
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

nodes.name: Bitmap / Bitset
nodes.what: Dense array of bits representing set membership or boolean flags by index, supporting bulk bitwise set operations word-at-a-time; compressed variants (Roaring, WAH) handle sparse ranges.
nodes.problem: Sets over a bounded integer universe cost far less as one bit per element than as pointer structures, and AND/OR/NOT over machine words gives vectorized set algebra (allocator maps, DB bitmap indexes, ECS masks).
nodes.named_in: Programming Pearls - Jon Bentley (1986)

nodes.name: Bitmap Index
nodes.what: An index that keeps, for each distinct value (or value range) of a column, a bitmap with one bit per row; multi-predicate queries are answered by bitwise AND/OR/NOT over the bitmaps before touching any rows.
nodes.problem: B-tree row-id lists are bulky and slow to intersect for low-cardinality columns and ad-hoc conjunctive predicates; per-value bitmaps make multi-column selection a stream of word-wide boolean operations and compress well on skewed data.
nodes.named_in: O'Neil — Model 204 Architecture and Performance, HPTS 1987; O'Neil & Quass — Improved Query Performance with Variant Indexes, SIGMOD 1997
nodes.borderline: distinct from bitmap-bitset (the raw data structure already in the index): this is the database index mechanism built from per-value bitmaps, with its own naming literature

nodes.name: Bloom Filter
nodes.what: Bit array plus k hash functions answering approximate set membership with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate.
nodes.problem: Storing full key sets to answer 'definitely absent?' wastes memory; a few bits per element let a component skip expensive lookups (disk reads, cache probes, network calls) for keys that cannot be present.
nodes.named_in: Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors - Burton H. Bloom (1970)

nodes.name: Bounding Volume Hierarchy
nodes.what: Tree whose nodes are bounding volumes (typically AABBs) enclosing their children, with scene objects at the leaves, letting intersection queries prune whole subtrees.
nodes.problem: Ray tracing and collision detection against thousands of objects cannot test each primitive; hierarchical bounds reduce intersection tests to a logarithmic descent.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Rendering - Akenine-Moller, Haines, Hoffman (2018)

nodes.name: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT)
aka: G-Counter / PN-Counter / G-Set / OR-Set / LWW-Register / RGA (family members, folded)
nodes.what: Family of replicated data types (counters, sets, registers, sequences) whose merge operations are commutative/associative/idempotent, so concurrently edited replicas converge without coordination.
nodes.problem: Multi-writer replication without locks or consensus produces conflicts; algebraically merge-safe state lets offline-first apps and collaborative editors converge deterministically.
nodes.named_in: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types - Shapiro, Preguica, Baquero, Zawirski (2011)
nodes.borderline: Charter mandates ONE element for the family; each replica's type is implementable in one component (IN), though the replication context shades distributed-systems territory.

nodes.name: Consistent Hashing
nodes.what: Hashing scheme placing keys and buckets on the same ring so each key maps to the nearest bucket, remapping only ~1/n of keys when a bucket joins or leaves; virtual nodes smooth the load.
nodes.problem: Modulo hashing reshuffles nearly every key when the bucket count changes; caches and partitioned stores need key-to-node assignment that is stable under membership churn.
nodes.named_in: Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web - Karger et al. (1997)
nodes.borderline: The ring structure is implementable inside one component (IN); its use as a cluster-partitioning scheme shades architectural - parked companion entry for Phase 3.

nodes.name: Copy-on-Write B-Tree
nodes.what: A B-tree whose updates never modify pages in place: changed pages and their ancestors up to the root are rewritten to new locations, and commit is an atomic root swap.
nodes.problem: Combines B-tree lookup with crash safety and lock-free readers (old roots stay valid snapshots) without a separate recovery log; used by LMDB and btrfs at the cost of write amplification.
nodes.named_in: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

nodes.name: Count-Min Sketch
nodes.what: Sub-linear 2-D counter array indexed by multiple hash functions that answers approximate frequency queries over a stream, with one-sided (over-count) error.
nodes.problem: Counting exact per-item frequencies over high-volume streams needs memory proportional to distinct items; a fixed small sketch bounds error probabilistically for heavy-hitter and frequency estimation.
nodes.named_in: An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications - Cormode & Muthukrishnan (2005)

nodes.name: Deque
nodes.what: Sequence container supporting O(1) insertion and removal at both ends, typically as a ring buffer or blocked array.
nodes.problem: Sliding windows, work-stealing schedulers, and undo histories need queue and stack behavior simultaneously; neither a plain stack nor a FIFO queue suffices.
nodes.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1: Fundamental Algorithms - Donald Knuth (1968)

nodes.name: Disjoint-Set (Union-Find)
nodes.what: Forest of trees tracking a partition of elements into disjoint sets, with union-by-rank and path compression making find/union near-constant amortized.
nodes.problem: Incremental equivalence tracking (connected components, type unification, Kruskal's MST, image segmentation) needs merge-and-query on partitions far faster than recomputing reachability.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

nodes.name: Dynamic Array
nodes.what: Contiguous array that grows by amortized capacity doubling (and optionally shrinks), preserving O(1) amortized append and O(1) random access.
nodes.problem: Fixed-size arrays force a size guess up front; linked structures sacrifice cache locality and random access. Amortized reallocation gives list flexibility at array speed.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

nodes.name: Embedded Pointer
nodes.what: Embed the pointers that maintain a collection directly into each member object instead of allocating external link nodes.
nodes.problem: External link nodes double the allocation count and memory overhead of collections; embedding the links in the objects removes per-node allocations (the intrusive-container idiom).
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Erase-Remove
nodes.what: Combine std::remove/remove_if (which compacts kept elements) with container erase to actually delete matching elements from a sequence container.
nodes.problem: STL algorithms cannot change container size; the two-step idiom is the established way to physically delete elements without quadratic cost.
nodes.named_in: Effective STL - Scott Meyers (2001)
nodes.borderline: A micro container-usage idiom rather than a design mechanism; kept as a canonical named C++ idiom (now std::erase_if).

nodes.name: Fenwick Tree
nodes.what: Implicit array-based tree exploiting binary index decomposition to maintain prefix sums with O(log n) point update and prefix query in n words of memory.
nodes.problem: The prefix-sum-with-updates role of a segment tree, in a fraction of the memory and code, when only invertible aggregates (sums, counts) are needed.
nodes.named_in: A New Data Structure for Cumulative Frequency Tables - Peter Fenwick (1994)
nodes.borderline: Near the research-zoo line; included because it is the named lighter-weight alternative designers actually reach for over segment trees for cumulative counts.

nodes.name: Fixed-Capacity Container
nodes.what: STL-style containers whose maximum capacity is a compile-time parameter, storing elements in embedded (static or stack) storage with no heap use.
nodes.problem: Standard containers allocate dynamically, which embedded and safety-critical code forbids; fixed-capacity variants keep container ergonomics with deterministic memory.
nodes.named_in: Embedded Template Library (ETL) documentation - Wellbelove (living)

nodes.name: Gap Buffer
nodes.what: Contiguous text buffer with a movable gap of free space at the cursor position, making localized insertions and deletions O(1) until the gap moves or fills.
nodes.problem: Text editing clusters around a cursor; keeping the free space there converts the common-case edit from an O(n) array shift into an in-place write (Emacs's buffer representation).
nodes.named_in: The Craft of Text Editing - Craig A. Finseth (1991)

nodes.name: Hash Array Mapped Trie (HAMT)
nodes.what: Trie over hash-code bit chunks using per-node bitmaps to compress sparse children, giving an efficiently persistent (structurally shared, immutable) hash map.
nodes.problem: Immutable/functional programs need maps whose 'updates' return new versions in O(log n) time and memory via structural sharing rather than full copies (Clojure, Scala, Immutable.js collections).
nodes.named_in: Ideal Hash Trees - Phil Bagwell (2001)

nodes.name: Hash Table
nodes.what: Key-value store mapping keys through a hash function into an array of buckets, with collisions resolved by separate chaining or open addressing (linear/quadratic probing, Robin Hood, cuckoo, Swiss-table variants folded here).
nodes.problem: Provides expected O(1) lookup, insert, and delete by key when key ordering is not needed, trading memory overhead and worst-case degradation for speed.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

nodes.name: HyperLogLog
nodes.what: Cardinality-estimation sketch that hashes items and records maximum leading-zero runs in a small register array, estimating distinct counts within a few percent using kilobytes.
nodes.problem: Exact distinct-count over large streams requires storing every seen key; probabilistic register merging gives mergeable, fixed-memory cardinality estimates (unique visitors, distinct keys).
nodes.named_in: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm - Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet, Meunier (2007)

nodes.name: Interval Tree
nodes.what: Search tree over intervals (typically a BST augmented with subtree max-endpoints) answering which stored intervals overlap a query point or interval in O(log n + k).
nodes.problem: Schedulers, editors (marker ranges), genomics, and calendars repeatedly ask 'what overlaps this range?', which sorted lists answer only by linear scan.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
nodes.borderline: Charter-flagged: kept IN - a recurring designer-reachable role (overlap queries), not just an algorithmics exercise.

nodes.name: Inverted Index
nodes.what: Mapping from each term to the sorted list of documents (and positions) containing it, the core structure of full-text search engines.
nodes.problem: Scanning documents per query is linear in corpus size; inverting the term-document relation makes multi-term queries an intersection/union of postings lists.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Information Retrieval - Manning, Raghavan, Schutze (2008)

nodes.name: k-d Tree
nodes.what: Binary space-partitioning tree that splits points on alternating coordinate axes, supporting nearest-neighbor and orthogonal range queries in low dimensions.
nodes.problem: Nearest-neighbor and range search over point sets is linear without an index; axis-aligned recursive splits prune most of the space per query.
nodes.named_in: Multidimensional Binary Search Trees Used for Associative Searching - Jon Bentley (1975)

nodes.name: Linked List
nodes.what: Sequence of nodes each holding an element and a pointer to the next (and optionally previous) node, giving O(1) insertion/removal at a known position without element movement.
nodes.problem: Sequences with frequent mid-stream splicing, stable element addresses, or no contiguous memory (allocators, kernels) cannot use arrays; pointer links trade locality for splice freedom.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
nodes.borderline: Near the lower altitude floor (elementary ADT) but unambiguously named, recurring, and a deliberate design choice versus arrays; kept IN.

nodes.name: Lock-Free FIFO Queue (Michael-Scott)
nodes.what: A linked-list MPMC queue where enqueue and dequeue advance head/tail with CAS, and threads help complete a lagging tail swing before proceeding.
nodes.problem: A shared FIFO whose operations never block: no lock-holder preemption stalls, safe in mixed-priority and signal contexts, scalable under moderate contention.
nodes.named_in: Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms - Michael & Scott (1996)

nodes.name: Lock-Free Stack (Treiber)
nodes.what: A linked LIFO where push and pop swing the top-of-stack pointer with a CAS retry loop (with an ABA guard when nodes are recycled).
nodes.problem: The minimal lock-free container: a shared free list or work stack usable from contexts where locking is forbidden or unscalable.
nodes.named_in: Systems Programming: Coping with Parallelism (IBM Research Report RJ 5118) - R. K. Treiber (1986)

nodes.name: LSM Tree
nodes.what: Write-optimized index that batches writes in an in-memory table, flushes them as sorted immutable runs (SSTables), and merges runs in the background via compaction.
nodes.problem: In-place index updates (B-trees) turn random writes into random I/O; sequential append plus deferred merge converts write-heavy workloads into sequential I/O at the cost of read amplification.
nodes.named_in: The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) - O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick, O'Neil (1996)

nodes.name: Merkle Tree
nodes.what: Tree whose leaves are hashes of data blocks and whose internal nodes hash their children, so one root hash authenticates the whole set and any block is verifiable with a log-length path.
nodes.problem: Verifying integrity or divergence of large or distributed data sets without transferring them; enables efficient tamper-evidence, sync anti-entropy, and inclusion proofs (Git, ZFS, certificate transparency, blockchains).
nodes.named_in: A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function - Ralph Merkle (1987)

nodes.name: MinHash
nodes.what: Similarity sketch storing the minimum hash values of a set under many hash functions, so sketch agreement estimates Jaccard similarity between sets.
nodes.problem: Near-duplicate detection and similarity search over huge document/set collections cannot compare full sets pairwise; small fixed sketches make similarity estimable in constant time.
nodes.named_in: On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents - Andrei Broder (1997)

nodes.name: Navigation Mesh
nodes.what: A data structure representing an environment's walkable space as connected convex polygons, over which agents path-find polygon-to-polygon and then smooth (e.g. string-pulling/funnel) within the free space.
nodes.problem: Waypoint graphs under-represent open walkable areas and force unnatural paths; a polygon mesh of free space supports arbitrary agent movement, cheap search over few polygons, and locally optimal smoothing.
nodes.named_in: Snook, 'Simplified 3D Movement and Pathfinding Using Navigation Meshes', Game Programming Gems, 2000

nodes.name: Persistent Data Structure
nodes.what: A data structure whose update operations return a new version while old versions remain valid, sharing unchanged substructure between versions.
nodes.problem: Provides safe sharing across threads and cheap history/undo without defensive copying, by making every version immutable and reusing common parts.
nodes.named_in: Making Data Structures Persistent - Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator, Tarjan (JCSS, 1989)

nodes.name: Piece Table
nodes.what: Edit representation keeping the original file and an append-only add buffer immutable, with the document described as a sequence of pieces (spans) into the two buffers.
nodes.problem: Editors need fast arbitrary edits, cheap undo, and untouched original file data; recording edits as span descriptors avoids moving text and makes undo a piece-list operation.
nodes.named_in: Data Structures for Text Sequences - Charles Crowley (1998)

nodes.name: Quadtree / Octree
nodes.what: Hierarchical spatial partition recursively subdividing 2D space into four quadrants (or 3D into eight octants) until cells meet an occupancy or depth bound.
nodes.problem: Spatial queries (culling, collision broad-phase, image regions, point clouds) over non-uniform data need adaptive subdivision that concentrates resolution where objects cluster.
nodes.named_in: Quad Trees: A Data Structure for Retrieval on Composite Keys - Finkel & Bentley (1974)

nodes.name: Queue (FIFO)
nodes.what: First-in-first-out collection with enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head, array- or list-backed.
nodes.problem: Order-preserving buffering between producers and consumers - task queues, BFS frontiers, request pipelines - requires arrival-order service as a structural guarantee.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
nodes.borderline: Elementary ADT at the band's floor; kept IN as the in-process structure (the message-queue mechanism and broker topology belong to other scouts/Phase 3).

nodes.name: R-tree
nodes.what: Balanced B-tree-like index of minimum bounding rectangles that may overlap, grouping nearby spatial objects for disk-friendly window and containment queries.
nodes.problem: Databases need paged, balanced indexing of extended spatial objects (rectangles, polygons) where point-based partitions fail; the standard spatial index of GIS databases.
nodes.named_in: R-Trees: A Dynamic Index Structure for Spatial Searching - Antonin Guttman (1984)

nodes.name: Rope
nodes.what: Balanced binary tree of string fragments representing a long string, making concatenation, insertion, and splitting O(log n) instead of O(n) copies.
nodes.problem: Flat strings make every edit of a large text a full copy; editors and string-heavy systems need sublinear splice operations and cheap substring sharing.
nodes.named_in: Ropes: an Alternative to Strings - Boehm, Atkinson, Plass (1995)

nodes.name: Scene Graph
nodes.what: Represent a scene as a hierarchy of nodes whose spatial transforms (and other attributes) compose parent-to-child, so moving a parent moves its whole subtree.
nodes.problem: Objects are naturally attached to one another (turret on tank, moon around planet); a hierarchy lets local transforms be authored independently while world transforms are derived by composition, and supports hierarchical culling and traversal.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Rendering - Akenine-Moller, Haines, Hoffman (2008, 3rd ed.)

nodes.name: Secondary Index
nodes.what: An auxiliary structure mapping non-primary-key attribute values to record locations (or primary keys), maintained alongside the base data on every write.
nodes.problem: Queries on attributes other than the primary access path degenerate to full scans; a redundant per-attribute index buys lookup speed at the cost of write amplification and consistency maintenance.
nodes.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)
nodes.borderline: Generic 'index' altitude is contested; kept because 'secondary index' names a specific recurring design decision (redundant derived access path maintained on write).

nodes.name: Segment Tree
nodes.what: Complete binary tree over an array where each node stores an aggregate (sum, min, max) of its range, giving O(log n) range queries and point/range updates.
nodes.problem: Alternating range-aggregate queries and updates over an array defeat both prefix-sum arrays (slow update) and raw arrays (slow query); the tree balances the two.
nodes.named_in: Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications - de Berg, Cheong, van Kreveld, Overmars (2008)
nodes.borderline: Charter-flagged research-zoo borderline: kept IN - named, recurring, and reached-for by role (range aggregate index) well beyond competitive programming; variants folded.

nodes.name: Skip List
nodes.what: Sorted linked list augmented with probabilistic express lanes at multiple levels, giving expected O(log n) search/insert/delete without rebalancing.
nodes.problem: Balanced trees achieve ordered O(log n) operations through intricate rebalancing; randomized levels achieve the same expectation with simpler code and easier concurrent (lock-free) implementation.
nodes.named_in: Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees - William Pugh (1990)

nodes.name: Slot Map
nodes.what: Contiguous object pool addressed by stable keys that pair a slot index with a generation counter, so freed-and-reused slots invalidate stale handles while keeping O(1) access and dense iteration.
nodes.problem: Game and systems code needs stable, dangle-proof references into pools of frequently created/destroyed objects without pointer invalidation or use-after-free; generations make stale handles detectable.
nodes.named_in: slot_map Container in C++ (WG21 P0661) - Allan Deutsch (2017)

nodes.name: Sparse Set
nodes.what: Pair of arrays (dense packed elements plus sparse index-by-value) representing an integer set with O(1) insert, delete, membership, and clear, and cache-friendly iteration over only the members.
nodes.problem: Sets over a bounded integer universe that are cleared and iterated constantly (compiler live-sets, ECS component membership) need O(1) clear and dense iteration, which bitmaps and hash sets lack.
nodes.named_in: An Efficient Representation for Sparse Sets - Briggs & Torczon (1993)

nodes.name: Spatial Partition
nodes.what: Store objects in a data structure organized by their spatial position (grid, quadtree, BSP, etc.) so that location-based queries need only examine nearby cells.
nodes.problem: Finding objects near a point or each other (collision, combat range, rendering culling) is O(n^2) by pairwise scan; position-keyed structures cut queries to near-constant or logarithmic cost. Concrete structures (quadtree, k-d tree, BSP) are enumerated in the datastructures corpus, not here.
nodes.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

nodes.name: Stack
nodes.what: Last-in-first-out collection with push/pop/peek at one end, whether array- or list-backed.
nodes.problem: Nested and reversible processes - call frames, undo, parsing, DFS, expression evaluation - need most-recent-first access as a structural guarantee.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
nodes.borderline: Elementary ADT at the band's floor; kept IN because designers reach for 'a stack' by role constantly and it anchors many other elements.

nodes.name: Suffix Array
nodes.what: Sorted array of all suffix start positions of a text, supporting binary-search substring queries; the array-based, cache-friendly successor to the suffix tree.
nodes.problem: Repeated arbitrary-substring search over a fixed large text (bioinformatics, plagiarism detection, search indexing) needs a full-text index cheaper than a suffix tree's pointers.
nodes.named_in: Suffix Arrays: A New Method for On-Line String Searches - Manber & Myers (1990)
nodes.borderline: Shades research-zoo; kept IN as the designer-reachable full-text-substring-index role, with suffix tree and FM-index folded as variants.

nodes.name: t-digest
nodes.what: Mergeable sketch of a numeric distribution built from size-varying centroid clusters, estimating quantiles (esp. extreme percentiles) accurately in constant memory.
nodes.problem: Monitoring systems need p99/p999 latency over unbounded streams and across shards; exact quantiles require storing all samples, and fixed-bin histograms lose tail accuracy.
nodes.named_in: Computing Extremely Accurate Quantiles Using t-Digests - Dunning & Ertl (2019)

nodes.name: Trie
nodes.what: Tree keyed by successive symbols of the key, so all descendants of a node share a common prefix; radix/Patricia variants compress single-child chains into one edge.
nodes.problem: Prefix lookup, autocomplete, longest-prefix match (IP routing), and ordered string sets need key-structure-aware indexing that comparison trees and hash tables do not give.
nodes.named_in: Trie Memory - Edward Fredkin (1960)

nodes.name: Uniform Spatial Hash Grid
nodes.what: Partition of space into uniform cells whose coordinates hash into buckets of contained objects, so neighborhood queries examine only nearby cells.
nodes.problem: Broad-phase collision and proximity queries need O(1) neighbor lookup for roughly uniformly-sized objects without the build cost or pointer-chasing of trees.
nodes.named_in: Optimized Spatial Hashing for Collision Detection of Deformable Objects - Teschner et al. (2003)

nodes.name: Zipper
nodes.what: A representation of a position inside an immutable structure as the focused element plus its inverted surrounding context, allowing O(1) local edits and navigation.
nodes.problem: Enables efficient localized updates and cursor-style navigation in purely functional trees and lists, where naive editing would rebuild the path from the root on every step.
nodes.named_in: The Zipper - Gérard Huet (Journal of Functional Programming, 1997)

nodes.name: Zone Map
nodes.what: A tiny per-block summary (typically min/max, optionally count/sum) kept for each zone of contiguously stored tuples; scans consult the summaries first and skip every block whose value range cannot satisfy the predicate.
nodes.problem: Full-precision secondary indexes on bulk-loaded analytic data are expensive to build and maintain; a few bytes of precomputed aggregate per block prunes most of a scan for range/equality predicates at near-zero load and storage cost.
nodes.named_in: Moerkotte — Small Materialized Aggregates: A Light Weight Index Structure for Data Warehousing, VLDB 1998 (naming source); 'zone map' is the Netezza-originated industry name (Ziauddin et al., Dimensions Based Data Clustering and Zone Maps, PVLDB 2017); PostgreSQL BRIN is the same mechanism

nodes.name: A/B Firmware Image Update
nodes.what: Keep two firmware image slots; write the new image into the inactive slot, verify it, then atomically switch the boot selection, keeping the old image as instant fallback.
nodes.problem: In-place firmware updates brick the device on power loss or a bad image; dual slots make updates atomic and reversible. Golden-image recovery slots, anti-rollback counters, and delta updates are folded here as variants.
nodes.named_in: Device Firmware Update Cookbook - Memfault Interrupt

nodes.name: Bootloader Jump / Handoff
nodes.what: A small boot program validates the application image, then hands off execution by loading the application's stack pointer and reset vector (relocating the vector table) and jumping to it with hardware in a known state.
nodes.problem: Field-updatable and multi-image devices need a trusted first stage that can select, verify, and start an application image; the disciplined SP/PC/vector handoff is the mechanism that makes the transition safe and restartable.
nodes.named_in: From Zero to main(): How to Write a Bootloader from Scratch - Memfault Interrupt (2019)

nodes.name: Deferred Interrupt Processing
nodes.what: Split interrupt handling into a minimal ISR that acknowledges the hardware and queues work, plus deferred task-level code that completes the processing later.
nodes.problem: Long ISRs increase interrupt latency and jitter for everything else; deferring the bulk of the work keeps interrupt context short while preserving responsiveness.
nodes.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

nodes.name: Device Driver
nodes.what: A module encapsulating all interaction with one device class behind a uniform operations interface (open/read/write/ioctl or vendor API).
nodes.problem: Hardware detail must be quarantined behind a stable interface so application logic stays portable and per-device knowledge lives in one place.
nodes.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini, Kroah-Hartman (2005)
nodes.borderline: A component role more than a mechanism, but named, recurring, and implementable as one module - passes the altitude test on balance.

nodes.name: Direct Memory Access (DMA) Transfer
nodes.what: Configuring a DMA controller to move data between peripherals and memory without CPU involvement, with completion signaled by interrupt; often paired with double buffering so one buffer fills while the other is processed.
nodes.problem: High-rate I/O consumes the CPU if every word is moved by software; offloading transfers frees cycles and meets throughput deadlines.
nodes.named_in: Making Embedded Systems - Elecia White (2024)

nodes.name: Hardware Adapter
nodes.what: An adapter layer that converts the interface a hardware device (or its proxy) actually offers into the interface the application expects.
nodes.problem: Applications written against one device interface must run with a different-but-similar device; the adapter absorbs the mismatch so neither client nor device code changes.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Hardware Proxy
nodes.what: A class/module that encapsulates all access to a hardware device behind a device-neutral interface, hiding register layout, encoding, and access mechanics.
nodes.problem: Clients scattered with direct register access break whenever the hardware changes; centralizing access in one proxy isolates hardware detail and eases porting and testing.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Interrupt Service Routine
nodes.what: Hardware-vectored handler code that preempts normal execution to service an event, doing minimal work at interrupt context before returning.
nodes.problem: Urgent, asynchronous hardware events must be handled with low latency without the CPU wasting cycles waiting for them.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
nodes.borderline: The handler construct itself is hardware-defined; included because ISR design rules (and ISR-with-deferred-work) are a named recurring design concern - the mission's anchor form.

nodes.name: Interrupt Vector Table
nodes.what: A table of handler entry addresses, indexed by exception/interrupt number, through which the CPU dispatches to the right ISR; firmware populates and sometimes relocates it (e.g. VTOR).
nodes.problem: Hardware must find the correct handler in bounded time for any interrupt source; a fixed-layout dispatch table is the universal mechanism, and its relocation underlies bootloaders and RAM-vectored systems.
nodes.named_in: The Definitive Guide to ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 Processors - Yiu (2013)
nodes.borderline: Hardware-defined structure at the floor of the design band - kept IN per charter as the named dispatch construct firmware designs around.

nodes.name: iohw.h Standard Hardware I/O Interface
nodes.what: A standardized C/C++ macro interface (iord/iowr on abstract register designators) that isolates device-register access from platform addressing details.
nodes.problem: Register-access code is inherently platform-specific; a standard indirection layer lets driver logic port across buses and toolchains unchanged.
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC TR 18015:2006 Technical Report on C++ Performance, hardware-interface chapter
nodes.borderline: A standardized API shape rather than a pattern; included as the TR-blessed portable hardware-access mechanism.

nodes.name: Memory-Mapped Register Access
nodes.what: Address peripheral hardware registers as (volatile-qualified) memory locations through typed pointers or structure overlays, with disciplined read/write ordering.
nodes.problem: Peripherals must be controlled from portable C/C++ without compiler-reordered or elided accesses; the volatile-pointer/struct-overlay discipline (plus hardware aids like Cortex-M bit-banding for atomic bit access) is the canonical mechanism.
nodes.named_in: Dan Saks embedded.com columns on memory-mapped devices in C and C++

nodes.name: PID Controller
nodes.what: A periodic feedback loop computing an actuator command as the weighted sum of proportional, integral, and derivative terms of the setpoint error, implemented as a fixed-rate update with output clamping, integrator anti-windup, and derivative filtering.
nodes.problem: Driving a physical process to a setpoint despite disturbances and lag needs a standard, tunable feedback structure; the discrete PID update is the established implementable one.
nodes.named_in: Åström & Hägglund, PID Controllers: Theory, Design, and Tuning (ISA, 1995); Wescott, 'PID Without a PhD' (Embedded Systems Programming, 2000); Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (Princeton UP)
nodes.borderline: control-theory algorithm rather than a software-structural pattern — included because embedded-software literature treats the discrete PID loop (anti-windup, derivative filtering, sample-time handling) as a named implementation-level building block a firmware designer reaches for

nodes.name: Polling
nodes.what: The software repeatedly samples device or data status - periodically on a timer or opportunistically in the main loop - instead of being interrupted.
nodes.problem: When events are frequent, non-urgent, or interrupts are unavailable/undesirable, checking on the program's own schedule is simpler and avoids preemption hazards.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Shadow Register
nodes.what: Maintain a RAM copy of a hardware register's intended contents, perform all read-modify-write logic on the copy, and write the whole copy to the device.
nodes.problem: Write-only registers cannot be read back and read-modify-write on live registers races with hardware (the PIC RMW problem); a software shadow makes register state knowable and updates atomic. Vendors also use 'shadow register' for hardware-buffered registers that latch atomically (e.g. PWM compare shadows) - noted as the hardware sense.
nodes.named_in: Shadow Register - ScienceDirect Topics (Elsevier embedded-systems references); PIC/AVR vendor documentation

nodes.name: Super Loop
nodes.what: Structure the whole application as one endless main loop that calls each task function in turn, with ISRs as the only asynchronous activity.
nodes.problem: Tiny systems need multitask-like behavior without the cost and complexity of an RTOS; a single repeating loop plus interrupts is the minimal, fully deterministic executive.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

nodes.name: Typesafe Register Access via C++ Templates
nodes.what: Hardware registers and bitfields modeled as template types so illegal accesses fail at compile time while generated code equals hand-written volatile pokes.
nodes.problem: Raw address-and-mask register code is unchecked and error-prone; encoding register semantics in the type system catches wrong-register/wrong-field bugs at zero runtime cost.
nodes.named_in: C++ Hardware Register Access Redux - Smith (2010)

nodes.name: Brown-Out Handling
nodes.what: Detect supply voltage sagging below a safe threshold (via an on-chip or external detector) and hold the MCU in reset or run a controlled shutdown until power is reliable.
nodes.problem: During sags the CPU and flash misbehave unpredictably (corrupted writes, erratic execution) without a clean power-off; explicit brown-out detection converts an undefined-behavior region into a defined reset or safe-save path.
nodes.named_in: AVR180: External Brown-out Protection - Atmel/Microchip application note

nodes.name: Built-In Self-Test
nodes.what: Firmware routines that exercise and verify the system's own hardware (RAM patterns, ROM checksums, register/ALU checks, peripheral loopbacks) at startup or periodically.
nodes.problem: Latent hardware faults otherwise surface only as mysterious runtime failures; explicit self-tests detect them at a moment the system can still report, refuse to run, or fail safe. RAM march tests and ROM CRC checks are folded here as variants.
nodes.named_in: Built-in self-test - Wikipedia

nodes.name: Circuit Breaker
nodes.what: A stateful wrapper around a failure-prone operation that trips open after a failure threshold, rejects calls while open, and probes recovery via a half-open state.
nodes.problem: Repeatedly calling a failing dependency wastes resources, slows callers, and hammers the struggling system; the breaker fails fast and gives the dependency time to recover.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

nodes.name: Cleanup Record
nodes.what: A variable records which acquisition steps succeeded so a single cleanup path can conditionally release exactly what was obtained.
nodes.problem: Multi-resource initialization in C must undo partial progress on failure without duplicating release logic per exit point.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Complete Parameter Checking
nodes.what: Validate all parameters and inputs at component boundaries every time, detecting errors close to their source at the cost of some performance.
nodes.problem: Faults manifest as bad values crossing interfaces; checking at the boundary shortens fault latency and stops propagation into the component.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Copy-and-Swap
nodes.what: Implement assignment by constructing a copy and swapping its guts with *this via a non-throwing swap, so the operation either fully succeeds or leaves the object untouched.
nodes.problem: Hand-written assignment operators struggle with self-assignment and partial-failure states; copy-and-swap gives the strong exception guarantee for free.
nodes.named_in: Exceptional C++ - Herb Sutter (1999)

nodes.name: Core Dump
nodes.what: On a fatal fault, a handler serializes the program's execution state (registers, stack, selected memory regions, fault status) to persistent storage or a host channel for postmortem analysis.
nodes.problem: Crashes in the field or in hard-to-reproduce conditions leave no debugger attached; capturing machine state at the moment of failure lets developers diagnose the fault after the fact instead of losing it to a silent reset.
nodes.named_in: white

nodes.name: Correcting Audits
nodes.what: Routinely scan in-memory or stored data for structural and semantic errors and repair them (rebuild links, reset invalid fields) as they are found.
nodes.problem: Data errors accumulate silently from faults elsewhere and eventually trigger failures; active auditing finds and corrects them before they are used.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Cyclic Redundancy Check
nodes.what: Data blocks carry a checksum computed by polynomial division over GF(2); the receiver/reader recomputes it to detect corruption in storage or transit.
nodes.problem: Large data regions and messages accumulate bit errors that simple parity misses; CRCs detect burst errors with small, cheaply computed check values.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Dead Letter Channel
nodes.what: A designated channel to which the messaging layer moves messages that cannot be delivered or processed, instead of dropping or endlessly retrying them.
nodes.problem: Undeliverable or repeatedly failing messages would otherwise poison the main queue or vanish silently; parking them aside preserves them for inspection and keeps the main flow healthy.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Deferred Validation
nodes.what: Delay comprehensive validity checking of captured data until an action requires it, scaling the rigor of the check to the consequences of that action (edit freely, validate on save/commit/publish).
nodes.problem: Eager validation at entry time rejects legitimately incomplete in-progress data and hard-codes one rigidity level; different actions need different degrees of integrity.
nodes.named_in: Cunningham, 'The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity' (PLoP 1994; c2.com/ppr/checks.html, loaded live)

nodes.name: Diagnostic Context
nodes.what: Attach per-thread/per-request key-value context (transaction id, user, request id) to a stash that the logging system automatically appends to every message emitted within that scope.
nodes.problem: Interleaved logs from concurrent activities are unattributable; carrying context explicitly through every call is invasive, so the logger holds it ambiently per execution scope.
nodes.named_in: Harrison, 'Patterns for Logging Diagnostic Messages', PLoPD3 (1997); canonical living form: log4j/logback/SLF4J MDC/NDC documentation

nodes.name: Diagnostic Logger
nodes.what: Route all diagnostic messages through a dedicated logger object that decouples message producers from output destinations, formats, and severity filtering.
nodes.problem: Ad-hoc prints scatter diagnostic policy through the code; a central logger lets destination, format, and level be configured without touching call sites.
nodes.named_in: Harrison, 'Patterns for Logging Diagnostic Messages', PLoPD3 (1997) (PLoPD3 ToC loaded live); living realizations: log4j/syslog-style logging frameworks

nodes.name: Error Handler
nodes.what: Concentrate error-processing logic in dedicated handler components/blocks separate from normal-flow code, invoked when errors are detected.
nodes.problem: Error handling interleaved with mainline logic is duplicated, inconsistent, and untestable; separating it gives one place to get recovery right.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Error Kernel
nodes.what: Keep the irreplaceable state and critical logic in a small, maximally simple core, delegating risky or failure-prone work to expendable child components that can crash and be restarted.
nodes.problem: If valuable state lives where risky work happens, every failure threatens it; pushing risk to the leaves lets crashes stay cheap while the kernel stays reliable.
nodes.named_in: Reactive Design Patterns - Kuhn, Hanafee, Allen (2017)

nodes.name: Escalation
nodes.what: When a recovery action fails to clear an error, escalate to a progressively more drastic action (retry -> restart task -> restart process -> reboot) up a defined ladder.
nodes.problem: No single recovery action handles all faults; an ordered ladder bounds recovery time while preferring the least disruptive action that works.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Exceptional Value
nodes.what: A distinguished value object representing missing or invalid input that flows through the domain model, absorbing or rejecting messages instead of raising errors.
nodes.problem: Real-world input contains blanks and illegible entries; letting a typed placeholder value propagate keeps exceptional-case handling concentrated near the UI instead of scattered through business logic, while still recording that the input was bad.
nodes.named_in: Cunningham, The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity (PLoP 1994; c2.com/ppr/checks.html)
nodes.borderline: adjacent to null-object and special-case (both indexed); kept as the CHECKS-named propagate-through-computation mechanism the mission explicitly seeds

nodes.name: Fail Fast
nodes.what: Check preconditions and resource availability up front and report failure immediately, rather than doing work that is doomed to fail slowly.
nodes.problem: Slow failures consume caller time and system resources; failing before acquiring resources preserves capacity and gives callers fast, actionable errors.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

nodes.name: Goto Cleanup
nodes.what: On failure, jump forward to a single labeled cleanup section at the end of the function that releases resources in reverse acquisition order.
nodes.problem: Multi-step acquisition in C needs unwinding on every failure path; one exit chain avoids duplicated cleanup code and leak-prone nested conditionals.
nodes.named_in: Linux kernel coding style (living); also Goto Error Handling in Fluent C - Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Guard Clause
aka: replace nested conditional with guard clauses
nodes.what: Check preconditions/special cases at the top of a function and return immediately, keeping the main path unindented.
nodes.problem: Deeply nested conditionals obscure the dominant path; guard clauses flatten control flow and make precondition handling explicit.
nodes.named_in: Refactoring - Martin Fowler (1999), 'Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses'; also Fluent C (2022)
nodes.borderline: Statement-level code-shaping idiom below typical design altitude; kept because two catalogs name it as a pattern.

nodes.name: Happy Eyeballs
nodes.what: Race connection attempts over alternative paths (canonically IPv6 vs IPv4) with small staggered delays, keep the first to succeed, and cancel the rest.
nodes.problem: Trying alternatives strictly in sequence makes users wait out full timeouts when the preferred path is broken; staggered parallel attempts hide failures at the cost of a little duplicate work.
nodes.named_in: RFC 8305: Happy Eyeballs Version 2: Better Connectivity Using Concurrency - Schinazi & Pauly (2017)

nodes.name: Heartbeat
nodes.what: A monitored component emits (or answers) a periodic signal; missing beats mark it as failed and trigger recovery.
nodes.problem: A silently dead task or peer is indistinguishable from a slow one without an agreed periodic liveness signal and timeout.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Leaky Bucket Counter
nodes.what: An error counter incremented on each fault and decremented ('leaked') periodically; recovery escalates only when the count crosses a threshold, i.e. errors arrive faster than they drain.
nodes.problem: Distinguishing an acceptable background rate of transient errors from a persistent fault requires rate, not count; the leak encodes the acceptable rate. Distinct from the leaky-bucket traffic shaper.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Let It Crash
nodes.what: On unexpected error, abandon in-process recovery: let the failing unit die immediately and rely on an external mechanism (supervisor, restart) to recreate it in a known-good state.
nodes.problem: Defensive recovery code for unanticipated errors is itself error-prone and can leave corrupt state; a clean crash-plus-restart returns to a verified initial state.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
nodes.borderline: Erlang-rooted philosophy verging on a design principle; kept because it names a concrete, recurring failure-handling mechanism (crash + supervised restart). Related: Candea & Fox crash-only software.

nodes.name: Log Errors
nodes.what: Record error details on a separate diagnostic channel (log file, console, trace buffer) at the point where the error occurs, instead of forcing all debug information through return values to the caller.
nodes.problem: Callers need only actionable error information, but programmers debugging the system need full detail; funneling both through return codes bloats APIs and loses context available only at the error site.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C ch. 2 (Preschern 2022); also 'Patterns for Returning Error Information in C' (Preschern, EuroPLoP 2019, ACM DL)

nodes.name: Loop Timeout
nodes.what: Bound every polling/wait loop with a software counter or hardware timer so the loop cannot hang forever if the awaited hardware condition never occurs.
nodes.problem: Unbounded waits on hardware flags hang the whole system when a peripheral fails; an explicit timeout converts a hang into a detectable, handleable error. Pont's HARDWARE TIMEOUT timer-based variant is folded here.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

nodes.name: Marked Data
nodes.what: Tag data elements known or suspected to be erroneous so subsequent processing can skip, repair, or handle them specially instead of propagating the corruption.
nodes.problem: Deleting bad data may be worse than keeping it; an explicit corruption mark contains the error while preserving structure and audit trail.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Meaningless Behavior
nodes.what: Write domain methods without defensive input checks; let computations on exceptional/missing values fail or yield meaningless results, and have the input/output boundary recover (e.g. display blank) instead.
nodes.problem: Defensive checks duplicated through every domain method obscure the model; centering recovery at the presentation boundary keeps domain code minimal while tolerating bad data.
nodes.named_in: Cunningham, 'The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity' (PLoP 1994; c2.com/ppr/checks.html, loaded live)

nodes.name: N-Version Programming
nodes.what: Run N independently developed implementations of the same specification and adjudicate their outputs by a voter to mask residual design faults.
nodes.problem: Identical redundant copies share design faults; diverse implementations plus majority voting tolerate faults no single version can. The voter/voting mechanism (Hanmer: Voting) is folded here.
nodes.named_in: The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software - Avizienis (1985)
nodes.borderline: Development-process-heavy (independent teams, common spec), but the runtime N-version-plus-voter execution is implementable inside one program; kept with tag rather than parked.

nodes.name: Notification
nodes.what: An object that accumulates errors and messages during an operation (typically validation) and is returned or passed across a layer boundary instead of throwing on first failure.
nodes.problem: Exceptions abort at the first problem and cross layer boundaries poorly; a notification gathers all failures so callers can report them together.
nodes.named_in: Notification - Martin Fowler, Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev)

nodes.name: Quarantine
nodes.what: Isolate a faulty element from the rest of the system - stop routing work to it, fence its outputs - so its errors cannot spread while diagnosis or recovery proceeds.
nodes.problem: A faulty unit that keeps participating spreads corrupt data and secondary failures; active isolation contains the damage.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
nodes.borderline: Presumes isolatable units, which shades architectural; kept because in-process quarantine (disabling a worker, fencing a plugin) is implementable in one component.

nodes.name: Railway-Oriented Programming
nodes.what: Composing a workflow as a chain of functions over a two-track success/failure type, where any failure switches the rest of the pipeline onto the error track automatically.
nodes.problem: Keeps multi-step validation/IO workflows linear and readable while still short-circuiting on the first failure and accumulating error information, without nested conditionals or exceptions.
nodes.named_in: Railway Oriented Programming - Scott Wlaschin (fsharpforfunandprofit.com / NDC, 2014)
nodes.borderline: Essentially a named usage idiom of the result type (monadic bind); kept as a separate entry because the name is established and widely taught, cross-linked to result-type.

nodes.name: Recovery Blocks
nodes.what: Execute a primary algorithm, validate its result with an acceptance test, and on failure roll back and run an alternate implementation of the same function.
nodes.problem: A single implementation may contain residual design faults; structured alternates plus an acceptance test give software fault tolerance within one program.
nodes.named_in: System Structure for Software Fault Tolerance - Randell (1975)

nodes.name: Restart
nodes.what: Recover from an unhandled or unrecoverable error by reinitializing the affected unit (task, process, component, or whole program) to its known-good initial state.
nodes.problem: Some errors leave state too corrupt to repair in place; restarting from verified initial conditions is the recovery of last resort with predictable cost.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Result Type
nodes.what: A sum type carrying either a success value or an error value, returned instead of throwing, so failure is part of the function's signature.
nodes.problem: Makes failure paths visible and composable in the type system, avoiding invisible exception control flow and forcing callers to acknowledge errors.
nodes.named_in: P1028 SG14 status_code and standard error object - Douglas (WG21, 2020)

nodes.name: Retry Budget
nodes.what: Cap retries globally as a fraction of primary requests (e.g. retries may add at most 10% extra load), disabling retry when the budget is exhausted.
nodes.problem: Per-request retry limits still multiply load during a broad outage; a system-wide budget prevents retry amplification from turning partial failure into total overload.
nodes.named_in: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems - Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy eds. (2016)

nodes.name: Retry with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
nodes.what: Retry a failed operation a bounded number of times, doubling the wait between attempts and randomizing (jittering) it to avoid synchronized retry storms.
nodes.problem: Immediate or fixed-interval retries from many clients synchronize into load spikes that prolong the outage they respond to; capped attempts (Hanmer: Limit Retries, folded here) prevent infinite retry loops.
nodes.named_in: Timeouts, Retries, and Backoff with Jitter - Brooker, AWS Builders' Library (2019)

nodes.name: Return Status Code
nodes.what: Functions return a numeric/enum status indicating success or a specific failure, delivering actual results through out-parameters.
nodes.problem: C has no exceptions; a uniform status-return channel makes failure explicit and checkable at every call boundary.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022); also Preschern's EuroPLoP error-handling pattern papers

nodes.name: Riding Over Transients
nodes.what: Deliberately ignore errors that are momentary and self-clearing, acting only when an error persists or recurs beyond a threshold.
nodes.problem: Reacting instantly to every transient glitch triggers needless recovery actions that cost more than the fault itself; filtering separates transient from persistent faults.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Roll-Forward
nodes.what: Recover from an error by advancing the system to a new consistent state ahead of the error point, reconstructing or discarding in-flight work rather than returning to a checkpoint.
nodes.problem: Rolling back can be impossible (real-time deadlines, external side effects already visible); moving forward to the next safe state keeps the system live.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Rollback
nodes.what: Recover from an error by restoring the system to a previously saved consistent state (a checkpoint) and resuming from there.
nodes.problem: An error may have corrupted current state; returning to a known-good earlier state removes the error's effects at the cost of redoing work.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Safe State
nodes.what: A predefined operating condition without unreasonable risk that the system deliberately enters on fault detection (outputs de-energized, actuators parked, subsystem disabled).
nodes.problem: When a fault makes continued normal operation untrustworthy, the firmware needs a designed, reachable state that minimizes harm; defining and driving to that state is the core functional-safety mechanism.
nodes.named_in: ISO 26262:2018 - Road vehicles - Functional safety
nodes.borderline: A system-safety concept as much as a code mechanism, but implemented as a concrete in-program transition routine - kept IN with the tag.

nodes.name: Samurai Principle
aka: return victorious or not at all
nodes.what: For errors the caller cannot meaningfully handle, do not return an error code - assert/abort at the failure point instead.
nodes.problem: Propagating unhandleable errors buries the fault and corrupts state downstream; failing fast at the point of detection preserves the evidence.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Sentinel Value
nodes.what: A special in-band value, distinct from all legal data, used to signal a condition such as end-of-data, absence, or failure (NUL terminator, -1, null pointer).
nodes.problem: When a channel or return type has no out-of-band way to signal termination or absence, a reserved value carries the signal without extra state or size bookkeeping.
nodes.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming Vol. 3: Sorting and Searching - Donald Knuth (1973); also Code Complete 2nd ed. - McConnell (2004)

nodes.name: setjmp/longjmp Error Handling
nodes.what: Macro-wrapped setjmp/longjmp implementing raise-and-catch non-local control transfer as an exception facility in C.
nodes.problem: Deeply nested call chains cannot practically thread error codes through every level; a structured non-local jump delivers errors straight to a handler.
nodes.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - Hanson (1996)

nodes.name: Software Rejuvenation
nodes.what: Proactively restart or reinitialize a long-running process on a schedule or on resource-degradation signals, before software aging (leaks, fragmentation, drift) causes failure.
nodes.problem: Long-running processes accumulate degradation that eventually causes outages at uncontrolled moments; planned rejuvenation converts that into cheap, scheduled downtime.
nodes.named_in: Software Rejuvenation: Analysis, Module and Applications - Huang, Kintala, Kolettis, Fulton (1995)

nodes.name: Special Return Value
nodes.what: Reserve one or more values of the normal return domain (NULL, -1, EOF) to signal failure in-band, avoiding a separate status channel.
nodes.problem: When the result domain has spare values, in-band signaling keeps APIs terse; the C-API-convention face of the general sentinel-value element.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Stack Painting / Watermarking
nodes.what: Fill each stack with a known pattern at startup and later scan for the deepest overwritten address to measure worst-case stack usage and detect near-overflow.
nodes.problem: Stack overflow in fixed-stack embedded systems corrupts adjacent memory silently; painting makes actual usage observable so stack sizes can be right-sized and overflows caught (complementary to canary/guard-zone checks).
nodes.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (stack overflow detection and uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark)

nodes.name: Supervisor
nodes.what: A component whose only job is to monitor child workers and apply a declared restart strategy (one-for-one, one-for-all, escalation to its own supervisor) when they crash.
nodes.problem: Let-it-crash needs someone to do the restarting; a hierarchy of supervisors turns individual crashes into localized, policy-driven recovery instead of whole-program failure.
nodes.named_in: OTP Design Principles (Erlang/OTP documentation) - Ericsson (living)

nodes.name: Timeout
nodes.what: Bound every blocking wait on an external resource or call with a maximum duration, treating expiry as failure.
nodes.problem: Unbounded waits on unresponsive dependencies tie up threads and connections, propagating a remote failure into local resource exhaustion and cascading failure.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

nodes.name: Active Object
nodes.what: Method invocation is decoupled from method execution: calls are reified as requests on an activation queue and executed by the object's own thread via a scheduler, with futures for results.
nodes.problem: An object needs its own thread of control so clients are not blocked and its internal state is accessed by one thread only, serializing concurrency at the object boundary.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)
nodes.borderline: In-process actor frameworks (Akka on one JVM, Erlang processes in one node, actor libraries in C++/Rust) pass the altitude test; distributed actor systems as deployment topology are architecture-level and belong to Phase 3.

nodes.name: Async-Await Model
nodes.what: A language-level model in which functions marked async are compiled into continuation/state-machine form so that awaiting an asynchronous result suspends the function without blocking its thread.
nodes.problem: Callback-based asynchronous code inverts control flow and destroys readability; async-await preserves sequential-looking code while keeping execution non-blocking.
nodes.named_in: The F# Asynchronous Programming Model - Syme, Petricek, Lomov (2011)

nodes.name: Asynchronous Completion Token
nodes.what: The initiator of an asynchronous operation passes along an opaque token that comes back with the completion event, letting the response be demultiplexed to the right state and actions in constant time.
nodes.problem: When responses to async operations arrive out of order, the receiver must efficiently re-associate each completion with the context needed to process it, without searching.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

nodes.name: Bytecode Virtual Machine
nodes.what: An interpreter that first compiles source to a compact linear instruction encoding (bytecode) and then executes it in a dispatch loop over a virtual instruction set, usually with an operand stack or virtual registers.
nodes.problem: Tree walking pays pointer-chasing and dynamic-dispatch costs on every node visit; a dense linear instruction stream improves locality and dispatch speed while remaining portable across host platforms.
nodes.named_in: Crafting Interpreters - Robert Nystrom (2021)

nodes.name: Cancellation Token
nodes.what: An explicit token/context object threaded through the call graph that carries a cancellation signal (and often a deadline) which long-running operations poll or subscribe to, exiting cooperatively when it fires.
nodes.problem: Work spawned on behalf of a request must stop promptly when the request is abandoned or times out; forced termination is unsafe, so a propagated, observable cancellation signal lets every participant release resources cooperatively.
nodes.named_in: Sameer Ajmani, 'Go Concurrency Patterns: Context' (Go blog, 2014-07-29); Microsoft Learn, 'Cancellation in Managed Threads' (CancellationToken)
nodes.borderline: Overlaps deadline-propagation (already in index) which covers the deadline/budget facet; this entry is the explicit cancellation-signal object itself. Also adjacent to two-phase-termination, which is the shutdown protocol rather than the propagated signal carrier.

nodes.name: Competing Consumers
nodes.what: Multiple concurrent consumers receive from the same point-to-point channel, each message going to exactly one of them, so throughput scales with consumer count.
nodes.problem: A single consumer cannot keep up with message arrival rate; letting a pool of consumers race for messages parallelizes processing while the queue preserves once-only delivery.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Coroutine
nodes.what: A routine that can suspend its own execution at yield points and later be resumed with its local state intact, enabling cooperative multitasking on one thread.
nodes.problem: Some computations (pipelines, state machines, async I/O) are naturally expressed as multiple interleaved control flows without the cost and preemption hazards of OS threads.
nodes.named_in: Design of a Separable Transition-Diagram Compiler - Conway (1963)

nodes.name: Deoptimization
aka: on-stack replacement (OSR, the frame-replacement mechanism, folded)
nodes.what: The runtime invalidates speculatively optimized compiled code and transfers a running activation back to unoptimized code (interpreter or baseline), reconstructing the equivalent stack frames and local state at a mapped program point; the same frame-replacement machinery run upward (OSR entry) promotes a hot running loop into optimized code.
nodes.problem: JIT compilers optimize on assumptions (class hierarchy, type profiles, no debugger) that can be invalidated at runtime, and debuggers need source-level state from optimized frames; the runtime must be able to abandon optimized frames mid-execution without losing correctness.
nodes.named_in: Hoelzle, Chambers & Ungar, 'Debugging Optimized Code with Dynamic Deoptimization', PLDI 1992 (verified live via selflanguage.org bibliography this session)

nodes.name: Event Loop
nodes.what: A single loop that waits for events (I/O readiness, messages, timers) and dispatches each to its handler, serializing all handler execution on one thread.
nodes.problem: Handling many concurrent event sources with one thread avoids locking and thread overhead, provided handlers never block the loop; the pattern form for demultiplexing is POSA2's Reactor.
nodes.named_in: Event loop - Wikipedia

nodes.name: Executor
nodes.what: An abstraction that decouples task submission from the policy of task execution (which thread, when, in what order), typically backed by a work queue and thread pool.
nodes.problem: Hard-coding 'new thread per task' couples application logic to an execution policy; an executor lets throughput, ordering, and resource policy vary independently of submitted work.
nodes.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

nodes.name: False-Sharing Avoidance via Cache-Line Padding
