nodes.problem: Generating HTML, code, or reports by string concatenation entangles logic with presentation; a template engine separates the output's static shape from the data that fills it, ideally enforcing strict model-view separation.
nodes.named_in: Parr, Enforcing Strict Model-View Separation in Template Engines (WWW 2004, StringTemplate); Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) names the web form 'Template View'

nodes.name: Tree-Walking Interpreter
nodes.what: An interpreter that executes a program by recursively traversing its abstract syntax tree, evaluating each node directly against a runtime environment.
nodes.problem: Compiling to another representation costs implementation effort; evaluating the AST directly is the simplest correct execution strategy and keeps the interpreter structurally isomorphic to the language grammar, at the cost of dispatch overhead.
nodes.named_in: Crafting Interpreters - Robert Nystrom (2021)

nodes.name: Active Record
nodes.what: An object that wraps one row of a database table, encapsulating the database access and adding domain logic on that data.
nodes.problem: For CRUD-shaped domains, separating data access from domain behavior adds indirection with little payoff; fusing row data, persistence methods, and logic in one class is the simplest thing that works.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Association Table Mapping
nodes.what: Maps a many-to-many association to a separate table holding pairs of foreign keys into the two associated tables.
nodes.problem: Relational schemas cannot store multivalued fields in a row; an intermediate link table represents the association that neither object's table can hold.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Checkpointing
nodes.what: Periodically record a consistent marker of which logged changes have reached the main data store, bounding how far back crash recovery must scan the log.
nodes.problem: Without checkpoints the recovery log grows without bound and restart must replay the whole history; a checkpoint truncates the redo horizon and caps recovery time.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Class Table Inheritance
nodes.what: Maps each class in an inheritance hierarchy to its own table holding only that class's fields, joined by shared primary key.
nodes.problem: One-table-per-hierarchy wastes columns and one-table-per-concrete-class duplicates them; a table per class keeps the schema normalized at the cost of joins to assemble an object.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Concrete Table Inheritance
nodes.what: Maps each concrete class in an inheritance hierarchy to its own table containing all its fields, inherited and declared.
nodes.problem: Loading an object of a known concrete class should touch one table only; duplicating inherited columns per concrete table removes joins at the cost of schema duplication and cross-table key discipline.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Content-Addressable Storage
nodes.what: Store immutable blocks/objects keyed by a cryptographic hash of their contents, so identical data coalesces, references are self-verifying, and writes are idempotent.
nodes.problem: Location-addressed storage cannot cheaply deduplicate, verify integrity, or share immutable history; hashing the content makes the identifier both the address and the checksum.
nodes.named_in: Quinlan & Dorward, 'Venti: A New Approach to Archival Storage', USENIX FAST 2002 (verified live); canonical modern realization: the Git object store

nodes.name: Data Mapper
nodes.what: A layer of mapper objects that moves data between in-memory objects and the database while keeping the two schemas independent of each other.
nodes.problem: Rich domain objects and relational schemas evolve differently; putting the transfer logic in dedicated mappers lets neither side know about the other.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Dependent Mapping
nodes.what: Has one class (the owner) perform the database mapping for a child class whose objects are accessed only through it.
nodes.problem: Objects that exist only within one owner (line items in an order) do not need their own mapper, identity map, or independent updates; letting the owner map them simplifies the machinery.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: EEPROM Emulation in Flash
nodes.what: Emulate byte-updatable EEPROM semantics on page-erasable flash by journaling variable records across reserved pages and swapping/compacting pages when full.
nodes.problem: Many MCUs lack true EEPROM while flash only erases in large pages with limited endurance; record journaling plus page rotation provides small-datum persistence with wear spreading and power-loss recovery.
nodes.named_in: AN2594 - EEPROM emulation in STM32F10x microcontrollers (STMicroelectronics)

nodes.name: Embedded Value
nodes.what: Maps a value object into the columns of its owner's table rather than giving it a table of its own.
nodes.problem: Small value objects (money, date range) do not merit their own tables and joins; flattening their fields into the owning record keeps the object model rich and the schema simple.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Event Sourcing
nodes.what: Captures every change to application state as an immutable event in an append-only log, so current state is derived by replaying the events rather than stored destructively.
nodes.problem: Update-in-place storage loses history, complicates audit, and makes past states unrecoverable; storing the events themselves makes state reconstruction, temporal queries, and replay-based recovery possible.
nodes.named_in: Event Sourcing, martinfowler.com (Further Enterprise Application Architecture development) - Martin Fowler (2005)
nodes.borderline: The in-component append-log persistence mechanism is IN; the system-wide event-sourced architecture style is parked for Phase 3.

nodes.name: Flash Translation Layer
nodes.what: A firmware layer that remaps logical block writes to out-of-place physical flash pages, maintaining a logical-to-physical mapping table plus garbage collection so erase-constrained flash presents an ordinary rewritable block device.
nodes.problem: NAND/NOR flash cannot rewrite in place and erases in large blocks with limited endurance; out-of-place remapping hides erase-before-write, enables wear leveling, and keeps a consistent mapping across power loss.
nodes.named_in: Intel 'Understanding the Flash Translation Layer (FTL) Specification' (AP-684, 1998); Chung et al., 'A survey of Flash Translation Layer', Journal of Systems Architecture 2009
nodes.borderline: composite mechanism (composes flash-wear-leveling + out-of-place update + garbage collection); kept because FTL is the established name for the mapping mechanism itself, which the existing flash-wear-leveling entry does not cover

nodes.name: Flash Wear Leveling
nodes.what: Distribute writes and erases evenly across flash pages/blocks (via remapping or rotation) so no single block exhausts its limited erase endurance prematurely.
nodes.problem: Flash blocks endure only a bounded number of erase cycles while write traffic is naturally skewed to hot data; leveling the wear multiplies effective device lifetime.
nodes.named_in: Wear leveling - Wikipedia; AN798 EEPROM Emulation with Wear-Leveling (Silicon Labs)

nodes.name: Foreign Key Mapping
nodes.what: Maps an object reference between objects to a foreign key column in the referring object's table.
nodes.problem: In-memory pointers do not exist in relational storage; translating references to keys on save and keys back to references on load preserves the object graph.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Group Commit
nodes.what: Accumulate the log records of several concurrently committing transactions and flush them to stable storage with a single synchronous write.
nodes.problem: One fsync per commit makes the log device the throughput ceiling; amortizing one flush over many commits trades a little latency for large gains in commit throughput.
nodes.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

nodes.name: Identity Field
nodes.what: Saves the database identity (primary key) as a field in the in-memory object to maintain the correspondence between object and row.
nodes.problem: Objects and rows must be matched reliably across loads and saves; storing the key in the object gives every domain object a durable identity handle.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Inheritance Mappers
nodes.what: A structure of mapper classes mirroring an inheritance hierarchy, so each domain class has a mapper that handles its own fields and delegates inherited ones upward.
nodes.problem: Mapping code for a class hierarchy duplicates superclass field handling in every concrete mapper; organizing the mappers as a parallel hierarchy factors the shared mapping once.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Log-Structured Storage
nodes.what: All updates are written as appends to the head of a sequential log divided into large segments; live data is never overwritten in place, and a cleaner process copies still-live records out of old segments to reclaim them.
nodes.problem: Small random writes waste disk/flash bandwidth on seeks and read-modify-write cycles, and in-place update complicates crash recovery; turning the entire store into a sequential log makes writes device-speed and recovery a log replay, at the cost of background cleaning.
nodes.named_in: Rosenblum & Ousterhout — The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System, SOSP 1991 / ACM TOCS 1992
tags: embedded (FTLs and flash filesystems are log-structured)
nodes.borderline: kept separate from lsm-tree: LSM is a sorted-run merge index structure; log-structured storage is the persistence mechanism (append-only segments + cleaning) usable with no sorted-merge component at all (LFS, FTLs, journal-based KV stores)

nodes.name: Memory Image
nodes.what: Keep the authoritative application state entirely in main memory and obtain durability by logging every state-changing event to persistent storage, replaying the log (accelerated by periodic snapshots) to rebuild state after restart.
nodes.problem: Routing all state through a database costs IO and mapping complexity; when the working set fits in RAM, an event log plus snapshots gives durability while the program works at memory speed with plain in-memory structures.
nodes.named_in: Fowler, bliki 'MemoryImage' (31 Aug 2011; loaded live — cites Prevayler/'system prevalence' and the LMAX architecture as realizations)
tags: borderline: composes event-sourcing + checkpointing/snapshot and Fowler frames it as an architectural approach; included because it is a single-process persistence mechanism with library-level realizations (Prevayler) and its own established name (system prevalence)

nodes.name: Metadata Mapping
nodes.what: Holds the object-relational mapping details as metadata (tables/files or annotations) interpreted or code-generated at runtime, instead of hand-coding each mapper.
nodes.problem: Dozens of hand-written mappers are repetitive and drift from the schema; expressing the mapping once as data lets generic code perform it uniformly.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
nodes.borderline: Shades toward ORM-framework architecture; included as the in-program metadata-interpretation mechanism.

nodes.name: Query Object
nodes.what: An object that represents a database query as a structure of criteria referring to domain classes, later translated into SQL.
nodes.problem: Embedding SQL strings couples domain code to table schemas and duplicates query logic; building queries as interpretable objects lets them be composed, checked, and retargeted.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Repository
nodes.what: Mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing and querying domain objects.
nodes.problem: Domain code that speaks SQL or mapper APIs directly couples business logic to storage; an in-memory-collection illusion isolates query construction and enables substitution in tests.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
nodes.borderline: Sits at the domain/persistence seam and is sometimes treated as a layer element, but it is a class-level construct implementable inside one component; also a DDD tactical pattern (Evans 2003).

nodes.name: Row Data Gateway
nodes.what: An object that acts as a gateway to a single database row, one instance per row, exposing the row's fields and its insert/update/delete operations.
nodes.problem: Code that manipulates individual records needs record-shaped access without embedding SQL at every use site; a per-row gateway object gives record semantics while confining the database code.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Shadow Paging
nodes.what: Perform updates on copies of pages and atomically switch a page-table root from the old (shadow) versions to the new ones at commit, never overwriting committed state in place.
nodes.problem: Gives atomic, no-log crash recovery: a crash before the root switch leaves the intact shadow state; the cost is copying pressure and lost clustering, the classic alternative to write-ahead logging.
nodes.named_in: Physical Integrity in a Large Segmented Database - Lorie (1977)

nodes.name: Single Table Inheritance
nodes.what: Maps all classes of an inheritance hierarchy to one table whose columns are the union of all fields, with a type discriminator column.
nodes.problem: Relational databases have no inheritance; one wide table avoids joins and moves objects between subclasses cheaply, at the cost of nullable unused columns.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Table Data Gateway
nodes.what: An object that acts as the single gateway to a database table, with one instance handling all the rows and methods for the table's SQL.
nodes.problem: Scattering SQL through application code makes schema change and testing painful; centralizing all queries for a table behind one stateless object confines the SQL to one place.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Tombstone
nodes.what: A persisted marker record written in place of an actual deletion in append-only or replicated storage, treated as a write that shadows earlier data and purged later by compaction after a grace period.
nodes.problem: Log-structured and replicated stores cannot delete in place; without an explicit durable marker, deleted data resurrects from older segments or from replicas that missed the delete.
nodes.named_in: Apache Cassandra documentation, 'Tombstones' (verified live); Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (log compaction chapter)

nodes.name: Unit of Work
nodes.what: Maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing out the changes and resolving concurrency problems in one commit.
nodes.problem: Writing objects back one at a time causes many small database calls, ordering problems, and inconsistent partial updates; changes must be tracked and flushed atomically.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Write-Ahead Log
nodes.what: Append every intended change to a sequential durable log and force it to stable storage before the corresponding in-place data update, so committed work can be redone and uncommitted work undone after a crash.
nodes.problem: In-place updates can be half-applied when a crash hits; sequential logging makes durability cheap (one sequential write) and gives recovery a total order of changes to replay or roll back.
nodes.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

nodes.name: Allocation Wrapper
nodes.what: Wrap the raw allocation/deallocation calls (malloc/free) in your own functions so every allocation flows through one place that can check for failure, add statistics, tagging, debugging hooks, or alternative backing allocators.
nodes.problem: Scattered direct malloc calls duplicate out-of-memory handling and make it impossible to instrument, audit, or retarget allocation behavior centrally.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)

nodes.name: Asset Streaming
nodes.what: The engine loads and unloads game assets (geometry, textures, audio, world chunks) asynchronously in the background, keyed to player position or predicted need, keeping only a sliding working set resident within a memory budget.
nodes.problem: Open worlds exceed RAM and load screens break immersion; position-driven background load/unload bounds memory while presenting a seamless world.
nodes.named_in: Gregory, Game Engine Architecture (resource management / streaming); Unreal Engine documentation, 'Level Streaming'
nodes.borderline: Near paging, prefetching, and resource-files (all in index); kept per charter as the named game-engine form: spatially keyed, budgeted, asynchronous load/unload of a world working set.

nodes.name: Boundary Tags
nodes.what: Size/status fields at both ends of each heap block let an allocator find and merge free neighbors in constant time on free.
nodes.problem: Coalescing adjacent free blocks is essential to fight fragmentation, but without boundary metadata a freeing block cannot locate its neighbors cheaply.
nodes.named_in: A Memory Allocator (dlmalloc essay) - Lea (2000); technique originally due to Knuth

nodes.name: Buddy Memory Allocation
nodes.what: Manage memory in power-of-two-sized blocks that split into two 'buddies' on allocation and coalesce back with their buddy on free, found by address arithmetic.
nodes.problem: General free-list allocators suffer slow coalescing and external fragmentation; restricting block sizes to powers of two makes split/merge O(1)-ish and bounds fragmentation predictably, at the price of internal fragmentation. Technique due to Knowlton (1965); named and analyzed by Knuth.
nodes.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1 - Donald E. Knuth (1968), sec. 2.5 'Dynamic Storage Allocation'

nodes.name: Bulkhead
nodes.what: Partition resources (thread pools, connection pools, memory) into isolated compartments per client or function so one compartment's exhaustion cannot sink the rest.
nodes.problem: A shared pool lets one misbehaving consumer or one slow dependency exhaust capacity for everyone; partitioning contains the damage.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
nodes.borderline: Also applied at deployment/cluster level (architecture); the in-process pool-partitioning form is squarely design-level.

nodes.name: Callee Allocates
nodes.what: The callee allocates the result buffer (of size only it knows) and returns it with a paired deallocation function the caller must invoke.
nodes.problem: When result size is unknown to the caller, callee allocation avoids guess-and-retry sizing at the cost of an explicit ownership-transfer contract.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Caller-Owned Buffer
nodes.what: The caller allocates and owns the buffer, passing pointer and size for the callee to fill.
nodes.problem: Callee-side allocation forces heap use and ambiguous ownership; caller-owned buffers keep allocation strategy (stack, static, pool) and lifetime with the caller - vital in embedded code.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Captain Oates
nodes.what: On memory pressure, have less vital components voluntarily sacrifice their memory (caches, optional buffers) so more important tasks can proceed.
nodes.problem: When memory runs out, failing the currently-allocating (possibly critical) task is the wrong victim choice; deliberately releasing low-value memory first preserves the vital functions.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Compaction
nodes.what: Move live objects together in memory to squeeze out the unused gaps between them, recovering memory lost to fragmentation.
nodes.problem: Long-running allocation and deallocation leaves free memory scattered in unusable fragments; relocating objects (usually via handles or indirection) coalesces free space into allocatable blocks.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Component Configurator
nodes.what: An application links and unlinks component implementations at runtime via a uniform component lifecycle interface (init, suspend, resume, fini) and a central configurator, without recompiling or restarting.
nodes.problem: Which component implementations run, and when, should be decided late (deployment/runtime) and be changeable dynamically, decoupling implementation from configuration time.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

nodes.name: Copy-on-Write
nodes.what: Share an object between clients until one needs to modify it, then transparently copy it and let the writer mutate the private copy.
nodes.problem: Eager copying wastes memory and time when most copies are never modified; deferring the copy to first write keeps sharing cheap while preserving value semantics.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Custom Allocator
nodes.what: Containers and subsystems take an allocator object/parameter so memory sourcing policy is chosen by the client, not hard-coded.
nodes.problem: One global heap cannot satisfy games/embedded constraints (budgets per subsystem, alignment, determinism); pluggable allocation decouples data structures from memory policy.
nodes.named_in: EASTL - Electronic Arts Standard Template Library (WG21 N2271) - Pedriana (2007)

nodes.name: Data Files
nodes.what: Process data a little at a time from secondary storage, keeping only the current working portion in main memory.
nodes.problem: Data sets that do not fit in RAM cannot be loaded whole; incremental streaming bounds the memory footprint regardless of data size.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Dedicated Ownership
nodes.what: Every allocation is assigned exactly one owner responsible for freeing it, with ownership transfer made explicit at API boundaries.
nodes.problem: Manual memory management fails through unclear responsibility (double free, leak); naming an owner per object makes deallocation auditable.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Dispose Pattern
nodes.what: Objects owning unmanaged resources expose an explicit Dispose/close method, invoked deterministically via language constructs (using / try-with-resources), with finalizers only as backstop.
nodes.problem: Garbage collection reclaims memory but not files, sockets, or handles at predictable times; the pattern restores deterministic cleanup in GC languages.
nodes.named_in: Framework Design Guidelines - Cwalina & Abrams (2005); Effective Java Item 9 (try-with-resources)

nodes.name: Eager Acquisition
nodes.what: Resources are acquired up front, before actual use (at startup or configuration time), and handed out from the pre-acquired set at run time.
nodes.problem: Acquisition at use time is too slow or can fail unpredictably; paying the cost early makes run-time access fast and deterministic - central to real-time and embedded design.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

nodes.name: Epoch-Based Reclamation
nodes.what: Threads announce a global epoch on entering read-side sections; retired nodes are freed only after all threads have advanced past the epoch in which the nodes were retired.
nodes.problem: Amortizes the cost of safe memory reclamation for lock-free structures: per-access publication (as in hazard pointers) is replaced by cheap per-critical-section epoch bookkeeping.
nodes.named_in: Practical Lock-Freedom (UCAM-CL-TR-579) - Keir Fraser (2004)

nodes.name: Evictor
nodes.what: An evictor monitors resource usage and, under a configurable strategy (LRU, LFU, priorities), releases or swaps out the least valuable resources to bound consumption.
nodes.problem: Long-running systems accumulate rarely used resources; systematic, policy-driven eviction prevents exhaustion while keeping hot resources available.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

nodes.name: Execute Around Method
nodes.what: A method (or scoped object) performs guaranteed paired actions - acquire/release, open/close, begin/end - around a client-supplied block of code.
nodes.problem: Clients forget or fail to perform the closing half of paired operations, especially on error paths; centralizing the pairing makes correct usage the only possible usage.
nodes.named_in: Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns - Kent Beck (1997)

nodes.name: Fixed Sized Buffer
nodes.what: Allocate memory only in one (or a few) fixed sizes - sized for the worst case - so freed blocks are always exactly reusable.
nodes.problem: Variable-size heap requests interleave into unusable fragments over time; uniform block sizes eliminate external fragmentation at the cost of internal waste.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Free List
nodes.what: Linked list threaded through unused memory blocks or object slots themselves, from which an allocator pops on allocate and onto which it pushes on free.
nodes.problem: Recycling fixed-size blocks in O(1) without heap traffic or fragmentation bookkeeping; the backbone of pool allocators, slab allocators, and embedded memory managers.
nodes.named_in: Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review - Wilson, Johnstone, Neely & Boles (1995)

nodes.name: Garbage Collection
nodes.what: A runtime mechanism that finds no-longer-referenced allocations and reclaims (and, in compacting variants, relocates) them without explicit frees.
nodes.problem: Manual deallocation causes leaks and dangling pointers; automated reclamation trades CPU time and determinism for memory safety. (Douglass catalogs both Garbage Collection and Garbage Compactor patterns; folded here as one mechanism with a compaction variant.)
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: GC Read Barrier
nodes.what: A small check or fixup executed on every (or selected) pointer load so a concurrent or moving collector can intercept reads of stale or unforwarded references.
nodes.problem: Concurrent and moving garbage collectors must keep the mutator from observing objects mid-move or mid-mark; intercepting reads lets the collector repair or redirect references lazily.
nodes.named_in: The Garbage Collection Handbook — Jones, Hosking, Moss (2011)

nodes.name: GC Write Barrier
aka: Yuasa barrier / Dijkstra barrier / Steele barrier (variants)
nodes.what: A small code sequence the compiler or runtime inserts on every pointer store that records or checks the mutated reference (e.g. by marking a card in a card table or appending to a remembered set), so the collector can find cross-generation or concurrently-mutated pointers without rescanning the whole heap.
nodes.problem: Generational and incremental/concurrent collectors must know which old-generation or already-scanned objects now point into the young generation or unscanned space; intercepting mutator writes is the only way to track this without full-heap scans.
nodes.named_in: Jones, Hosking & Moss, 'The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management' (2011), sect. 11.8 'Write barrier mechanisms' incl. 'Card tables' (verified live via O'Reilly index/ToC this session)

nodes.name: Hazard Pointers
nodes.what: Each thread publishes single-writer pointers naming the nodes it is currently accessing; reclaimers defer freeing any node named in a hazard pointer.
nodes.problem: Safe memory reclamation for lock-free data structures: a node removed from the structure may still be dereferenced by a concurrent reader, so freeing must wait until no reader can hold it.
nodes.named_in: Hazard Pointers: Safe Memory Reclamation for Lock-Free Objects - Maged M. Michael (2004)

nodes.name: Hooks
nodes.what: Access read-only information through hooks (pointers or jump slots) held in writable storage, so changing the hooks gives the illusion of changing ROM content.
nodes.problem: Information baked into ROM cannot be updated in the field; a small writable indirection layer allows patching and extension without rewriting read-only storage.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Lazy Cleanup
aka: let the OS reclaim at exit
nodes.what: Deliberately never free dynamically allocated memory whose lifetime spans the whole program run, relying on the operating system to reclaim it at process exit.
nodes.problem: Explicit deallocation of long-lived allocations adds code, ownership bookkeeping, and dangling-pointer risk for memory the process needs until it dies anyway; skipping the free removes that entire error class at the cost of unbounded-lifetime allocations.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)
nodes.borderline: distinct from Eternal Memory / static allocation (already in index under static-allocation): here memory IS dynamically allocated, only the cleanup is skipped

nodes.name: Leasing
nodes.what: A resource is granted for a limited time; the holder must renew the lease to keep it, and expiry releases the resource automatically.
nodes.problem: Resource holders that crash or forget to release cause leaks in loosely coupled systems; time-bounded grants make reclamation the default rather than the exception.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

nodes.name: List Virtualization
nodes.what: Renders only the subset of a long scrollable list that is visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer), creating, recycling, and repositioning a fixed pool of item views as the user scrolls.
nodes.problem: Instantiating a widget per item makes large lists consume unbounded memory and layout time; virtualizing bounds live widget count to the viewport size. Named across stacks: WPF UI virtualization, Android RecyclerView view recycling, react-window windowing, CDK virtual scrolling.
nodes.named_in: Optimizing Performance: Controls (UI Virtualization) - WPF documentation - Microsoft

nodes.name: Lookup
nodes.what: Resource providers register references with a lookup service under known names or properties; users query the service to find and access the resources.
nodes.problem: Resource users should not hard-code the identity or location of providers; a mediating registry decouples acquisition from provider placement and lifetime.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)
nodes.borderline: Often distribution-flavored (naming services), but equally an in-process service registry; POSA3 documents it as a resource-acquisition design pattern.

nodes.name: Memory Arena
nodes.what: Allocate objects by bumping a pointer through a large block and free them all at once by resetting or discarding the whole arena.
nodes.problem: Per-object malloc/free is slow and error-prone when many objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compilation pass); grouping them into one region makes allocation a pointer increment and deallocation a single bulk release. Canonical name decided as 'memory arena' (mission anchor; Hanson's Arena interface); region/bump/linear/frame allocator folded as aka.
nodes.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996), ch. 'Arenas'

nodes.name: Memory Discard
nodes.what: Allocate temporary objects from a temporary workspace and reclaim them all at once by discarding the whole workspace.
nodes.problem: Freeing many short-lived temporaries individually is slow and error-prone; discarding an entire scratch region on completion reclaims everything in one cheap operation.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Memory Limit
nodes.what: Set an explicit memory budget for each component and fail allocations that would exceed the component's limit.
nodes.problem: Competing components can starve each other of memory unpredictably; enforced per-component limits contain failures and make memory use plannable.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)
nodes.borderline: Closer to a budgeting policy than a code mechanism, but pattern-cataloged and implemented via allocator quota checks - kept IN.

nodes.name: Memory Overlay
nodes.what: Divide a program into sections that share the same memory region, loading each overlay from secondary storage into the shared region only when its code/data is needed.
nodes.problem: The program is larger than the memory it must run in; time-multiplexing one region among mutually exclusive sections fits large programs into small RAM, predating and paralleling virtual memory.
nodes.named_in: Linkers and Loaders - Levine (1999)
nodes.borderline: Realized through linker machinery (ops territory), but choosing an overlay scheme is a genuine program-level memory-design decision.

nodes.name: Object Manager
nodes.what: A manager component separate from both clients and managed objects controls the objects' creation, access, and destruction, issuing references while owning the lifecycle.
nodes.problem: When object lifetime is governed by application-wide concerns rather than any single client, per-client ownership fails; a dedicated manager centralizes lifecycle policy.
nodes.named_in: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)

nodes.name: Paging
nodes.what: Keep code and data on secondary storage and move fixed-size pages in and out of main memory on demand, giving the illusion of more memory.
nodes.problem: The working set exceeds physical RAM; paging trades access latency for effectively unbounded addressable data (the OS virtual-memory realization is the system-level cousin).
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Partial Acquisition
nodes.what: A large resource is acquired in stages - only the part needed now, with further parts acquired progressively (e.g. lazy-loading pages of an image or file).
nodes.problem: A resource may be too large or costly to acquire whole, yet partially usable; staged acquisition balances memory, latency, and availability.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

nodes.name: Pool Allocation
nodes.what: Pre-allocated pools of fixed-size blocks (often one pool per object type/size) from which objects are checked out and returned in O(1).
nodes.problem: General-purpose heap allocation fragments memory and has variable timing; pools give deterministic allocation with bounded memory per type.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Pooling
nodes.what: Released resources are recycled into a pool and handed out again on demand, amortizing acquisition/release cost across many uses; the pool manages size and eviction.
nodes.problem: Frequent creation and destruction of expensive, identity-free resources (threads, connections, buffers, objects) wastes time and fragments memory.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

nodes.name: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)
nodes.what: Tie a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime so acquisition happens in the constructor and release happens deterministically in the destructor at scope exit.
nodes.problem: Manual release paths leak resources on early returns and exceptions; RAII makes cleanup automatic and exception-safe.
nodes.named_in: The Design and Evolution of C++ - Stroustrup (1994)

nodes.name: Read-Only Memory
nodes.what: Place read-only code and constant data in ROM/flash rather than RAM, reserving scarce writable memory for mutable state.
nodes.problem: RAM is the scarcest memory on small systems while ROM/flash is comparatively plentiful; segregating immutable content into read-only memory frees RAM.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Reference Counting
nodes.what: A handle class embeds a reference counter in (or beside) a dynamically allocated body object, updating it on copy/assignment/destruction and deleting the body when the count reaches zero.
nodes.problem: Shared dynamically allocated objects in C++ need deterministic deallocation without ownership ambiguity, dangling pointers, or leaks.
nodes.named_in: A Method for Overlapping and Erasure of Lists - George E. Collins (1960)

nodes.name: Resource Files
nodes.what: Keep configuration data and read-only resources in files on secondary storage, loading and discarding each item as needed.
nodes.problem: Keeping all configuration and UI resources resident wastes RAM and hard-codes content; externalized, demand-loaded resources cut memory use and ease localization/updates.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Resource Lifecycle Manager
nodes.what: A dedicated manager component centrally controls the whole lifecycle of a class of resources - acquisition, coordination, optimization, and release - decoupling lifecycle from resource use.
nodes.problem: When many users share many resources, per-user lifecycle handling causes leaks and conflicting policies; centralizing lifecycle management enables global optimization.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

nodes.name: Rule of Three/Five/Zero
aka: rule of the big four (and a half)
nodes.what: If a class defines any of destructor/copy/move special members it should deliberately define the whole set (three/five) - or own no resources directly and define none (zero).
nodes.problem: Compiler-generated special members silently mismanage owned resources (double frees, slicing of ownership semantics); the rule makes ownership responsibilities explicit.
nodes.named_in: C++ Core Guidelines (C.20/C.21) - Stroustrup & Sutter (living)
nodes.borderline: A coding guideline about special members rather than a standalone mechanism; kept because it is the named contract governing RAII-style ownership.

nodes.name: Scope Guard
nodes.what: An ad-hoc RAII object that runs an arbitrary cleanup or rollback action when a scope exits, optionally dismissible on success.
nodes.problem: One-off cleanup/rollback obligations (not tied to a reusable resource class) must still run on every exit path including exceptions.
nodes.named_in: Generic<Programming>: Change the Way You Write Exception-Safe Code - Forever - Andrei Alexandrescu & Petru Marginean, Dr. Dobb's/CUJ (2000)

nodes.name: Sharing
nodes.what: Store one copy of identical information and reference it from everywhere it is needed instead of duplicating it.
nodes.problem: Multiple copies of the same data multiply memory cost; sharing a single instance removes the duplication at the price of managing shared ownership and mutation (closely related to GoF Flyweight).
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Slab Allocator
nodes.what: Carve memory into per-type slabs of preconstructed, fixed-size objects and cache freed objects in initialized state for immediate reuse.
nodes.problem: Frequently allocated kernel objects pay repeated construction/destruction and fragmentation costs under a general allocator; caching constructed objects per type removes both and improves locality. Slab coloring and the later magazine/vmem layer (Bonwick & Adams 2001) are folded here as variants.
nodes.named_in: The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator - Jeff Bonwick (1994)

nodes.name: Small Buffer Optimization
nodes.what: A container or wrapper embeds a small fixed-size buffer inside itself and only falls back to heap allocation when contents exceed it.
nodes.problem: Heap allocation dominates cost for typically-small payloads (short strings, small callables); inline storage removes the allocation and improves locality.
nodes.named_in: C++ Software Design - Iglberger (2022)

nodes.name: Smart Pointer
nodes.what: A pointer-like object that wraps a raw pointer, validity-checks access, and manages the pointee's lifetime (typically by reference counting), releasing it when the last reference disappears.
nodes.problem: Raw pointers invite dangling access, double free, and leaks; wrapping pointer mechanics in an object enforces the ownership rules mechanically.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Stack First
nodes.what: Default data placement on the call stack (automatic storage), reaching for static or heap storage only when lifetime or size demands it.
nodes.problem: Heap allocation on constrained systems risks fragmentation, leaks, and nondeterminism; stack allocation is self-releasing and timing-safe.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Static Allocation
nodes.what: All objects and buffers are allocated at compile/link time or once at startup, and the heap is never used afterwards.
nodes.problem: Dynamic allocation brings fragmentation, nondeterministic timing, and out-of-memory failures that safety-critical and long-running embedded systems cannot tolerate.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Steady State
nodes.what: For every mechanism that accumulates a resource (log files, cache entries, rows, temp files), pair a mechanism that recycles or purges it, so the program can run indefinitely without human cleanup.
nodes.problem: Unbounded accumulation (logs filling disks, caches growing without eviction) eventually kills long-running systems and forces routine human intervention.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
nodes.borderline: Close to an operability principle, but kept: it prescribes concrete in-program purge/rotation/eviction mechanisms.

nodes.name: Two-Level Segregated Fit Allocator (TLSF)
nodes.what: A dynamic allocator using a two-level bitmap-indexed segregated-fit structure giving O(1) worst-case malloc and free.
nodes.problem: Real-time systems need dynamic allocation with a hard constant-time bound and low fragmentation, which classic best-fit/first-fit heaps cannot guarantee.
nodes.named_in: TLSF: a New Dynamic Memory Allocator for Real-Time Systems - Masmano, Ripoll, Crespo, Real (ECRTS 2004)

nodes.name: Variable Allocation
nodes.what: Allocate and deallocate variable-sized objects on demand from a heap as the program needs them.
nodes.problem: Fixed pre-allocation wastes memory on empty reserved space; allocating only what is needed, when needed, avoids unused headroom at the cost of allocation failure handling and fragmentation.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Weak Reference
nodes.what: A reference that does not keep its target alive: it can be dereferenced only while the target still exists and observably lapses when the target is reclaimed.
nodes.problem: Reference-counted or traced object graphs with back-pointers, caches, or observer lists otherwise leak via cycles or unwanted retention; a non-owning, lapse-aware reference breaks the cycle while remaining safe to use. Kept as a separate element from reference counting per decision log (distinct mechanism, also exists in tracing-GC runtimes).
nodes.named_in: The Garbage Collection Handbook - Jones, Hosking & Moss (2011)

nodes.name: Access Control List
nodes.what: Store, with each protected object, the list of subjects and the operations each may perform on it; checks consult the object's list.
nodes.problem: The full subject-by-object access matrix is sparse; attaching permissions to the object makes per-object review and revocation direct (the column-slice of Lampson's access matrix).
nodes.named_in: Lampson, Protection (1971, access matrix); Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); standard OS textbooks

nodes.name: Allowlist Input Validation
aka: Intercepting Validator (placement variant, Core Security Patterns)
nodes.what: Validate untrusted input by accepting only what matches an explicit specification of the known-good (type, length, range, grammar) and rejecting everything else.
nodes.problem: Enumerating bad input (denylist) always misses encodings and novel attacks; specifying the accepted language flips the default to reject-unknown.
nodes.named_in: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet; Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns (2005)
nodes.borderline: Overlaps index entry complete-parameter-checking (Hanmer, fault-tolerance framing); kept because the positive-security-model discipline against adversarial input is the distinctly named security mechanism

nodes.name: Audit Log
nodes.what: An append-only record of security-relevant events (who did what, when, from where), written at the point of action for later reconstruction and accountability.
nodes.problem: After a fault or breach you must reconstruct what happened; ordinary debug logging is neither complete, attributable, nor protected against tampering.
nodes.named_in: Fowler, Audit Log (martinfowler.com eaaDev); Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns (2005, 'Secure Logger'); Schneier & Kelsey (1999, secure audit logs)

nodes.name: Authenticated Encryption
nodes.what: Encrypt and authenticate a message in one construction (optionally binding unencrypted associated data), so ciphertext cannot be undetectably modified.
nodes.problem: Encryption alone is malleable — attackers can flip ciphertext bits meaningfully; ad hoc MAC+encrypt compositions have failed repeatedly (padding oracles), so the combined primitive is the designer-facing element.
nodes.named_in: RFC 5116 (An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption, 2008); Rogaway AEAD literature
nodes.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; included as the modern reach-for-by-role encryption element

nodes.name: Canonicalization Before Validation
nodes.what: Reduce input (paths, URLs, Unicode strings) to its single canonical form before applying validation or access checks, so equivalent encodings cannot slip past the check.
nodes.problem: The same resource or string has many encodings (../, %2e%2e, Unicode homoglyphs, symlinks); validating a non-canonical form lets an equivalent alias bypass the filter after the check.
nodes.named_in: SEI CERT rules IDS01-J (normalize before validating) / FIO02-C (canonicalize path names); OWASP Input Validation guidance; Seacord, Secure Coding in C and C++

nodes.name: Capability
nodes.what: An unforgeable token/reference that both designates an object and carries the authority to use it; possession is permission (the row-slice of the access matrix).
nodes.problem: Checking identity against lists on every access needs ambient authority and a subject database; handing out unforgeable, delegatable, attenuable references makes authority flow with the references themselves.
nodes.named_in: Dennis & Van Horn, Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations (CACM 1966); Miller, Robust Composition (2006, object-capability)
nodes.borderline: OS-level origin, but in-language object-capability discipline (E, Caja, handle-based APIs) is an established in-process form

nodes.name: Check Point
nodes.what: A single configurable object/component that concentrates authentication, authorization and violation-response decisions, so the security policy can change without touching callers.
nodes.problem: Security policy evolves and differs per deployment; hard-coding checks throughout the application makes policy change and penalization logic unmaintainable. PAM-style pluggable authentication is a canonical realization.
nodes.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006)

nodes.name: Constant-Time Comparison
nodes.what: Compare secret-dependent data (MACs, tokens, passwords hashes) with an algorithm whose running time and memory access pattern are independent of the data values.
nodes.problem: Early-exit comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing, letting attackers recover secrets byte by byte; data-independent execution closes the side channel.
nodes.named_in: BearSSL: Constant-Time Crypto - Pornin (living)

nodes.name: Cryptographic Hash Function
nodes.what: A fixed-size digest function that is one-way and collision-resistant, used for integrity fingerprints, content addressing, commitment, and as a building block for MACs and signatures.
nodes.problem: CRCs and checksums detect accidental corruption only; against an adversary who can recompute them, integrity requires a digest that cannot be forged or collided.
nodes.named_in: Menezes, van Oorschot & Vanstone, Handbook of Applied Cryptography (1996, ch. 9); FIPS 180 (Secure Hash Standard)
nodes.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; included because index elements (merkle-tree, constant-time-comparison) already presuppose it and CRC is in the catalog

nodes.name: Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generator
nodes.what: A random generator whose output is computationally unpredictable even to an observer of prior output, seeded from real entropy, for keys, tokens, nonces and salts.
nodes.problem: Ordinary PRNGs (linear congruential, Mersenne Twister) are predictable from a few outputs; any security value derived from them (session ids, keys) is guessable.
nodes.named_in: NIST SP 800-90A (DRBG); RFC 4086 (Randomness Requirements for Security)
nodes.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; note the index has no PRNG element at all — the whole random-generation band is absent

nodes.name: Defensive Copy
nodes.what: Copy mutable inputs on receipt and mutable internal state on return, so external aliases can never mutate an object's invariant-protected state.
nodes.problem: Sharing references to mutable components lets callers corrupt invariants (time-of-check/time-of-use attacks); copying at the boundary restores encapsulation.
nodes.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2001; 3rd ed. Item 50)

nodes.name: Dual Channel
nodes.what: Two parallel channels (identical or diversely implemented) process the same inputs, with comparison or switchover logic detecting faults and continuing or safing on disagreement.
nodes.problem: Single-channel systems cannot keep operating through a channel fault; replication (homogeneous for random faults, heterogeneous for systematic ones) buys fault tolerance with hardware/software cost.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
nodes.borderline: Sits at the design/architecture boundary - kept per the DPESC safety-pattern canon; the system-scale redundancy variants are parked for Phase 3.

nodes.name: Full View With Errors
nodes.what: Show users the complete set of operations/data and reject unauthorized attempts with explicit errors at use time.
nodes.problem: Tailoring the interface per user is complex; presenting everything and enforcing at the action point is simpler and keeps the enforcement in one place, at the cost of revealing what exists.
nodes.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006)
nodes.borderline: UI-policy flavored, but an in-application enforcement-placement mechanism; dual of Limited View

nodes.name: Guard Page
nodes.what: Place an inaccessible (or trap-on-touch) memory page or poisoned band adjacent to a stack or allocation so that overrun/overflow faults immediately at the boundary instead of corrupting neighbors.
nodes.problem: Buffer and stack overflows silently corrupt adjacent memory and surface far from the bug; a trapping boundary converts the overrun into an immediate, located fault (and enables lazy stack growth). Allocator redzones (ASan-style poisoned bands) folded as aka; distinct from the ABI 'red zone' stack optimization.
nodes.named_in: Creating Guard Pages - Microsoft Win32 documentation (live)
nodes.borderline: Relies on MMU protection, so it straddles the OS/hardware boundary - but it is set up inside one program (allocator, runtime, thread library), so kept IN.

nodes.name: HTML Sanitization
nodes.what: Parse untrusted markup into a DOM and rebuild it keeping only an allowlist of safe elements/attributes, yielding markup that renders but cannot execute script.
nodes.problem: When users must be allowed to supply rich markup, output encoding would destroy it; regex filtering of markup is reliably bypassable, so parse-filter-serialize is the established defense.
nodes.named_in: OWASP HTML Sanitization guidance (XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet); OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer; WHATWG HTML Sanitizer API (draft)
nodes.borderline: Distinct from index entry escape-sequence: sanitization filters a parsed structure rather than encoding characters

nodes.name: Limited View
nodes.what: Present users only the operations and data their permissions allow, so unauthorized actions cannot even be attempted.
nodes.problem: Letting users attempt forbidden operations and then failing them leaks structure and frustrates; filtering the view by permission prevents the attempt, at the cost of computing per-user views.
nodes.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006, 'Limited Access')
nodes.borderline: UI-policy flavored, but an in-application enforcement-placement mechanism; dual of Full View With Errors

nodes.name: Memory Poisoning
nodes.what: Fills freed or uninitialized memory with a recognizable poison pattern and verifies it later (on reallocation or access), so stale reads, use-after-free, and buffer overruns surface as the pattern or its corruption.
nodes.problem: Memory-lifetime bugs are silent and nondeterministic; deterministic poison patterns make invalid accesses detectable, reproducible, and diagnosable from a crash dump.
nodes.named_in: Linux kernel CONFIG_PAGE_POISONING and slab-poisoning documentation (verified live); also AddressSanitizer shadow-poisoning terminology (Serebryany et al., USENIX ATC 2012)
nodes.borderline: distinct from stack-painting (usage watermarking), guard-page (trapping region), and marked-data (flagging known-corrupt application data)

nodes.name: Message Authentication Code
nodes.what: A keyed digest over a message that only holders of the secret key can produce or verify, authenticating both integrity and origin.
nodes.problem: A plain hash of a message can be recomputed by anyone, so it proves nothing about who produced it; binding the digest to a shared secret defeats tampering and forgery in transit or at rest.
nodes.named_in: RFC 2104 (HMAC, 1997); Handbook of Applied Cryptography ch. 9
nodes.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; the index's constant-time-comparison exists chiefly to compare MAC tags safely

nodes.name: Nonce
nodes.what: A value used exactly once within a security context (random, counter, or timestamp-based) so that replayed or duplicated messages/operations are detectable and rejected.
nodes.problem: A verifier cannot otherwise distinguish a fresh legitimate message from a captured-and-replayed one; uniqueness per interaction restores freshness.
nodes.named_in: RFC 4949 (Internet Security Glossary); Handbook of Applied Cryptography ch. 10
nodes.borderline: Protocol-element flavored, but implemented and checked in-process; sibling of index entries idempotency key and serial-number-arithmetic

nodes.name: One's Complement Data Storage
nodes.what: Critical data is stored twice - once normally, once bit-inverted - and every read verifies the pair still complement each other before use.
nodes.problem: Memory corruption (EMI, cosmic rays, stuck bits, wild pointers) silently alters safety-relevant values; a complemented copy detects corruption at each access.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Parameterized Query
nodes.what: Send the query text and the data values to the interpreter separately, so values are bound as data and can never be parsed as code.
nodes.problem: Building queries by string concatenation lets attacker-controlled input change the query structure (SQL injection); separating code from data removes the injection channel by construction.
nodes.named_in: OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet / OWASP Top 10 injection guidance; every major database API

nodes.name: Pointer Check
nodes.what: Explicitly set pointers to an invalid value (NULL) when uninitialized or freed, and check pointers against that invalid value before dereferencing them.
nodes.problem: Dangling and uninitialized pointers cause corruption far from the defect site; pairing deliberate invalidation with checks before use converts silent memory corruption into detectable, handleable conditions.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)
nodes.borderline: overlaps sanity-check and complete-parameter-checking in the index; kept separate because the mechanism is the invalidate-on-free/init + check-before-use pairing specific to raw-pointer lifetime, not general input validation

nodes.name: Privilege Bracketing
nodes.what: Hold elevated privilege only across the exact operations that need it: raise at the last possible moment, perform the action, drop immediately after (and permanently once never needed again).
nodes.problem: A process that keeps privileges it rarely needs turns every bug into a privileged bug; bracketing minimizes the window in which a fault or exploit runs privileged.
nodes.named_in: Oracle Solaris Developer's Guide to Security ('privilege bracketing'); Viega & Messier, Secure Programming Cookbook for C and C++ (2003, dropping privileges in setuid programs)

nodes.name: Privilege Separation
nodes.what: Split one application into a small privileged process and unprivileged worker processes that request sensitive operations over a narrow IPC interface, so a compromise of the exposed code yields no privileges.
nodes.problem: Monolithic privileged programs let any exploited parsing/network-facing code inherit full privileges; confining privileges to a minimal monitor bounds the damage.
nodes.named_in: Provos, Friedl, Honeyman, 'Preventing Privilege Escalation', 12th USENIX Security Symposium 2003 (verified live)
tags: borderline: multi-process internal structure edges toward architecture; kept design-realm because it is a named mechanism implemented within one application (privilege-bracketing covers only the temporal form)

nodes.name: Program Sequence Monitoring
nodes.what: Instrument checkpoints along required execution paths and have a monitor (often the watchdog manager) verify that checkpoints occur in the legal order and cadence.
nodes.problem: A timing watchdog alone cannot detect code that runs on time but in the wrong order (skipped safety checks, corrupted control flow); sequence monitoring detects illegal execution paths.
nodes.named_in: IEC 61508-7:2010 - program sequence monitoring technique

nodes.name: Protected Single Channel
nodes.what: A single end-to-end data/processing channel augmented with integrity checks at one or more points (CRCs, range checks, monitoring) so faults are detected even without redundant channels.
nodes.problem: Full channel redundancy is costly; when fail-safe (not fail-operational) behavior suffices, one channel plus systematic checking detects faults at lower recurring cost.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
nodes.borderline: Channel-scale structure verging on architecture, but implementable within one component and cataloged by Douglass as a design-level safety pattern.

nodes.name: Reference Monitor
aka: policy enforcement point / policy decision point (operational split)
nodes.what: A component that mediates every access by subjects to protected objects, checking each request against the authorization rules before allowing it.
nodes.problem: Access checks sprinkled through code can be skipped or diverge from policy; complete mediation requires one tamper-evident chokepoint that is always invoked and small enough to verify.
nodes.named_in: Anderson, Computer Security Technology Planning Study (1972); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006, 'Reference Monitor')

nodes.name: Role-Based Access Control
nodes.what: Authorization is granted to named roles rather than individual users; users acquire permissions by role membership, with optional role hierarchies.
nodes.problem: Per-user permission assignment does not scale and drifts; grouping privileges into roles matches organizational structure and makes review/revocation tractable.
nodes.named_in: Ferraiolo & Kuhn, Role-Based Access Controls (NIST, 1992); ANSI INCITS 359; Yoder & Barcalow 'Roles' (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006)

nodes.name: Salted Password Hashing
nodes.what: Store passwords only as the output of a deliberately slow one-way function over password plus per-entry random salt, so verification is possible but recovery and precomputation are not.
nodes.problem: Stored plaintext or fast unsalted hashes fall to theft, rainbow tables and cross-user cracking; per-user salt defeats precomputation and cost-tunable hashing keeps brute force expensive as hardware improves.
nodes.named_in: Morris & Thompson, Password Security: A Case History (CACM 1979, introduces salt); OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet

nodes.name: Sanity Check
nodes.what: A lightweight independent monitor verifies that outputs or system state remain within physically/logically plausible bounds, triggering fault handling when they do not.
nodes.problem: Full result verification is often infeasible, but gross faults are cheap to catch; checking plausibility gives broad fault coverage at minimal cost.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
nodes.borderline: Adjacent to the raw assert language facility; included as the named defensive-design mechanism (Hanson's Assert interface, design-by-contract lite).

nodes.name: Secure Access Layer
nodes.what: An application-internal layer that wraps the security mechanisms of the platforms it sits on (OS, database, network APIs), giving the application one coherent security interface.
nodes.problem: Application security is only as strong as its integration with lower-level security; scattering raw platform security calls through the code couples it to each platform and invites misuse.
nodes.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997)
nodes.borderline: Layer-shaped; kept design-side as an in-application integration layer on the HAL/wrapper-facade precedent — Phase 3 may claim it upward

nodes.name: Secure Boot Image Verification
nodes.what: Before transferring control, the bootloader cryptographically verifies the next stage or application image against a trusted public key, refusing or falling back on failure.
nodes.problem: A CRC (already in the index) only catches corruption; against malicious firmware replacement the boot stage must verify authenticity, anchoring each stage in the previous one.
nodes.named_in: UEFI Specification (Secure Boot); Android Verified Boot documentation; embedded bootloader literature (e.g. MCUboot documentation)
nodes.borderline: The full chain-of-trust across stages is architecture; the in-bootloader verify-then-jump step is the in-process element (complements index entries bootloader-jump-handoff and a-b-firmware-image-update)

nodes.name: Secure Zeroization
nodes.what: Erase sensitive data (keys, passwords) from memory using an operation the compiler cannot optimize away, immediately after last use.
nodes.problem: Ordinary memset before free is dead-store-eliminated by optimizers, leaving secrets recoverable from memory dumps, swap, or reuse; guaranteed-erase primitives close the gap.
nodes.named_in: The CERT C Coding Standard, 2nd ed. - Seacord (2014)

nodes.name: Security Session
nodes.what: An object holding an authenticated subject's identity and security attributes across a sequence of actions, so each request need not re-authenticate or re-derive permissions.
nodes.problem: Distributing a user's security state across many interactions invites inconsistency and repeated credential handling; one session object localizes it and gives it a lifetime (timeout, invalidation).
nodes.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006, 'Security Session')

nodes.name: Single Access Point
aka: one entry point for security checks
nodes.what: Route all entry into a program or module through one guarded entry point where identity and validity checks run before anything else executes.
nodes.problem: Multiple scattered entrances make security checks inconsistent and individually bypassable; a single funnel makes the check set complete and auditable.
nodes.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow, Architectural Patterns for Enabling Application Security (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006)

nodes.name: Smart Data
nodes.what: Data types that carry their own validity metadata (ranges, units, CRC) and check every set/get operation, rejecting or flagging out-of-range values.
nodes.problem: Plain C data accepts any bit pattern, so faults propagate silently; building the checks into the data type enforces validity at every touch point.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Stack Canary
nodes.what: Place a secret guard value between a stack frame's buffers and its control data (return address); verify it before returning, aborting if a buffer overflow overwrote it.
nodes.problem: Stack buffer overflows silently overwrite return addresses, enabling control-flow hijack; a checked sentinel converts the overwrite into a detected crash.
nodes.named_in: StackGuard: Automatic Adaptive Detection and Prevention of Buffer-Overflow Attacks - Cowan et al. (1998)

nodes.name: Synchronizer Token Pattern
nodes.what: Embed a per-session (or per-request) unpredictable token in each legitimate form/request and verify it server-side, so cross-site forged requests lacking the token are rejected.
nodes.problem: Browsers attach ambient credentials (cookies) to any request, letting a hostile page forge state-changing requests; a secret the attacker cannot read distinguishes genuine requests.
nodes.named_in: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet ('Synchronizer Token Pattern')

nodes.name: Taint Checking
nodes.what: Mark data from untrusted sources as tainted, propagate the mark through computations, and refuse (or flag) its use in sensitive sinks until it passes an explicit untainting step.
nodes.problem: Manually tracking which values derive from untrusted input across a codebase fails silently; making trust a tracked property of the data enforces the source-to-sink discipline mechanically.
nodes.named_in: Perl perlsec (taint mode); Ruby $SAFE taint (historical); Schwartz & Christiansen Perl literature; dynamic taint analysis literature (Newsome & Song 2005)

nodes.name: Watchdog
nodes.what: A hardware or software timer that must be periodically serviced ('kicked') by correctly running software; missing the deadline triggers reset or a safety action.
nodes.problem: Hung, livelocked, or timing-broken software cannot report its own failure; an independent timer converts liveness violations into detectable, recoverable events.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Cyclic Executive
nodes.what: A fixed infinite loop that runs each task to completion in a predetermined order every cycle, with no preemption.
nodes.problem: Small systems with stable, known task sets need utterly predictable, low-overhead scheduling without an RTOS.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Deadline Propagation
nodes.what: Carry an absolute deadline (or remaining budget) with each request and pass it down the call chain; every stage checks it and aborts work whose deadline has already passed.
nodes.problem: Independent per-hop timeouts let deep call chains do work the original caller has already abandoned; a propagated deadline stops wasted work everywhere at once.
nodes.named_in: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems - Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy eds. (2016)
nodes.borderline: Spans a call chain across services, but each hop implements it locally (check-and-forward); kept as design-level with tag.

nodes.name: Debouncing
nodes.what: Filtering the intermittent make/break bounce of mechanical inputs (or noisy edges generally) by accepting a state change only after it is stable for a defined interval.
nodes.problem: Mechanical switches and noisy signals produce bursts of spurious transitions per actuation; naive edge handling registers many false events.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: Deferrable Work
nodes.what: Classify work as essential vs deferrable and, under overload, postpone deferrable tasks (audits, housekeeping, statistics) until load subsides.
nodes.problem: Under overload every cycle matters; explicitly deferring non-urgent work preserves capacity for revenue/critical processing without dropping it entirely.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
nodes.borderline: An overload policy inside one component; near operational policy but named and mechanically implementable (priority demotion, deferral queues).

nodes.name: Dynamic Priority Scheduling
nodes.what: Task priorities are recomputed at runtime from urgency - classically earliest-deadline-first, where the task with the nearest deadline runs.
nodes.problem: Fixed priorities cannot always achieve full utilization or handle aperiodic arrivals; deadline-driven priorities schedule optimally on one processor at the cost of predictability under overload.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Fixed Timestep
nodes.what: Advance the simulation in constant-size time increments driven by an accumulator of elapsed real time, decoupling the simulation rate from the (variable) render rate, typically with interpolation of the leftover fraction for display.
nodes.problem: Variable delta-time updates make physics non-deterministic, unstable at low frame rates, and irreproducible; a fixed step gives determinism and stability while the accumulator keeps game time synchronized with wall-clock time.
nodes.named_in: Fix Your Timestep! - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2004)

nodes.name: Governor
nodes.what: Cap the rate or scope of automated actions (restarts, scale-downs, config pushes) so automation cannot do damage faster than humans can react.
nodes.problem: Automation acts at machine speed; a runaway control loop can destroy capacity in seconds, so its actuation rate is deliberately slowed like an engine governor.
nodes.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
nodes.borderline: Governs ops automation, verging on operations tooling; kept as a named implementable rate-limiting mechanism from a pattern catalog.

nodes.name: Idle Task Hook
nodes.what: A user callback invoked repeatedly from the RTOS idle task (the lowest-priority always-ready task), used to run work that should consume only otherwise-idle cycles: low-power sleep entry, background self-tests, stack watermark checks.
nodes.problem: Firmware has background work and power-management actions that must run only when nothing else is runnable, without a dedicated task or any interference with real-time work.
nodes.named_in: freertos.org 'The Idle Task and the Idle Task Hook'; Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel; uC/OS-II OSTaskIdleHook
nodes.borderline: arguably just a registered callback (hook method) into the scheduler; kept because idle-context background processing is a named, recurring firmware mechanism across RTOSes (FreeRTOS idle hook, Zephyr idle thread, uC/OS idle hook) with distinct constraints (must not block)

nodes.name: Interrupt Coalescing
nodes.what: Hold back events that would each raise an interrupt until a count threshold or timeout is reached, then deliver one interrupt for the whole batch.
nodes.problem: Per-event interrupts under high event rates (e.g. NIC packet arrival) swamp the CPU with context switches; batching trades a bounded latency increase for an order-of-magnitude drop in interrupt load. NAPI-style hybrid interrupt/polling is the software realization folded here.
nodes.named_in: Interrupt coalescing - Wikipedia (live)

nodes.name: Leaky Bucket
nodes.what: Arriving work enters a bounded bucket that drains at a constant rate; overflow is rejected, converting bursty input into a smooth constant-rate output.
nodes.problem: Downstream stages that cannot absorb bursts need arrival smoothing; the bucket enforces a hard output rate regardless of input burstiness. Distinct from Hanmer's Leaky Bucket Counter (error counting).
nodes.named_in: New Directions in Communications (or Which Way to the Information Age?) - Turner (1986)

nodes.name: Round Robin Scheduling
nodes.what: The scheduler grants each ready task a turn (optionally a fixed time slice) in rotating order, giving fairness rather than urgency-driven preference.
nodes.problem: When tasks have comparable importance and no hard deadlines, fair progress for all is preferable to priority starvation.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Sandwich Delay
nodes.what: Wrap a code section between a hardware-timer start and a wait-for-timer end so the section always consumes the same wall-clock duration regardless of path taken.
nodes.problem: Variable execution paths introduce task jitter that degrades time-triggered control and sampling quality; padding every path to a fixed duration with a timer equalizes timing.
nodes.named_in: Meeting Real-Time Constraints Using 'Sandwich Delays' - Pont, Kurian & Bautista (EuroPLoP 2006)

nodes.name: Schedule Table
nodes.what: A statically configured table of expiry points on a counter, each releasing tasks or setting events at fixed offsets, cyclically or once, as an OS-level time-triggered dispatch mechanism.
nodes.problem: Periodic activations with precise relative phasing are clumsy to build from individual alarms; a schedule table expresses the whole time-triggered activation pattern declaratively and synchronizably (e.g. to a global time base).
nodes.named_in: AUTOSAR Specification of Operating System (schedule tables); OSEK/VDX time-triggered OS

nodes.name: Scheduler
nodes.what: An object that explicitly sequences waiting threads' access to a resource according to a scheduling policy (FIFO, priority, deadline) instead of leaving the order to the lock implementation.
nodes.problem: When the order in which contending threads proceed matters (fairness, priorities, deadlines), the policy must be lifted out of the lock and made an explicit, pluggable decision.
nodes.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

nodes.name: Software Timer
nodes.what: Kernel facility multiplexing many logical one-shot or auto-reload callback timers onto a single hardware tick/timer, with expiry callbacks typically executed by a timer-service (daemon) task rather than in interrupt context.
nodes.problem: Applications need many independent timed callbacks but hardware timers are scarce; a software timer layer provides unlimited cheap timers without dedicating a hardware timer or a task per delay.
nodes.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (software timers chapter)
nodes.borderline: decision logged: index has timer-wheel, but that is an implementation data structure for large timer populations; the RTOS software-timer kernel facility (one-shot/auto-reload objects + timer daemon) is the mechanism designers name and reach for, so a separate element is warranted

nodes.name: Static Priority Scheduling
nodes.what: Tasks receive fixed, design-time priorities and a preemptive scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task; rate-monotonic assignment (priority by period) is the classic policy.
nodes.problem: Concurrent tasks with different urgencies must meet deadlines; fixed priorities give analyzable, predictable preemption behavior.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

nodes.name: System Tick
nodes.what: A periodic timer interrupt increments a monotonic tick counter that serves as the system's software time base, driving timekeeping, timeouts, and scheduler preemption decisions.
nodes.problem: Bare-metal and RTOS code needs a cheap, uniform notion of elapsed time without dedicating a hardware timer per consumer; a single periodic tick gives every timeout, delay, software timer, and time-slice decision one shared clock.
nodes.named_in: white

nodes.name: Throttle
nodes.what: Ensure a function or action executes at most once per interval, discarding or coalescing invocations that arrive faster.
nodes.problem: High-frequency event streams (scroll, sensor readings, status updates) would trigger expensive handlers far faster than useful; throttling caps the execution rate while keeping periodic updates.
nodes.named_in: Debouncing and Throttling Explained Through Examples - Corbacho, CSS-Tricks (2016)

nodes.name: Tickless Idle
nodes.what: Suppress the periodic scheduler tick during idle, program a one-shot wakeup for the next deadline, and sleep the CPU in a low-power mode until then.
nodes.problem: A free-running tick interrupt wakes the CPU pointlessly and dominates power draw in mostly-idle systems; eliminating idle ticks lets the MCU stay in deep sleep between real events.
nodes.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (tickless idle mode)

nodes.name: Time to Live (TTL)
nodes.what: Attach a lifetime to a datum, message, or entry; holders treat it as invalid (and evict or drop it) once the lifetime elapses.
