nodes.problem: Keeping rarely used services running wastes memory and startup capacity, but clients must still be able to reach them at any time; an activation intermediary buys resource economy at the cost of first-request latency.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Adapter (container)
nodes.what: A sidecar variant that presents a standardized interface (e.g., uniform metrics/log format) over a heterogeneous application to the rest of the system.
nodes.problem: Uniform monitoring/management across services built differently, without modifying each service.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Container-based Distributed Systems - Burns & Oppenheimer (HotCloud 2016)
nodes.borderline: Shares the GoF Adapter name; kept separate: this is a deployment-unit structure, not an object-interface mechanism.

nodes.name: Ambassador
nodes.what: A sidecar variant that proxies the application's outbound connections to the outside world, hiding discovery, sharding, or protocol detail.
nodes.problem: Let a component talk to remote dependencies as if local and unsharded; the ambassador absorbs routing/resilience client logic.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Auto-Scaling
nodes.what: The instance pool grows and shrinks automatically, driven by metrics or schedules evaluated against scaling policies.
nodes.problem: Static provisioning wastes capacity at trough and fails at peak; policy-driven elasticity matches deployed capacity to demand without operator action.
nodes.named_in: Autoscaling guidance - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (living); also AWS Auto Scaling documentation

nodes.name: Blue-Green Deployment
nodes.what: Two identical production environments are maintained and releases go live by switching traffic from the active (blue) to the newly deployed (green) environment.
nodes.problem: Releasing in place risks downtime and slow rollback; keeping a fully deployed standby environment makes cutover and rollback a routing switch instead of a redeploy.
nodes.named_in: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010); also BlueGreenDeployment - Fowler bliki (2010)

nodes.name: Bootloader-Application Split
nodes.what: Partitioning firmware into a small, rarely-changed bootloader image and one or more application images in separate flash regions, with the bootloader validating, selecting, updating, and jumping to the application.
nodes.problem: Field-updatable devices must survive a failed or interrupted update; keeping an immutable boot stage that can verify images and fall back (golden image, A/B banks) makes the update path recoverable and the root of trust small.
nodes.named_in: From Zero to main() series - Memfault Interrupt (2019)

nodes.name: Bootloader (boot-stage architecture)
nodes.what: A dedicated boot-stage program that initializes the platform, selects/validates an application image, and hands off execution to it.
nodes.problem: Field update, image validation and bring-up need a stage that is independent of - and can replace - the application image.
nodes.named_in: From Zero to main() series - Memfault (2019)

nodes.name: Canary Release
aka: incremental rollout to a user subset
nodes.what: A new version is deployed to a small slice of production servers or users and observed before the rollout is widened to the whole fleet.
nodes.problem: Full-fleet releases expose every user to an undetected defect at once; a canary bounds the blast radius and turns release into a monitored experiment.
nodes.named_in: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010); also Site Reliability Engineering - Beyer et al. (2016)

nodes.name: Cell-Based Architecture
nodes.what: Workload deployed as multiple isolated, self-sufficient instances (cells), each serving a partition of requests, with a thin router directing traffic to cells.
nodes.problem: Reduce blast radius: a failure or bad deployment is contained to one cell's share of traffic; fault-isolation bulkheads at workload level.
nodes.named_in: Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture - AWS Well-Architected (2023)

nodes.name: Container
nodes.what: An execution environment that hosts application components and transparently provides them the technical services they need - lifecycle, transactions, security, persistence, resource access - via contracts the components declare.
nodes.problem: Domain components should not each reimplement cross-cutting runtime services; hosting them in a managing container buys uniform infrastructure and deploy-time configuration at the cost of conforming to the container's component model. Distinct from OS-level containers (Docker-style isolation), which are a separate deployment element.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Compute Resource Consolidation
nodes.what: Multiple tasks or operations are consolidated into shared compute units to raise utilization and cut cost.
nodes.problem: One deployment unit per small task wastes allocated capacity; packing trades isolation for density.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Deployment Pipeline
nodes.what: An automated, staged structure through which every change flows from commit to production - build, automated test stages, and deployment stages, each gating promotion of the same artifact.
nodes.problem: Manual, ad-hoc release paths make delivery slow and unrepeatable; a single automated pipeline makes the route to production an inspectable, versioned system structure.
nodes.named_in: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010), ch. 5 'Anatomy of the Deployment Pipeline'
nodes.borderline: Practice-adjacent (CI/CD is pass-7 territory), but the pipeline itself is a named, recurring structure - stages, gates, artifact promotion - not just a practice; included as the structural core of the CD literature.

nodes.name: Deployment Stamps
nodes.what: The full solution is replicated as identical scale-unit deployments (stamps), each hosting a subset of tenants/load, with routing in front.
nodes.problem: Scale beyond a single deployment's limits and isolate tenants by adding units instead of growing one deployment.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Deployment Stamps - Azure Architecture Center (living)

nodes.name: External Configuration Store
nodes.what: Configuration for all application instances is moved to a central external store fetched at startup/run time.
nodes.problem: Per-deployment config files diverge across instances and redeploys; centralization gives one managed source.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Feature-Flag-Driven Release
nodes.what: Code ships to production dark behind runtime toggles, and release becomes a configuration act - enabling the flag for cohorts, rings, or percentages - independent of deployment.
nodes.problem: Coupling release to deployment forces long-lived branches and big-bang exposure; runtime toggles let incomplete or risky features ride mainline deploys and be exposed, tested, and killed selectively.
nodes.named_in: Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags) - Hodgson (2017); also Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm has feature-flag (the in-code toggle point/router mechanism); this entry is the release-strategy structure built on it. Kept per the same-name rule.

nodes.name: Gatekeeper
nodes.what: A dedicated hardened host between clients and backends validates and sanitizes all requests, holding no keys or sensitive data itself.
nodes.problem: Exposing application hosts directly widens the attack surface; a minimal broker instance absorbs first contact.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Geodes
nodes.what: Identical active-active deployments distributed across geographic regions, each able to serve any user, backed by globally replicated data.
nodes.problem: Serve a global user base with low regional latency and region-loss tolerance, instead of active-passive DR.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Geodes - Azure Architecture Center (living)
nodes.borderline: Name currency is largely Azure-specific; the structure (geo-distributed active-active units) is real and bridgeable, so kept with the caveat.

nodes.name: Immutable Infrastructure
nodes.what: Deployed servers/images are never modified in place; every change produces a new image that replaces the old instance wholesale.
nodes.problem: In-place patching accumulates configuration drift and snowflake servers; rebuilding from a versioned image makes every environment reproducible and rollback a redeploy of the previous image.
nodes.named_in: ImmutableServer - Kief Morris (martinfowler.com bliki, 2013); also Infrastructure as Code - Morris (2016)
nodes.borderline: Practice-vs-structure judged: kept because it names a deployment structure (versioned images replacing mutable servers), not merely a working habit; the enclosing infrastructure-as-code practice is rejected below.

nodes.name: Load Balancer
aka: server farm behind a virtual IP
nodes.what: An intermediary distributes incoming requests across a pool of equivalent service instances, presenting the pool as one logical endpoint.
nodes.problem: A single instance limits capacity and is a single point of failure; a fronting distributor lets capacity scale horizontally and routes around dead instances.
nodes.named_in: Release It! - Nygard (2007/2018)

nodes.name: OS Container
nodes.what: An OS-level isolated execution unit packaging an application with its dependencies, sharing the host kernel, used as the standard unit of deployment and scheduling.
nodes.problem: Deployable units need environment-independent packaging and fast, dense isolation without full-VM overhead; containers make the deployment topology reproducible and orchestratable.
nodes.named_in: Design Patterns for Container-based Distributed Systems - Burns & Oppenheimer (USENIX HotCloud 2016)

nodes.name: Rolling Deployment
nodes.what: Instances in a load-balanced pool are replaced with the new version a few at a time, keeping the service up while old and new versions briefly coexist.
nodes.problem: Replacing an entire fleet at once requires downtime or double capacity; rolling replacement trades a window of mixed-version operation for zero-downtime upgrades within existing capacity.
nodes.named_in: Kubernetes Documentation - Deployments (RollingUpdate strategy) (living)

nodes.name: Scale Cube
aka: X-axis cloning / Y-axis functional decomposition / Z-axis data partitioning
nodes.what: A three-axis model of scaling structures: X - cloning identical instances behind a load balancer, Y - splitting by function/service, Z - partitioning by data/customer subset.
nodes.problem: Systems that only clone hit data and code-complexity limits; naming the three orthogonal scaling structures lets architects combine duplication, decomposition, and sharding deliberately.
nodes.named_in: The Art of Scalability - Abbott & Fisher (2009; 2nd ed. 2015)
nodes.borderline: A named model organizing three scaling structures rather than a single mechanism; included because it is the established name for the trio and each axis is a concrete, bridgeable deployment structure (sharding and functional-split design elements bridge to its axes). Verified live at akfpartners.com this session.

nodes.name: Serverless / Function-as-a-Service
nodes.what: Application logic deployed as provider-managed, event-triggered ephemeral functions (plus managed backend services), with no server capacity owned by the team.
nodes.problem: Eliminate server provisioning and idle cost; scale-to-zero and per-invocation billing, traded against cold starts, execution limits, and provider coupling.
nodes.named_in: Serverless Architectures - Roberts (martinfowler.com, 2016)

nodes.name: Service Mesh
nodes.what: Dedicated infrastructure layer of per-service proxies (data plane) plus a control plane that transparently handles inter-service traffic: routing, retries, mTLS, telemetry.
nodes.problem: Move reliability and security of service-to-service communication out of every application's code into uniform, operable infrastructure.
nodes.named_in: What's a service mesh? And why do I need one? - Morgan (Buoyant, 2017)

nodes.name: Sidecar
nodes.what: A helper process/container co-deployed with an application instance, sharing its lifecycle and local resources to extend it (proxying, logging, config).
nodes.problem: Add cross-cutting capabilities to heterogeneous services without changing their code or language; per-instance co-location keeps latency and fate-sharing local.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Static Content Hosting
nodes.what: Static content is served from dedicated storage/CDN services instead of the application's compute instances.
nodes.problem: Serving immutable assets from application servers wastes expensive compute on cacheable bytes.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: 4+1 View Model
nodes.what: A fixed viewpoint set — logical, process, development, and physical views, plus scenarios (the +1) that tie them together — for describing a software architecture.
nodes.problem: Single-diagram architecture descriptions overload one drawing with every stakeholder's concerns; a small fixed set of concurrent views, validated by use-case scenarios, covers the stakeholder spectrum without conflating concerns.
nodes.named_in: Architectural Blueprints — The 4+1 View Model of Software Architecture — Kruchten (1995)

nodes.name: Allocation View
nodes.what: A view type mapping software elements onto structures in the system's environment — hardware and networks (deployment), file systems (implementation), and teams (work assignment).
nodes.problem: Neither module nor runtime structure says where software executes, lives on disk, or who builds it; a dedicated mapping view type carries the software-to-environment correspondences these concerns need.
nodes.named_in: Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond, 2nd ed. — Clements et al. (2010)

nodes.name: Architectural Perspective
nodes.what: A collection of activities, tactics, and guidelines for ensuring that a system exhibits a particular quality property, applied across all of a description's views rather than forming a view of its own.
nodes.problem: Quality attributes (security, performance, availability, evolution) cut across every view; treating each as yet another view duplicates content, so a cross-cutting construct is applied to existing views instead. Highly bridgeable: perspective instances map onto quality attributes and their tactics.
nodes.named_in: Software Systems Architecture, 2nd ed. — Rozanski & Woods (2011)

nodes.name: Architecture Decision Record
nodes.what: A short, versioned document capturing one architecturally significant decision together with its context, status, and consequences.
nodes.problem: Design rationale evaporates as teams change; later maintainers see what was decided but not why, and either cargo-cult the decision or blindly reverse it. A lightweight per-decision record kept with the code preserves the why at low cost.
nodes.named_in: Documenting Architecture Decisions — Michael Nygard (2011)

nodes.name: Architecture Description
nodes.what: The concrete work product (documents, models, views) used to express the architecture of a system of interest.
nodes.problem: An architecture is intangible and lives partly in architects' heads; stakeholders need a durable, reviewable artifact that expresses it and can be checked for concern coverage.
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description

nodes.name: Architecture Description Language
nodes.what: A formal notation whose first-class constructs are architectural — components, connectors, configurations — used to model and analyze a software architecture.
nodes.problem: Box-and-line diagrams lack defined semantics, so descriptions cannot be analyzed or checked for consistency; an ADL gives architectural constructs a defined syntax and semantics amenable to tooling (instances — AADL, Wright, Rapide, Darwin, ACME — stay works; AADL is corpus work feilergluch).
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description

nodes.name: Architecture Framework
nodes.what: An established package of conventions, principles, viewpoints, and practices for architecture description within a specific domain or stakeholder community.
nodes.problem: Communities and organizations repeatedly need the same viewpoints and description conventions; packaging them as a reusable framework standardizes descriptions across projects (instances such as TOGAF or DoDAF stay works, not elements).
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description

nodes.name: Architecture View
nodes.what: A representation of a system's architecture from the perspective of a related set of concerns, composed of one or more architecture models.
nodes.problem: No single representation can serve all stakeholders; splitting the description into concern-focused views keeps each representation coherent, readable, and auditable against the concerns it frames.
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description

nodes.name: Architecture Viewpoint
nodes.what: A reusable work product establishing the conventions — model kinds, notations, methods — for constructing, interpreting, and using views that frame a specific set of stakeholder concerns.
nodes.problem: Views built ad hoc are inconsistent across systems and teams; making the conventions first-class lets viewpoints be declared, reused, and conformance-checked independently of any one system.
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description

nodes.name: Component-and-Connector View
nodes.what: A view type documenting the system's runtime elements (components) and their interaction pathways (connectors) — pipes-and-filters, client-server, publish-subscribe structures and the like.
nodes.problem: Static module structure says little about runtime behavior, concurrency, or data flow; a dedicated runtime view type is where architectural styles and connector choices become visible and analyzable.
nodes.named_in: Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond, 2nd ed. — Clements et al. (2010)

nodes.name: Context Map
nodes.what: A documented map of the system's bounded contexts and the relationship type at each seam (partnership, customer-supplier, conformist, ACL, ...).
nodes.problem: Teams need a shared, honest picture of model boundaries and inter-context translation obligations to coordinate integration.
nodes.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)
nodes.borderline: An architecture-description artifact rather than a runtime structure; kind description per 42010-style constructs.

nodes.name: Interface Definition Language
nodes.what: A language-neutral contract describing component interfaces and data types from which stubs, skeletons and serializers are generated.
nodes.problem: Cross-language, cross-component boundaries need a single authoritative contract rather than per-language duplication.
nodes.named_in: The Common Object Request Broker: Architecture and Specification - OMG (1991)
nodes.borderline: A contract-and-toolchain construct rather than a runtime structure, but the established architecture-level boundary description mechanism.

nodes.name: Model Kind
nodes.what: The conventions (notation, modeling template, analytic methods) for one type of architecture model used within a viewpoint, e.g. a state-machine or dataflow model kind.
nodes.problem: A viewpoint typically needs several distinct model types; declaring each model type's conventions separately keeps individual models checkable and lets model kinds be reused across viewpoints.
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description

nodes.name: Module View
nodes.what: A view type documenting the system's units of implementation (modules) and their static relations — decomposition, uses, layering, generalization, data-model.
nodes.problem: Stakeholders doing construction, modification-impact analysis, and work assignment reason about code structure, not runtime; a dedicated static-structure view type keeps implementation-unit concerns separate from runtime concerns.
nodes.named_in: Documenting Software Architectures: Views and Beyond, 2nd ed. — Clements et al. (2010)

nodes.name: Rozanski–Woods Viewpoint Catalog
nodes.what: A catalog of seven viewpoints — context, functional, information, concurrency, development, deployment, operational — for describing information-system architectures.
nodes.problem: Architects reinvent view structure per project; a checklist-strength, reusable viewpoint catalog with defined models and pitfalls per viewpoint standardizes coverage. Granularity call: the catalog is one element, not seven — per-viewpoint entries would balloon the realm without adding bridge endpoints beyond what 4+1 and the Views-and-Beyond viewtypes already give.
nodes.named_in: Software Systems Architecture, 2nd ed. — Rozanski & Woods (2011)

nodes.name: Stakeholder Concern
nodes.what: An interest in the system relevant to one or more stakeholders, used to scope which viewpoints and views an architecture description must provide.
nodes.problem: Architecture descriptions must demonstrably address what matters to whom; naming concerns explicitly lets viewpoint selection be justified and concern coverage be audited.
nodes.named_in: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 — Architecture description
nodes.borderline: Concept-vs-construct call: included as a construct because ISO 42010 defines it normatively and viewpoints are specified by the concerns they frame; bridging value to design elements is low — bridge indirectly via quality attributes where applicable.

nodes.name: Anti-Corruption Layer
nodes.what: An isolating translation layer between two bounded contexts (typically new model and legacy/external system) that converts between the two models.
nodes.problem: Integrate with a system whose model you must not absorb; keeps the foreign model from leaking into and corrupting your own.
nodes.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

nodes.name: API Composition
nodes.what: A composer queries multiple services and joins their results in memory to answer a query that spans service-owned databases.
nodes.problem: Queries crossing database-per-service boundaries need an answer without shared storage; simple but limited by in-memory join cost.
nodes.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - API Composition - Richardson (living)

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.what: Single entry point that routes, composes, and adapts client requests to backend services, and absorbs cross-cutting edge concerns (auth, TLS, rate limits).
nodes.problem: Clients should not know service decomposition or make chatty cross-service calls; edge concerns should not be re-implemented per service.
nodes.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - API Gateway - Richardson (living)

nodes.name: Application Controller
nodes.what: A centralized component owns the application's screen navigation and action flow, deciding which domain logic and view follow each input.
nodes.problem: Wizard-like or state-dependent navigation duplicated across input controllers becomes inconsistent.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Application Switching
nodes.what: Splits the system into independent executables of which only one runs at a time, each fitting the memory budget alone.
nodes.problem: Total functionality exceeds memory; sequential exclusive programs trade concurrency for footprint.
nodes.named_in: Small Memory Software - Noble & Weir (2000)

nodes.name: Asynchronous Request-Reply
nodes.what: A client-facing request is accepted immediately with a status/result endpoint while backend processing completes asynchronously.
nodes.problem: Long-running backend work cannot hold client connections open; the reply channel is decoupled from the request.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Authoritative Server
nodes.what: One server owns the true game/simulation state; clients send inputs and locally predict, then reconcile against authoritative snapshots.
nodes.problem: Trusting clients invites cheating and divergence, but pure server authority feels laggy - prediction plus reconciliation resolves both.
nodes.named_in: Latency Compensating Methods in Client/Server In-game Protocol Design and Optimization - Bernier (2001)

nodes.name: Authorization (security pattern)
nodes.what: A system-level structure defining which subjects may perform which actions on which protected resources, enforced at guarded access points.
nodes.problem: Ad hoc permission checks scattered through a system are inconsistent and unauditable; the rights structure must be explicit.
nodes.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

nodes.name: Backends for Frontends
nodes.what: One purpose-built edge/API backend per frontend type (mobile, web, ...), each owned by the corresponding frontend team.
nodes.problem: A single general-purpose gateway becomes a contended, lowest-common-denominator bottleneck when client types have divergent needs.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Board Support Package
nodes.what: The packaging of all board-specific software - boot code, clock and pin configuration, device drivers, memory maps - into one named unit that adapts an OS or firmware stack to a particular hardware board.
nodes.problem: An OS or product firmware must run on many boards; isolating everything board-specific into a replaceable package makes 'support a new board' a bounded, well-understood unit of work.
nodes.named_in: Mastering Embedded Linux Programming, 3rd ed. - Simmonds (2021)

nodes.name: Bodyguard
nodes.what: Shares objects across address spaces without full RPC by attaching a guard that intercepts and validates operations on the shared object.
nodes.problem: Distributed object sharing needs protection against misbehaving remote clients without heavyweight middleware.
nodes.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 - das Neves & Garrido (1997)

nodes.name: Bounded Context
nodes.what: An explicit boundary within which a domain model and its ubiquitous language apply consistently; large systems are partitioned into several.
nodes.problem: One unified enterprise model fails at scale; explicit context boundaries prevent model corruption and define natural service/ownership seams.
nodes.named_in: Domain-Driven Design - Evans (2003)

nodes.name: Bulkhead (deployment isolation)
nodes.what: System capacity (instances, pools, clusters) is partitioned into isolated compartments per client, workload, or function so one compartment's failure cannot exhaust the rest.
nodes.problem: Shared capacity lets one misbehaving consumer or dependency sink the whole system; compartments cap the blast radius.
nodes.named_in: Release It! - Nygard (2007)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's bulkhead is the in-process resource-partitioning mechanism (pools, queues); this is the deployment/topology sense.

nodes.name: Canonical Data Model
nodes.what: An application-independent shared data model for the messages exchanged across an integration solution; every application translates only between its internal format and the canonical one.
nodes.problem: Translating directly between every pair of application formats needs O(N^2) translators and couples applications' formats to each other; a canonical hub format reduces this to 2N translations and decouples applications' data models enterprise-wide.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)
nodes.borderline: Data-governance flavored, but an established EIP structural pattern with clear bridge endpoints (message-translator, normalizer).

nodes.name: Chained Processors
nodes.what: Arranges multiple processors in a chain where a small always-on processor handles front-line work and wakes or feeds larger downstream processors only when needed.
nodes.problem: Running the big processor continuously wastes power; delegating vigil duty to a tiny processor cuts system energy dramatically.
nodes.named_in: Making Embedded Systems, 2nd ed. - White (2024)

nodes.name: Channel Adapter
nodes.what: A component that connects an application never built for messaging to the messaging system, translating between the application's API/data/database/UI surface and messages on a channel.
nodes.problem: Integration must reach packaged, legacy, or third-party applications that cannot be modified to speak messaging; an adapter at the boundary buys their participation at the cost of an extra mediation component per application.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Choreography
nodes.what: Multi-service workflows emerge from services publishing and reacting to each other's events, with no central coordinator.
nodes.problem: Avoid a coordination bottleneck and keep services autonomous; trades away a single place to see and control workflow state.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Choreography - Azure Architecture Center (living)

nodes.name: Client Proxy (remoting)
nodes.what: A local object presenting the remote component's interface inside the client process, forwarding invocations to the remoting machinery.
nodes.problem: Clients should program against ordinary local interfaces while calls actually cross the network.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Client Request Handler
nodes.what: Client-side middleware component that manages network resources, sends request messages and receives replies for requestors.
nodes.problem: Connection management, timeouts and transport details belong in one reusable client-side layer.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Client Session State
nodes.what: Session state is held on the client (cookies, hidden fields, client storage) and sent with each request; servers stay stateless.
nodes.problem: Server statelessness for scale-out and failover; trades bandwidth, security exposure, and size limits on session data.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Competing Consumers (system scale)
nodes.what: Multiple service instances concurrently consume from one shared channel, each message going to exactly one of them.
nodes.problem: Throughput and availability of message processing must scale by adding instances without coordination between them.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
nodes.borderline: Design realm carries competing-consumers (in-process form); this is the multi-instance system form - same-name-two-realms.

nodes.name: Competing Consumers (system topology)
nodes.what: Multiple independently deployed consumer instances pull from one shared message channel, so load spreads and any instance's failure is absorbed by the rest.
nodes.problem: Scale-out and resilience of asynchronous message processing across nodes without a dispatcher knowing the consumers.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's competing-consumers is the in-process worker-pool-on-queue mechanism; this entry is the multi-instance topology sense (per charter judgment call).

nodes.name: Control Bus
nodes.what: A separate messaging channel overlay used to send configuration, heartbeat, test, and monitoring traffic to every component of a distributed messaging solution, distinct from the application-data channels.
nodes.problem: A distributed integration solution spanning many machines must be administered and observed as one system; a dedicated control plane buys manageability without polluting or depending on the data plane it manages.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: CQRS
nodes.what: The system's write model (commands) and read model (queries) are separated into distinct models, often with distinct stores kept in sync asynchronously.
nodes.problem: Read and write workloads have divergent shapes and scale; one canonical model serves both poorly. Costs eventual consistency between models.
nodes.named_in: CQRS Documents - Young (2010); also CQRS - Fowler (bliki, 2011)

nodes.name: Crash-Only Software
nodes.what: A system is structured so its components have exactly one stop method (crash) and one start method (recover), making crash-restart the universal, well-tested recovery path.
nodes.problem: Separate clean-shutdown and crash-recovery code paths mean the rarely exercised one is broken when needed; designing for crash as the only stop makes recovery the routine path and enables microreboots of subcomponents.
nodes.named_in: Crash-Only Software - Candea & Fox (HotOS IX, 2003)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm's let-it-crash carries 'crash-only software' as an aka for the in-program supervisor/restart idiom; Candea-Fox's sense is a system-structure commitment (crash-only components, microrebootable architecture) and earns the architecture entry.

nodes.name: Data Bus (RTDP)
nodes.what: A system-wide shared bus abstraction through which components publish and read common data instead of holding pairwise links.
nodes.problem: N-squared point-to-point connections between subsystems are unmaintainable; a common backbone decouples producers from consumers.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Database per Service
nodes.what: Each service exclusively owns its persistent data; other services access it only through the service's API.
nodes.problem: Shared databases couple services at the schema level; private data enables independent evolution and technology choice, at the cost of cross-service queries/transactions.
nodes.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Database per Service - Richardson (living)

nodes.name: Database Session State
nodes.what: Session state is committed to shared persistent storage between requests, keyed by session, readable by any server instance.
nodes.problem: Session survival across server failures and free request routing; costs a database round-trip per request and cleanup of dead sessions.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Datatype Channel
nodes.what: The channel topology is organized so each channel carries messages of exactly one data type, letting receivers know a message's type from the channel it arrived on.
nodes.problem: Receivers must know how to interpret incoming messages without inspecting each one; dedicating channels per type buys implicit typing and simple receivers at the cost of channel proliferation and topology-wide naming discipline.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)
nodes.borderline: A channel-topology organizing convention rather than a mechanism or whole topology; kept with honest tag per the over-inclusion rule (parked upward by the Phase 1 EIP scout as a channel-topology design decision).

nodes.name: Demilitarized Zone
nodes.what: Externally reachable services are placed in a separate network segment between two firewall layers, isolating them from both the internet and the internal network.
nodes.problem: Public-facing servers are the most exposed components; segregating them means their compromise does not grant direct access to internal systems.
nodes.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

nodes.name: Distributed Hash Table
nodes.what: Nodes form a self-organizing overlay in which consistent-hashing-based routing locates the node responsible for any key in O(log n) hops.
nodes.problem: Decentralized lookup at scale must survive churn without any directory server.
nodes.named_in: Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications - Stoica et al. (2001)

nodes.name: Distributed Snapshot
nodes.what: Marker messages flow through a distributed system's channels so each node records a mutually consistent cut of global state without stopping the world.
nodes.problem: Consistent global checkpoints for recovery/exactly-once processing when no node can observe the whole system at one instant.
nodes.named_in: Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems - Chandy & Lamport (ACM TOCS, 1985)

nodes.name: Distributed Tracing
nodes.what: Every external request gets a trace id propagated through all service hops; per-hop spans are collected centrally to reconstruct the end-to-end path.
nodes.problem: In a request that crosses many services, latency and failure localization are impossible from per-service logs alone.
nodes.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Distributed Tracing - Richardson (living); canonical system: Dapper - Sigelman et al. (Google, 2010)
nodes.borderline: Observability infrastructure sits near operations; kept as it is a named cross-cutting system structure and the bridge endpoint for the design realm's correlation-id mechanisms.

nodes.name: Domain Model
nodes.what: Organizes domain logic as an interconnected object model where each object carries the data and behavior of one domain concept.
nodes.problem: Complex, rule-heavy business logic becomes unmanageable as procedures; an object model localizes each rule with its data.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Domain Object (POSA4)
nodes.what: Encapsulates each distinct unit of application functionality as a self-contained component behind an explicit interface, as the root partitioning move of a distributed design.
nodes.problem: Distributed systems need functional partitioning into cohesive, independently deployable units before any infrastructure decisions.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Dual-Core Lockstep
nodes.what: Two identical processor cores execute the same instruction stream cycle-aligned (one delayed a few cycles) while comparators check their outputs every cycle, signaling a fault on any divergence.
nodes.problem: Software-visible redundancy cannot catch transient hardware faults inside the CPU with low latency; cycle-level comparison of redundant cores detects them immediately and transparently to software, at the cost of doubled silicon.
nodes.named_in: Cortex-R5 and Cortex-R5F Technical Reference Manual - Arm (2011)
nodes.borderline: Hardware-adjacent: the structure lives in silicon, but it is a named system-architecture option that safety firmware is designed around (fault response, self-test hooks) and a bridge endpoint for error-detection design elements; distinct from the design realm's deterministic-lockstep (game networking).

nodes.name: Durable Subscriber
nodes.what: The messaging infrastructure persists a subscriber's subscription so that messages published while the subscriber is disconnected are saved and delivered when it reconnects.
nodes.problem: Publish-subscribe normally delivers only to currently connected subscribers; when a subscriber must miss nothing across downtime, the infrastructure - not the application - has to hold its messages, trading broker storage and cleanup obligations for completeness.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)
nodes.borderline: Endpoint-scoped QoS rather than a topology; kept architecture-level because the durability obligation lives in the messaging infrastructure, not in application code (parked upward by the Phase 1 EIP scout).

nodes.name: Event-Carried State Transfer
nodes.what: Events carry the full changed state so consumers maintain local replicas and need not call back to the source system.
nodes.problem: Decouple availability and latency of consumers from the source system; trades data duplication and eventual consistency for autonomy.
nodes.named_in: What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'? - Fowler (martinfowler.com, 2017)

nodes.name: Event Collaboration
nodes.what: Components collaborate by broadcasting events about what happened rather than requesting each other to act, each maintaining its own state from the stream.
nodes.problem: Request-based collaboration couples callers to responsibilities; event collaboration inverts dependencies at the cost of harder reasoning about flow.
nodes.named_in: Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev) - Fowler (2005)

nodes.name: Fault Containment Region
nodes.what: A set of components (typically a node computer) engineered so that the immediate consequences of an internal fault stay inside the region's boundary, which is defined and enforced architecturally.
nodes.problem: Without designated containment boundaries a single fault can corrupt arbitrary parts of a distributed system, defeating redundancy; partitioning the system into independent FCRs is the precondition for any fault-tolerance argument.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

nodes.name: Fault Observer
nodes.what: A system-wide component that collects fault reports from everywhere and publishes them to interested parties (operators, loggers, recovery agents).
nodes.problem: Fault information scattered across reporters never forms a coherent picture for diagnosis and response.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Fault-Tolerant Unit
nodes.what: A group of replica-deterministic fault containment regions that produce the same outputs so that the failure of a member is masked by the remaining replicas (duplex fail-silent or triplicated voting configurations).
nodes.problem: Individual nodes fail; grouping FCRs into an FTU lets the architecture deliver correct service despite the failure of any single member without involving the application.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

nodes.name: Federated Identity
nodes.what: Authentication is delegated to a separate identity provider that the application trusts, receiving identity claims/tokens instead of managing credentials itself.
nodes.problem: Per-application credential stores multiply attack surface and user friction; trusting an external identity authority centralizes authentication and enables single sign-on across systems.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (living)

nodes.name: Firewall
nodes.what: A barrier that restricts access to designated resources (typically processors, memory, and network connections); a specific realization of the security Limit Access tactic used to keep unsafe effects from propagating.
nodes.problem: Once part of a system misbehaves, unrestricted access lets the damage spread; a barrier confines it.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Five-Layer Architecture (RTDP)
nodes.what: A concrete whole-system layering template for real-time embedded applications (application, UI, communication, abstract OS, abstract hardware).
nodes.problem: Embedded systems need a standard portable stratification separating application concerns from OS and hardware dependencies.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Flux
nodes.what: App structure with a strict one-way cycle: views dispatch actions, a dispatcher routes them to stores, stores update and re-render views.
nodes.problem: Tame cascading, hard-to-trace two-way binding updates in complex UIs by forcing all state change through one auditable direction.
nodes.named_in: Flux: In-Depth Overview - Facebook (2014)

nodes.name: Front Controller
nodes.what: One handler receives every request for a web application, performing common processing and dispatching to per-request commands or handlers.
nodes.problem: Duplicating security, i18n and routing logic across per-page handlers is unmaintainable; centralize the request entry point.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Functional Redundancy
nodes.what: Provide redundant components that are diversely designed and implemented but must produce the same output for the same input.
nodes.problem: Common-mode failures defeat identical replicas because copies sharing an implementation fail together; diversity in the redundancy addresses systematic design faults, at higher development and verification cost.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm has n-version-programming (error-handling); Avizienis frames NVP explicitly as a fault-tolerant software architecture (versions + execution environment + adjudicator), which is this entry. Overlaps the RTDP Heterogeneous Redundancy pattern parked to the douglass/resilience scout - flag for merge-time dedup.

nodes.name: Gateway Aggregation
nodes.what: A gateway fans one client request out to multiple backend services and aggregates their results into a single response.
nodes.problem: Chatty client-to-many-services interaction over high-latency links must be collapsed at the system edge.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Gateway Offloading
nodes.what: Shared edge functionality (TLS termination, authentication, compression) is offloaded from services into the gateway.
nodes.problem: Duplicating edge concerns in every service wastes effort and spreads security-critical code.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Gateway Routing
nodes.what: A gateway routes requests to different backend services from a single endpoint based on request attributes.
nodes.problem: Clients should keep one stable address while backends split, move and re-version behind it.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Guaranteed Delivery
nodes.what: The messaging system persists every message to a local data store at each hop before acknowledging, and deletes it only after successful handoff to the next store, so messages survive crashes and outages end to end.
nodes.problem: Asynchronous integration is only trustworthy if a sent message cannot be lost while machines and networks fail; per-hop persistence buys the delivery guarantee at the cost of throughput and storage.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)
nodes.borderline: A quality-of-service guarantee of the messaging infrastructure rather than a topology; kept architecture-level because it mandates persistent-store structure at every hop of the system (parked upward by the Phase 1 EIP scout).

nodes.name: Half-Object plus Protocol (distribution structure)
nodes.what: Splits one logical object into coordinated halves in two address spaces with a private protocol keeping them consistent.
nodes.problem: An object needed with low latency on both sides of a distribution boundary can live wholly on neither.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)
nodes.borderline: Design realm carries half-object-plus-protocol (object-level mechanism); this is the distribution-structure reading - same-name-two-realms.

nodes.name: Half-Sync/Half-Async (system layering)
nodes.what: Layers a concurrent system into a synchronous service layer and an asynchronous event layer mediated by a queueing layer.
nodes.problem: Synchronous code is simpler but async I/O is more efficient; the layering lets each part of the system use the model that suits it.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2 - Schmidt et al. (2000)
nodes.borderline: Same name exists in the design realm (half-sync-half-async); POSA2 labels it an architectural pattern - cataloged in both realms per the same-name-two-realms rule.

nodes.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer (architectural layer)
nodes.what: A dedicated layer in the firmware stack that presents hardware-independent interfaces for all peripheral and processor access, so every layer above it is portable across boards and silicon.
nodes.problem: Direct register access scattered through application code welds the product to one chip; concentrating hardware knowledge in one boundary layer makes ports, test doubles, and vendor changes tractable.
nodes.named_in: Reusable Firmware Development: A Practical Approach to APIs, HALs and Drivers - Beningo (2017)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm catalogs hardware-abstraction-layer as an API-shape mechanism; this entry is the layer as a position in the system's layer stack (parked from Phase 1, admitted here).

nodes.name: Health Check API
nodes.what: Each service exposes an endpoint reporting its own liveness/readiness, polled by orchestrators and load balancers to route around unhealthy instances.
nodes.problem: Infrastructure must distinguish a live-but-degraded instance from a dead one to place traffic and restarts correctly; a self-reported health contract makes that decision mechanical.
nodes.named_in: Microservices Patterns - Richardson (2018), Health check API pattern

nodes.name: Health Endpoint Monitoring
nodes.what: Services expose endpoints reporting their own health; external agents (monitors, orchestrators, load balancers) probe them to route or restart.
nodes.problem: A process can be up yet unable to serve; standardized self-reported checks let infrastructure detect and react to partial failure.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Health Endpoint Monitoring - Azure Architecture Center (living)
nodes.borderline: Design realm carries heartbeat (in-process liveness); this is the service-topology contract - related but distinct.

nodes.name: Health Monitor (ARINC 653)
nodes.what: A standardized architectural function that detects and reports faults at process, partition, and module level and applies configured recovery actions (restart, stop, switch) per level, defined by configuration tables rather than application code.
nodes.problem: In a partitioned system, error handling must itself be partition-aware and criticality-aware; a system-level, table-driven monitor keeps fault escalation and recovery policy out of individual applications and under certification control.
nodes.named_in: ARINC 653 - Avionics Application Standard Software Interface - AEEC (living)

nodes.name: Hierarchical Control (RTDP)
nodes.what: Distributes control policy across a hierarchy in which upper controllers set goals/modes and lower controllers execute them locally.
nodes.problem: Centralizing all control logic does not scale and mixing policy with actuation entangles concerns.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Index Table
nodes.what: Maintains separate tables keyed by frequently queried fields over a data store that lacks native secondary indexes.
nodes.problem: Key-value and partitioned stores answer non-key queries only via full scans unless the application maintains its own indexes.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Intrusion Detection System
nodes.what: A dedicated component observes network traffic or host activity and flags (or blocks, as IPS) patterns indicating attack or misuse.
nodes.problem: Preventive controls fail silently; a separate observing component turns compromise attempts into detectable, alertable events.
nodes.named_in: An Intrusion-Detection Model - Denning (IEEE Trans. Software Engineering, 1987)

nodes.name: Invoker
nodes.what: Server-side middleware component that receives invocations, unmarshals them and dispatches to the target remote object's method.
nodes.problem: Servers need generic machinery mapping wire requests onto object operations.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Islands Architecture
nodes.what: Server-rendered pages contain isolated interactive islands that hydrate independently, leaving the rest static HTML.
nodes.problem: Hydrating a whole page for a few interactive widgets wastes bandwidth and startup time.
nodes.named_in: Islands Architecture - Jason Miller (2020)

nodes.name: Kernel-Bypass Networking
nodes.what: Restructures the I/O path so the application drives the NIC from user space via polled queues, bypassing the kernel network stack.
nodes.problem: Kernel crossings and interrupts dominate latency/throughput at high packet rates; moving the dataplane into the application removes them.
nodes.named_in: DPDK Programmer's Guide (dpdk.org)

nodes.name: Leader Election
nodes.what: Cooperating instances select exactly one of themselves as coordinator for a role, and re-elect when the leader fails.
nodes.problem: Some actions must be done by exactly one instance in a fleet of equals; election plus failure detection avoids both split-brain and a fixed single point of failure.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Leader Election - Azure Architecture Center (living)

nodes.name: Leaderless Replication
nodes.what: Clients (or coordinators) write to and read from multiple replicas directly, using read/write quorums, read repair, and hinted handoff instead of a leader.
nodes.problem: High write availability under node failure and partition without failover machinery; trades strict ordering for quorum-tunable consistency.
nodes.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

nodes.name: Log Aggregation
nodes.what: All services ship logs to a central searchable store rather than keeping them on individual hosts.
nodes.problem: Per-host logs are useless when instances are ephemeral and requests span services; central aggregation restores a single queryable operational record.
nodes.named_in: Microservices Patterns - Richardson (2018), Log aggregation pattern

nodes.name: MooN Voting Architecture
nodes.what: The safety-instrumented channel topologies named MooN in IEC 61508: N channels of which M must agree/demand for the safety function to act (1oo1, 1oo2, 2oo2, 2oo3, 1oo2D...), each with defined diagnostic and voting arrangements.
nodes.problem: Safe-failure and dangerous-failure probabilities pull channel topology in opposite directions (spurious trips vs missed demands); the MooN family names the standard trade-off points and the standard's SIL tables quantify them.
nodes.named_in: IEC 61508:2010 - Functional safety of E/E/PE safety-related systems - IEC (2010)

nodes.name: Maintenance Interface
nodes.what: A separate interface/channel dedicated to administration, diagnosis and maintenance, distinct from the application service interface.
nodes.problem: Mixing management traffic with application traffic obscures both and blocks maintenance exactly when the service path is congested or broken.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Master-Worker
nodes.what: A master component partitions work into independent tasks and dispatches them to a pool of identical worker components, then collects and combines their results.
nodes.problem: A large, largely-independent, throughput-bound workload must be spread across many workers with dynamic load balancing and without workers coordinating with one another; a master centralizes task hand-out and result collection.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders & Massingill (2004), Master/Worker pattern

nodes.name: Materialized View (architecture pattern)
nodes.what: Precomputed, query-shaped copies of data are generated and refreshed from source-of-truth stores to serve reads the source format handles poorly.
nodes.problem: Query shapes that would need expensive joins/scans against the write-optimized store; trades staleness and refresh machinery for read performance.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Materialized View - Azure Architecture Center (living)
nodes.borderline: The database-internal materialized view is a storage mechanism; kept here in its architecture-pattern sense (cross-store derived read models), per parked data-tier decision.

nodes.name: Message Broker
nodes.what: A central intermediary receives messages from all senders and routes (and often transforms) them to the appropriate receivers, so every application couples only to the hub.
nodes.problem: Point-to-point integration of N applications explodes into N^2 connections; a hub-and-spoke broker buys maintainable topology and central routing logic at the cost of a potential bottleneck and single point of failure. Distinct from POSA1 Broker: routes asynchronous messages rather than mediating remote invocations.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Message Endpoint
nodes.what: The component that connects an application to a messaging channel, encapsulating send/receive mechanics at the application boundary.
nodes.problem: Application code should not be written against raw messaging APIs throughout; the endpoint isolates the messaging boundary.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Message Router
nodes.what: A component that consumes messages from one channel and republishes them to different channels according to routing conditions.
nodes.problem: Senders should not need to know which consumer must handle each message; routing knowledge is centralized.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Messaging Bridge
nodes.what: A set of connected channel pairs (or a broker-to-broker connector) that replicates messages between two distinct messaging systems so each behaves as an extension of the other.
nodes.problem: Organizations end up with multiple messaging infrastructures (mergers, vendors, platforms) whose applications must still exchange messages; a bridge buys interoperation without migrating either side, at the cost of mapping between two messaging semantics.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Model-View-Controller
nodes.what: Decomposes an interactive application into a model holding core data and logic, views presenting it, and controllers handling user input, with a change-propagation mechanism keeping them consistent.
nodes.problem: User interfaces change far more often than the domain core and the same information needs multiple simultaneous presentations; separating model from presentation lets UIs be added or changed without touching the core. GoF ch.1 decomposes MVC into Observer, Composite, and Strategy - the design-realm bridge endpoints.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: Model-View-Intent
nodes.what: Structures the app as a reactive cycle: intents (user input streams) feed a model function producing state streams that the view renders.
nodes.problem: Expressing the whole UI as composed observable streams removes callback wiring and mutable view state.
nodes.named_in: Model-View-Intent - Cycle.js documentation (Staltz)

nodes.name: Model-View-Presenter
nodes.what: UI structure where a presenter mediates all interaction between a (possibly passive) view and the model, absorbing presentation logic.
nodes.problem: Make GUI logic testable and views thin by moving decision logic out of widgets into a mediating presenter.
nodes.named_in: MVP: Model-View-Presenter - Potel (Taligent, 1996)

nodes.name: Model-View-ViewModel
nodes.what: UI structure where a view binds declaratively (data binding) to a view-model exposing view-shaped state and commands over the model.
nodes.problem: Exploit data-binding frameworks so views need no imperative glue code and presentation state is testable without the UI toolkit.
nodes.named_in: Introduction to Model/View/ViewModel pattern - Gossman (Microsoft blog, 2005)

nodes.name: Monitor-Actuator
aka: actuation channel with independent monitoring channel
nodes.what: A two-channel structure separating the actuation channel from an independent monitoring channel that checks the actuator's physical effect against setpoints and forces a fail-safe state on divergence.
nodes.problem: A single channel that both acts and checks itself shares failure modes between the two duties; an independent monitor with its own sensing detects actuation-channel faults without doubling the actuation hardware.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Multi-Leader Replication
nodes.what: Several nodes accept writes concurrently and asynchronously replicate to each other, requiring conflict resolution.
nodes.problem: Accept writes in multiple datacenters or offline clients; trades single-writer simplicity for write availability plus conflict handling.
nodes.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

nodes.name: Object Synchronizer
nodes.what: Decouples object replicas' synchronization policy from their functionality, coordinating state updates between distributed replicas.
nodes.problem: Replica consistency strategies must be swappable without rewriting the replicated objects.
nodes.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 4 - Silva, Pereira & Marques (2000)

nodes.name: Page Controller
nodes.what: Each page or action of a web application has its own controller object handling its requests.
nodes.problem: Simple sites are clearer with one input path per page than with a central dispatcher.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Policy Decision Point / Policy Enforcement Point
nodes.what: Authorization is externalized: enforcement points embedded at resource boundaries defer every access decision to a central policy decision point that evaluates declarative policy.
nodes.problem: Authorization logic scattered through components is inconsistent and unauditable; separating decision from enforcement centralizes policy while keeping enforcement local to each resource.
nodes.named_in: eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) 3.0 - OASIS Standard (2013); terminology from IETF RFC 2753
nodes.borderline: Design realm holds reference-monitor (with PDP/PEP noted in its aka as the operational split); this entry catalogs the distributed authorization topology itself, the sense Phase 1's security scout parked upward.

nodes.name: Polyglot Persistence
nodes.what: A system deliberately uses multiple storage technologies, matching each data-management need to the store best suited for it.
nodes.problem: One database type fits neither graph, document, relational, and cache workloads all at once; trades operational diversity for per-need fit.
nodes.named_in: PolyglotPersistence - Fowler (bliki, 2011)

nodes.name: Preforked / Prethreaded Server
nodes.what: The server creates a pool of processes or threads at startup that take turns accepting and serving connections.
nodes.problem: Per-connection fork/create cost and unbounded concurrency are avoided by amortizing workers across connections.
nodes.named_in: UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1, 3rd ed. - Stevens, Fenner & Rudoff (2003)

nodes.name: Presentation-Abstraction-Control
nodes.what: Structures an interactive system as a hierarchy of cooperating agents, each with its own presentation, abstraction, and control facet, communicating only through the control facets.
nodes.problem: Interactive systems built from semi-autonomous subtasks (multiple tools, views, input modalities) need each agent independently developed and composed; full per-agent PAC triads buy composability at the cost of many small components and longer control paths.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: Presentation Model
nodes.what: A self-contained class holding all view state and behavior, which the view synchronizes with; the toolkit-independent predecessor of MVVM.
nodes.problem: Pull view state and logic out of widgets into a testable object when the toolkit lacks data binding.
nodes.named_in: Further Enterprise Application Architecture development - Fowler (eaaDev, 2004)

nodes.name: Primary-Replica Replication
nodes.what: One node accepts all writes and streams its change log to replicas, which serve reads and can be promoted on failure.
nodes.problem: Read scale-out and failover for a single-writer dataset while keeping a simple consistency story on the write path.
nodes.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

nodes.name: Privilege Separation
nodes.what: Splits a program into a small privileged monitor process and unprivileged worker processes that request privileged operations over a narrow channel.
nodes.problem: A compromise of the bulk of the code must not yield the process's privileges; the split confines them to a minimal auditable part.
nodes.named_in: Preventing Privilege Escalation - Provos, Friedl & Honeyman (2003)

nodes.name: Process Manager
nodes.what: A central component maintains the state of each multi-step process instance and determines, step by step, which processing unit to invoke next based on intermediate results.
nodes.problem: Multi-step message flows whose routing cannot be fixed at design time need central sequencing, state, and error handling; an orchestrator buys visibility and flexible flow control at the cost of a hub that all steps depend on. The structural alternative is itinerary-based routing (Routing Slip) or pure choreography.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Process Pairs
nodes.what: A primary process executes while a backup process on another node receives checkpoints and takes over transparently when the primary fails.
nodes.problem: Single-process services die with their host and lose in-flight state; a checkpointed backup converts host failure into a fast, state-preserving takeover.
nodes.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992); named earlier in Gray's 'Why Do Computers Stop' (1985)

nodes.name: Proxy-Based Firewall
nodes.what: A firewall that terminates connections and re-issues them via per-protocol proxies, inspecting traffic at application level.
nodes.problem: Packet-level rules cannot judge application-protocol content; proxying enables semantic filtering at the boundary.
nodes.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

nodes.name: Recursive Containment (RTDP)
nodes.what: Decomposes the system recursively into parts that are themselves structured like systems, to any needed depth.
nodes.problem: Very large systems need a uniform decomposition discipline so every level presents the same structural concepts.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Recursive Control
nodes.what: Structures a real-time control system as a recursive hierarchy in which every component pairs its functional part with a control part, uniformly at all levels.
nodes.problem: Startup, shutdown, failure and mode handling pervade control systems; making control structure recursive keeps it uniform and analyzable.
nodes.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 - Selic (1997)

nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.what: Splits a system into a base level doing the application work and a meta level holding a self-representation (metaobjects) whose modification changes the base level's behavior and structure at runtime.
nodes.problem: Systems that must change structure or behavior dynamically (type discovery, marshalling, adaptation) need change without editing and redeploying base code; an explicit meta level makes the software self-aware and modifiable at the price of complexity and opacity.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: Remote Facade
nodes.what: A coarse-grained facade over fine-grained objects provides the remote interface, bundling many small interactions into few large calls.
nodes.problem: Fine-grained object interfaces are unusable across a network; call granularity must change at the distribution boundary.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Replicated Component Group
nodes.what: Deploys a component as a coordinated group of replicas presented as one logical component, for availability or load distribution.
nodes.problem: A single component instance is a single point of failure and a throughput ceiling.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Replication
nodes.what: Provide multiple identical copies of a component so their results can be voted on or a copy can take over; effective against random hardware faults.
nodes.problem: Random hardware failures can silently corrupt a single component's behavior; pure replication offers no diversity, so it does not protect against design or implementation faults.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Reporting Database
nodes.what: A separate database, fed from the operational store, structured and indexed for reporting/analytics queries.
nodes.problem: Reporting workloads distort and degrade the operational schema and its performance; offloading isolates both.
nodes.named_in: ReportingDatabase - Fowler (bliki, 2004)

nodes.name: Requestor
nodes.what: Client-side middleware component that constructs and sends remote invocations on behalf of proxies, handling marshaling and result delivery.
nodes.problem: Invocation construction, marshaling and transport must be reusable machinery, not per-interface code.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Routing Slip
nodes.what: Each message carries its own list of processing steps; every step consumes its entry and forwards the message to the next step on the slip, so the route is decided once up front and no central router is consulted en route.
nodes.problem: Message flows that vary per message but are computable at entry need sequential routing without a central orchestration bottleneck; the attached itinerary buys decentralized flow at the cost of no mid-flight re-planning and harder flow visibility.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Safety Executive
nodes.what: A centralized component that tracks safety-relevant events and coordinates all shutdown, recovery, and fail-safe transitions for the system, separating safety policy from the functional channels it supervises.
nodes.problem: When safety measures are scattered across subsystems, complex shutdown sequences and cross-subsystem fault policy become inconsistent and unverifiable; centralizing them in one executive makes the safety logic auditable.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Saga
nodes.what: A multi-step business transaction implemented as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to semantically undo it on failure.
nodes.problem: Atomic distributed transactions (2PC) are unavailable or too coupling across services; sagas trade isolation for availability with explicit compensation.
nodes.named_in: Sagas - Garcia-Molina & Salem (SIGMOD 1987)

nodes.name: Sandbox
nodes.what: Isolate an instance of the system from the real world so it can be experimented on without permanent consequences, including virtualizing uncontrollable resources (system clock, memory, battery, network); stubs, mocks, and dependency injection are simple virtualization forms.
nodes.problem: Testing against real resources with real consequences is dangerous or impossible (e.g. waiting for a real time boundary); a consequence-free, controllable replica removes the constraint.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Scheduler Agent Supervisor
nodes.what: A scheduler drives distributed steps via agents while a supervisor tracks step state and triggers recovery or compensation for failed steps.
nodes.problem: Distributed workflows need built-in observation and self-healing when individual remote actions fail.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Secrets Management Service
nodes.what: Credentials, keys, and tokens are held in a dedicated hardened service that issues them to workloads at runtime under authentication, audit, and rotation policies.
nodes.problem: Secrets embedded in code, images, or config sprawl and leak; centralizing issuance gives one place for encryption at rest, access control, rotation, and audit.
nodes.named_in: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
nodes.borderline: Named primarily in living vendor/platform documentation rather than a catalog work; kept because the component category is established across independent platforms and was parked by Phase 1's security scout.

nodes.name: Self-Contained Component
nodes.what: Organizes code into components each owning its directory, exposing one header interface, with dependencies pointing only toward more fundamental components.
nodes.problem: Without enforced component boundaries and dependency direction, C codebases decay into cyclic tangles.
nodes.named_in: Fluent C - Preschern (2022)

nodes.name: Sequential Convoy
nodes.what: Related messages are grouped into convoys processed in order by a single consumer, while unrelated convoys proceed in parallel.
nodes.problem: Per-key ordering must survive in a competing-consumers world that otherwise destroys sequence.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Server Request Handler
nodes.what: Server-side middleware component that accepts connections, receives request messages and hands them to invokers, returning replies.
nodes.problem: Server transport concerns (demuxing, concurrency, buffering) need a dedicated reusable layer below dispatch.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4 - Buschmann, Henney & Schmidt (2007)

nodes.name: Server Session State
nodes.what: Session state is kept in the application server's memory (possibly serialized or replicated) between requests.
nodes.problem: Simplest handling of rich session data; costs sticky routing or replication and complicates failover and scale-out.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Service Layer
nodes.what: A layer of application services defines the system's available operations, coordinating domain logic, transactions and responses per operation.
nodes.problem: Multiple interface kinds (UI, API, batch) must share one authoritative boundary of application operations.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Service Registry
nodes.what: A continually-updated database of available service instances and their network locations, which instances register with on startup and which clients or routers query to discover where to send requests.
nodes.problem: In a dynamic deployment where instances come and go and change location, clients cannot hard-code endpoints; a registry holds the current authoritative map that service discovery uses to route requests.
nodes.named_in: Microservices Patterns - Richardson (2018), Service registry / Service discovery patterns

nodes.name: Sharding
nodes.what: A dataset is split by key across nodes (range or hash partitioning) so each shard is stored and served independently, with rebalancing and request routing.
nodes.problem: Data or write volume exceeds one node; partitioning scales linearly but introduces routing, rebalancing, hot spots, and cross-shard operations.
nodes.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

nodes.name: Single Sign-On
nodes.what: One authentication event with a trusted authority yields tokens/tickets accepted by many independent systems.
nodes.problem: Per-system logins multiply credentials and attack surface; centralizing authentication trades in a single trusted authority.
nodes.named_in: Core Security Patterns - Steel, Nagappan & Lai (2005)

nodes.name: Someone in Charge
nodes.what: For every fault-tolerance activity some identified component is in charge of seeing it through to completion.
nodes.problem: Recovery actions with no owner stall when the initiating component itself fails.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Strangler Fig
nodes.what: Incrementally build the new system around the edges of the old, intercepting and redirecting functionality until the legacy system is fully displaced.
nodes.problem: Big-bang rewrites fail; this gives continuously shippable migration with reversible steps and a shrinking legacy core.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Supervision Tree (OTP)
nodes.what: Workers are organized under a tree of supervisors whose only job is to monitor children and apply restart strategies (one-for-one, one-for-all, rest-for-one).
nodes.problem: Let-it-crash fault handling needs a system-wide structure that turns individual process failures into controlled restarts.
nodes.named_in: OTP Design Principles - Erlang/OTP System Documentation
nodes.borderline: Design realm carries supervisor (the restart mechanism); this is the whole-system supervision topology - same-name-two-realms.

nodes.name: Table Module
nodes.what: Organizes domain logic with one class per database table, each instance handling all rows of its table.
nodes.problem: A middle ground between transaction scripts and a full domain model that maps directly onto record-set infrastructure.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Template View
nodes.what: Renders web pages from static markup templates with embedded markers that are filled with dynamic content.
nodes.problem: Page structure should be editable as markup by non-programmers while dynamic data slots in cleanly.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: The Elm Architecture
nodes.what: App structured as an immutable model, a pure update function folding messages into the model, and a pure view function rendering it.
nodes.problem: Make whole-app state transitions pure, replayable, and exhaustively type-checked; the functional refinement of unidirectional data flow.
nodes.named_in: The Elm Architecture - Czaplicki (Official Elm Guide, living)

nodes.name: Thread-per-Connection Server
nodes.what: The server dedicates a freshly created process or thread to each accepted connection for its lifetime.
nodes.problem: Serving clients concurrently with straightforward sequential per-client code, at the cost of per-connection resource use.
nodes.named_in: UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1, 3rd ed. - Stevens, Fenner & Rudoff (2003)

nodes.name: Time and Space Partitioning
