nodes.what: An operating-system-enforced structure in which applications run in partitions with statically allocated memory regions (space) and fixed cyclic execution windows (time), so no partition can affect another's resources or timing.
nodes.problem: Hosting multiple applications of different criticality on one computer risks interference; enforced partitioning lets mixed-criticality software share hardware while preserving the independence that certification requires.
nodes.named_in: ARINC 653 - Avionics Application Standard Software Interface - AEEC (living)

nodes.name: Transaction Script
nodes.what: Organizes all domain logic as one procedure per business transaction, each handling its request from presentation to database.
nodes.problem: For simple logic, straight procedures are cheaper and clearer than an object model.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Transactional Outbox
nodes.what: Service writes outgoing messages into an outbox table within the local database transaction; a relay publishes them to the broker afterwards.
nodes.problem: Atomically update state and publish an event without distributed transactions across a database and a message broker.
nodes.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Transactional Outbox - Richardson (living)

nodes.name: Transform View
nodes.what: Renders output by programmatically transforming each domain data element into its presentation form.
nodes.problem: When output structure follows data structure, a transform is more testable and composable than a template.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Triple Modular Redundancy
nodes.what: Three identical channels compute in parallel and a voter forwards the majority result, masking any single channel failure without interruption of service.
nodes.problem: Fail-over redundancy has a detection-and-switch gap; majority voting removes the gap by masking the fault instantly, at the price of triple resources plus a voter that becomes the critical element.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Trusted Execution Environment
nodes.what: A hardware-isolated execution partition runs security-critical code and holds secrets, exposing only a narrow call interface to the untrusted rich OS beside it.
nodes.problem: Keys and critical logic cannot be protected by an OS that may itself be compromised; a hardware-enforced parallel world keeps them safe even under full OS compromise.
nodes.named_in: TEE System Architecture - GlobalPlatform (living specification)
nodes.borderline: Hardware-adjacent as charter notes, but the split into secure-world and normal-world software with a defined boundary is a software architecture structure, first-class for the corpus's embedded center of gravity.

nodes.name: Two-Phase Commit
nodes.what: A coordinator drives distributed atomic commit: participants first vote prepared, then all commit or all abort on the coordinator's decision.
nodes.problem: Atomicity across multiple resource managers; the price is blocking on coordinator failure and latency of two round trips.
nodes.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017); original treatment: Gray, Notes on Data Base Operating Systems (1978)

nodes.name: Two Step View
nodes.what: Renders pages in two stages: first a logical presentation independent of look, then a formatting stage applying the site appearance.
nodes.problem: A consistent site-wide look must be changeable in one place across many page types.
nodes.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Fowler (2002)

nodes.name: Units of Mitigation
nodes.what: Divides the system into the units within which errors are contained and recovery is performed - the granularity of restart and repair.
nodes.problem: Recovery scope must be decided architecturally: too large and everything restarts, too small and coordination explodes.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Valet Key
nodes.what: The application issues clients a restricted token granting direct, time-limited access to a specific resource or store, bypassing the application for data transfer.
nodes.problem: Proxying bulk data through the application wastes its capacity; scoped tokens grant safe direct access.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

nodes.name: Watchdog (architecture pattern)
nodes.what: A system-level supervision structure: an independent watchdog component (often on separate hardware with its own time base) receives liveness/sanity evidence from the supervised channels and initiates recovery or fail-safe shutdown when evidence stops or fails checks.
nodes.problem: A hung or corrupted system cannot rescue itself from within; placing the last-resort monitor outside the supervised computation, with an independent clock, keeps recovery credible under common-mode failure.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's watchdog is the timer mechanism and its kick discipline; Douglass's RTDP Watchdog Pattern is the system-level supervision structure cataloged here.

nodes.name: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform
nodes.what: The POSIX-based automotive reference architecture for high-performance ECUs: dynamically scheduled applications communicate via service-oriented ara::com middleware (SOME/IP) instead of the Classic platform's static signal routing.
nodes.problem: Autonomous-driving and connectivity functions need dynamic deployment, high compute, and update-over-the-air, which the statically configured Classic platform cannot provide; the Adaptive platform standardizes a service-oriented alternative alongside it.
nodes.named_in: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform - Explanation of Adaptive and Classic Platform Software Architectural Decisions - AUTOSAR (living)

nodes.name: AUTOSAR Layered Software Architecture
nodes.what: The automotive reference layering for ECU software: application layer above the RTE, above basic software split into services, ECU abstraction, and microcontroller abstraction (MCAL) layers, plus complex device drivers as a sanctioned bypass.
nodes.problem: Automotive software must be portable across ECUs and suppliers; a standardized layer stack with fixed interface contracts decouples application components from hardware and lets OEMs integrate multi-vendor code.
nodes.named_in: AUTOSAR Classic Platform - Layered Software Architecture - AUTOSAR (living)

nodes.name: Data Mesh
nodes.what: Analytical data architecture decentralized into domain-owned data products with self-serve platform and federated governance, instead of one central lake/warehouse.
nodes.problem: Central data teams become bottlenecks and lose domain context at scale; aligns data ownership with domain (bounded-context) boundaries.
nodes.named_in: How to Move Beyond a Monolithic Data Lake to a Distributed Data Mesh - Dehghani (martinfowler.com, 2019)
nodes.borderline: Organizational/socio-technical as much as structural; kept because it is an established named reference structure and a bridge endpoint for bounded-context-aligned data elements.

nodes.name: Domain-Specific Software Architecture
nodes.what: A reference structure specialized to one application domain (e.g. avionics, vehicle management) that fixes the component types, coordination model, and configuration rules that products in that domain instantiate.
nodes.problem: How to exploit deep domain regularities for reuse and generation across a product family, trading generality for the power to derive concrete systems (semi-)automatically from the architecture.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: Federated Avionics Architecture
nodes.what: The traditional avionics system structure in which each function runs on its own dedicated computer with private resources, integrated only through inter-box data buses.
nodes.problem: Physical separation gives inherent fault containment and simple per-box certification, at the cost of hardware proliferation; it is the named baseline against which IMA and partitioned architectures are defined.
nodes.named_in: DO-297 - Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) Development Guidance and Certification Considerations - RTCA (2005)
nodes.borderline: Named mostly as the contrast concept to IMA; kept because avionics sources name it as an architecture in its own right and dedicated-hardware design elements need a specific bridge endpoint.

nodes.name: HLA Federation
nodes.what: Independent simulators (federates) interoperate through a Run-Time Infrastructure under a federation object model and interface specification.
nodes.problem: Heterogeneous simulations must interoperate and be reused across federations without pairwise integration.
nodes.named_in: IEEE 1516-2010 - High Level Architecture (HLA)

nodes.name: Integrated Modular Avionics
nodes.what: A domain reference architecture in which multiple avionics functions, formerly on dedicated boxes, are hosted as partitioned applications on a shared set of common computing modules with standardized interfaces (ARINC 653 APEX) and defined supplier roles.
nodes.problem: Federated one-function-one-computer designs multiply size, weight, power, and spares; IMA consolidates functions onto shared platforms while preserving per-function independence through robust partitioning and incremental certification.
nodes.named_in: DO-297 - Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) Development Guidance and Certification Considerations - RTCA (2005)

nodes.name: Layered Game Engine Architecture
nodes.what: The canonical layering of a game engine runtime: platform independence layer, core systems, resource management, rendering/physics/audio, gameplay foundations, game-specific code.
nodes.problem: Game engines recur in structure; the reference layering keeps engine subsystems independent of game code and platform.
nodes.named_in: Game Engine Architecture, 4th ed. - Gregory (2026)

nodes.name: Multi-Pass Compiler Pipeline
nodes.what: The canonical decomposition of a compiler into sequential phases (lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, IR optimization, code generation) over shared intermediate representations.
nodes.problem: Language translation is intractable as one step; the phase structure isolates concerns and enables retargeting front and back ends.
nodes.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, 2nd ed. - Aho, Lam, Sethi & Ullman (2006)

nodes.name: Relational DBMS Reference Architecture
aka: query processor / transactional storage manager decomposition
nodes.what: The canonical decomposition of a DBMS into process manager, query processor (parser, rewriter, optimizer, executor), transactional storage manager, and shared utilities.
nodes.problem: Database engines recur in structure; the reference decomposition names the component roles every implementation fills.
nodes.named_in: Architecture of a Database System - Hellerstein, Stonebraker & Hamilton (2007)

nodes.name: Actor-Based Architecture
nodes.what: Organizes the whole system as actors that own their state and interact only via asynchronous messages processed run-to-completion from per-actor mailboxes.
nodes.problem: Shared-state concurrency does not scale in complexity; message-owned state removes locks and makes distribution and supervision natural.
nodes.named_in: A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence - Hewitt, Bishop & Steiger (1973)

nodes.name: Adaptive Object Model
nodes.what: Represents classes, attributes and rules as runtime data (metadata) interpreted by a generic engine, so the domain model is changed by users, not by code.
nodes.problem: Businesses whose types and rules change constantly cannot afford recompile-redeploy for every change.
nodes.named_in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 5 - Riehle, Tilman & Johnson (2006)

nodes.name: Batch Sequential
nodes.what: A degenerate data-flow organization in which each processing step runs to completion on the entire data set before passing the complete result to the next step.
nodes.problem: How to structure data processing when steps need the whole input (or when interactive incremental flow is unnecessary); loses the incremental delivery and concurrency of pipes-and-filters but simplifies each stage.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: Blackboard
nodes.what: Independent specialized knowledge sources cooperate by reading and writing partial solutions on a shared data structure (the blackboard) under a control component's opportunistic scheduling.
nodes.problem: For problems with no deterministic solution strategy (signal interpretation, recognition), no fixed control flow can be designed up front; opportunistic, data-driven cooperation of partial experts replaces a hardwired pipeline.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: Blockchain
nodes.what: A peer-to-peer system maintains a replicated append-only ledger of Merkle-chained blocks agreed by a consensus mechanism.
nodes.problem: Mutually distrusting parties need a tamper-evident shared history without a trusted central authority.
nodes.named_in: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System - Nakamoto (2008)

nodes.name: Broker
nodes.what: Structures a distributed system around an intermediary component that coordinates remote service invocations - locating servers, marshalling requests/replies, and reporting errors - so clients and servers stay decoupled from location and transport.
nodes.problem: Components of a distributed system should interact by service request without hardwiring host, transport, or wire format into every participant; the broker centralizes registration, lookup, and forwarding (CORBA/DCOM lineage). Distinct from EIP's Message Broker: this brokers request/reply remote invocations, not asynchronous message routing.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: C2
nodes.what: A layered, message-based style in which components communicate only through explicit connectors via asynchronous notifications (downward) and requests (upward), under a strict substrate-independence rule: a component may know services above it but nothing below.
nodes.problem: How to build flexible, distributable GUI-centric systems from reusable off-the-shelf components whose parts can be replaced or rewired at runtime; requires all interaction to be mediated, prohibiting direct component links and shared address-space assumptions.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Channel Architecture
nodes.what: Organizing the system as one or more end-to-end channels, each a sequential chain of data transformations from sensing to actuation, so that redundancy and safety measures can be applied per-channel.
nodes.problem: Safety and reliability engineering needs a unit to replicate, diversify, or protect; structuring the system as identifiable channels creates that unit and localizes data flow for analysis.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Douglass (2002)

nodes.name: Clean Architecture
nodes.what: Concentric layers (entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks) with all source dependencies pointing inward toward policy.
nodes.problem: Keep business rules independent of frameworks, UI, and databases so they outlive delivery mechanisms; generalizes hexagonal/onion into one dependency discipline.
nodes.named_in: Clean Architecture - Martin (2017)

nodes.name: Client-Server
nodes.what: Server components provide services at known locations while client components initiate requests for them, typically via remote procedure call or request/response protocols, with the server unaware of client identities in advance.
nodes.problem: How to share centralized resources and services among many distributed consumers; centralizes state and administration at the cost of a scalability and availability bottleneck at the server.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: Code-on-Demand
nodes.what: A mobile-code style in which a client that has the data and processing resources requests executable code (know-how) from a remote server and runs it locally, as with scripts delivered to a browser.
nodes.problem: How to extend a deployed client's functionality without redeployment, moving computation to where the data and interaction are; introduces trust, versioning, and sandboxing obligations on the receiving site.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Component-Based Architecture
nodes.what: Structures the whole system as replaceable components with explicit provided/required interfaces (ROOM: capsules with ports and protocols).
nodes.problem: Monolithic structure prevents unit substitution, reuse and independent development of system parts.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Object-Oriented Modeling - Selic, Gullekson & Ward (1994)

nodes.name: Data-Parallel Architecture
nodes.what: The same program is applied concurrently across partitions of a large regular data set, each unit of execution running identical code over its own data slice (SPMD / geometric decomposition).
nodes.problem: A computation over a large regular data structure must exploit many processing units; partitioning the data and running one program across all partitions converts data size into parallelism while keeping the code single-sourced.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Parallel Programming - Mattson, Sanders & Massingill (2004), SPMD & Geometric Decomposition patterns

nodes.name: Dataflow Architecture
nodes.what: Organizes the whole system around the availability and movement of data through transforming nodes rather than control flow.
nodes.problem: Transformation-dominated systems are clearer and more parallelizable when structure follows the data path.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)

nodes.name: Distributed Commit Log
nodes.what: A partitioned, replicated append-only log serves as the system's ordering and integration backbone; producers append, consumers replay at their own pace.
nodes.problem: Give many decoupled systems one durable, ordered, replayable record of what happened, unifying messaging, replication, and stream processing.
nodes.named_in: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction - Kreps (LinkedIn Engineering, 2013)

nodes.name: Distributed Objects
nodes.what: System functionality is partitioned into objects whose methods can be invoked across process and machine boundaries through proxies and an object request broker, preserving OO interfaces over the network.
nodes.problem: How to extend object-oriented organization to distributed systems while hiding location and transport; masks but does not remove the latency, partial-failure, and concurrency differences between local and remote calls.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Distributed Processes
nodes.what: The system is a set of independent processes, typically on multiple processors, interacting by message passing under some topological organization (ring, star, arbitrary graph).
nodes.problem: How to structure systems whose components are inherently concurrent and physically distributed; the architecture must state both the topology and the communication protocol because no shared state exists.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: Event-Based Implicit Invocation
nodes.what: Components announce (broadcast) events instead of invoking procedures directly; the system implicitly invokes every procedure registered as interested in that event.
nodes.problem: How to integrate components without hard-wiring caller-callee identities; announcers gain strong decoupling but surrender control over which handlers run, in what order, and whether they run at all.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: Event-Driven Architecture
nodes.what: The system is organized around the production, detection, and asynchronous reaction to events, with components emitting and subscribing to event notifications through a mediator or broker rather than calling each other directly.
nodes.problem: Components must stay decoupled and independently scalable while reacting to state changes whose timing and origin they do not control; routing interactions as asynchronous events removes direct dependencies and lets producers and consumers evolve and scale separately.
nodes.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020), Event-Driven Architecture Style

nodes.name: Event Sourcing (architecture style)
aka: event store as system of record
nodes.what: System-level persistence strategy where the event log is the source of truth for whole services and downstream projections/read models are derived from it.
nodes.problem: Full audit/history, temporal queries, and rebuildable projections across a system; couples consumers to event schemas over time.
nodes.named_in: Event Sourcing - Fowler (eaaDev, 2005)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's event-sourcing entry is the in-component persist-as-events mechanism; this entry is the system-level style built on it.

nodes.name: Event-Triggered Architecture
nodes.what: System-level organization in which communication and task activation are initiated by the occurrence of significant events (interrupts, message arrivals) rather than by a global clock; Kopetz names it as the counterpoint to time-triggered control.
nodes.problem: Sporadic, low-rate, or unpredictable stimuli waste bandwidth and CPU under static time-triggered schedules; event triggering gives flexibility and responsiveness at the cost of harder worst-case analysis and possible event showers.
nodes.named_in: Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications - Kopetz & Steiner (2022)

nodes.name: File Transfer
nodes.what: Applications integrate by one producing files of shared data and others consuming them, with an agreed format and transfer/processing cadence.
nodes.problem: Independently built applications must share information with maximum decoupling and no shared infrastructure; files buy universality and loose coupling at the cost of staleness, format-agreement effort, and no transactional coordination.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Function-Queue-Scheduling Architecture
nodes.what: A system structure in which interrupts enqueue pointers to task functions and the main loop dequeues and runs them to completion, allowing priority ordering of the queue without a preemptive kernel.
nodes.problem: Round-robin loops cannot prioritize urgent work and full RTOS preemption may be overkill; queueing work as functions gives priority control and bounded response with cooperative simplicity.
nodes.named_in: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)

nodes.name: Hexagonal Architecture
nodes.what: Application core exposes technology-neutral ports; adapters translate between each external actor (UI, DB, tests, other systems) and the ports.
nodes.problem: Let the application be driven equally by users, programs, or tests, and keep infrastructure swappable; kills business-logic leakage into UI and DB code.
nodes.named_in: Hexagonal Architecture - Cockburn (alistair.cockburn.us, 2005)

nodes.name: Interpreter (Architectural Style)
nodes.what: The system is organized as a virtual machine: an interpretation engine, the pseudo-program it executes, and the engine's and program's state, closing the gap between the execution platform and the desired semantics.
nodes.problem: How to execute programs for a machine that does not exist in hardware, or to make behavior data-driven and portable; the extra level of interpretation trades performance for flexibility.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)
nodes.borderline: Same NAME as the design-realm GoF 'interpreter' pattern - the architectural style structures a whole system as a virtual machine; both kept, id suffixed.

nodes.name: Kappa Architecture
nodes.what: Everything is a stream: a single stream-processing pipeline over a replayable log serves both real-time and reprocessing needs, eliminating the separate batch layer.
nodes.problem: Avoid maintaining dual batch/speed code paths of the lambda architecture; reprocessing is replaying the log through the same pipeline.
nodes.named_in: Questioning the Lambda Architecture - Kreps (O'Reilly Radar, 2014)

nodes.name: Lambda Architecture
nodes.what: Data system split into a batch layer (immutable master dataset, recomputed views), a speed layer (incremental real-time views), and a serving layer merging both.
nodes.problem: Combine the accuracy/robustness of batch recomputation with low-latency access to recent data.
nodes.named_in: Big Data: Principles and best practices of scalable realtime data systems - Marz & Warren (2015)

nodes.name: Layers
nodes.what: Structures a whole system as a hierarchy of abstraction levels in which each layer offers services to the layer above and uses only the layer(s) below.
nodes.problem: A large system mixes concerns at very different abstraction levels (hardware access, mechanism, policy, UI); one-way layered dependencies buy exchangeability, portability, and independent evolution at the cost of indirection and pass-through overhead.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

nodes.name: LMAX Architecture
aka: business logic processor with input/output disruptors
nodes.what: A single-threaded in-memory business logic processor is fed and drained by ring-buffer (Disruptor) pipelines, with event sourcing for durability.
nodes.problem: Extreme-throughput low-latency processing is defeated by locks and database round-trips; single-writer in-memory design removes both.
nodes.named_in: The LMAX Architecture - Martin Fowler (2011)

nodes.name: Main Program and Subroutines
nodes.what: A single main program drives the system by calling a hierarchy of subroutines, with control returning up the call tree after each call.
nodes.problem: How to organize a computation-dominant system when the decomposition follows functional refinement; correctness of a component depends only on the subroutines it calls, but data flow through shared parameters/globals resists change.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: MapReduce
nodes.what: Batch computation structured as a parallel map phase over partitioned input, a shuffle, and a reduce phase, scheduled across a cluster by a framework.
nodes.problem: Run large-scale data processing on commodity clusters while the framework handles partitioning, scheduling, and fault recovery.
nodes.named_in: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters - Dean & Ghemawat (OSDI 2004)

nodes.name: Message Bus
nodes.what: A shared messaging backbone - common channels, a common data model, and a common command set - that all applications plug into to interoperate, joining or leaving without affecting the others.
nodes.problem: An enterprise of separate applications must work as one system while letting individual systems be added, removed, or replaced; a common bus buys plug-in interoperability at the cost of enterprise-wide agreement on the shared contract.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Messaging
nodes.what: Applications integrate by exchanging discrete asynchronous messages over channels provided by a messaging infrastructure, decoupling senders from receivers in time and availability.
nodes.problem: Integration must be frequent, immediate-enough, and reliable between systems that cannot assume each other's availability; asynchronous channels buy decoupling and reliability at the cost of eventual consistency and harder end-to-end reasoning.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Micro Frontends
nodes.what: Frontend decomposed into independently built and deployed UI fragments owned end-to-end by the teams owning the corresponding backend services.
nodes.problem: Extend microservice-style team autonomy through the UI layer instead of funneling all teams through one frontend monolith.
nodes.named_in: Micro Frontends - Jackson (martinfowler.com, 2019)

nodes.name: Microkernel
nodes.what: Separates a minimal functional core (fundamental services, communication, extension management) from extended functionality delivered as internal/external servers or plug-ins loaded onto the core.
nodes.problem: A platform or product family must adapt to changing requirements and support many variants; keeping the core minimal and pushing features into replaceable extensions buys portability and product-line flexibility at the cost of extra indirection through the core.
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: Microservices
nodes.what: Suite of small, independently deployable services, each owning its data, communicating over lightweight network mechanisms, organized around business capabilities.
nodes.problem: Independent deployability, team autonomy, and heterogeneous technology per service; trades operational and distribution complexity for decoupling.
nodes.named_in: Microservices - Lewis & Fowler (martinfowler.com, 2014)

nodes.name: Mobile Agent
nodes.what: A mobile-code style in which an entire computational unit - code, execution state, and data - migrates itself from site to site, resuming execution at each destination.
nodes.problem: How to sustain a long-lived computation across intermittently connected or resource-shifting hosts; state capture, migration transparency, and security of both agent and host dominate the design.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Modular Monolith
nodes.what: Single deployable unit whose interior is decomposed into strictly encapsulated modules with enforced boundaries.
nodes.problem: Keep monolith deployment simplicity while getting service-like boundary discipline; a stepping stone to (or alternative to) microservices.
nodes.named_in: Monolith to Microservices - Newman (2019)

nodes.name: Monolithic Architecture
nodes.what: The whole application is built and deployed as a single deployable unit.
nodes.problem: Simplicity of development, testing, and deployment for one team/one unit; the named baseline against which service decomposition trades off.
nodes.named_in: microservices.io: Pattern - Monolithic Architecture - Richardson (living)

nodes.name: N-Tier Client-Server
nodes.what: Client-server generalized to a chain of tiers (e.g. presentation, business logic, data management), each acting as server to the tier before it and client of the tier after it, deployable on separate machines.
nodes.problem: How to scale, secure, and independently evolve the presentation, application, and data concerns of an enterprise system; each added tier buys isolation and scaling at the price of latency and deployment complexity.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Object-Oriented Organization
nodes.what: The system is organized as a collection of abstract-data-type instances (objects) that hide their representations and interact by invoking each other's operations.
nodes.problem: How to localize the effects of representation change; encapsulation lets internals evolve freely, at the cost that every caller must know the identity of the object it invokes.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: Peer-to-Peer
nodes.what: Networked components (peers) act as both clients and servers of one another, discovering and exchanging services directly without a distinguished central server.
nodes.problem: How to achieve scalability, resilience, and resource pooling when no node can be trusted or provisioned as a permanent center; pays for decentralization with discovery, consistency, and trust problems.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Pipes and Filters
nodes.what: Organizes a processing system as a chain of independent filter components connected by pipes that carry a data stream from source to sink.
nodes.problem: A whole processing task must be decomposable, recombination-friendly, and incrementally streamable; independent filters buy reuse, reordering, and parallel deployment at the cost of shared-format agreement and per-stage transfer overhead. EIP restates the same macro structure at inter-application integration scale (steps joined by message channels).
nodes.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann et al (1996)

nodes.name: Process Control (Feedback Control Loop)
nodes.what: The system is organized around a control loop: a controller reads process variables from sensors, compares them to set points, and adjusts manipulated variables to keep a physical or continuing process on target.
nodes.problem: How to maintain specified properties of an ongoing process in the face of external disturbances that cannot be predicted, using open- vs closed-loop and feedback vs feedforward variants; the architecture must make the loop, not the call graph, the primary structure.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)

nodes.name: Protocol Layering
nodes.what: Structures communication software as a stack of protocol layers, each providing services to the layer above and encapsulating its PDU inside the layer below.
nodes.problem: Communication concerns (framing, routing, reliability, sessions) must evolve independently; strict layering with encapsulation isolates them.
nodes.named_in: Computer Networks, 6th ed. - Tanenbaum, Feamster & Wetherall (2021)

nodes.name: Publish-Subscribe (Architectural Style)
nodes.what: Publishers emit messages classified by topic or content to an intermediary event service, which delivers them to all components that have subscribed, so producers and consumers never address each other.
nodes.problem: How to decouple many-to-many information flow in space, time, and synchronization across a distributed system; delivery ordering, reliability, and subscription management move into the connector.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)
nodes.borderline: Same NAME as the design realm's in-process publish-subscribe (observer / event-aggregator / publish-subscribe-channel); this is the system-scale style with a distributed event service - both kept, id suffixed.

nodes.name: Remote Evaluation
nodes.what: A mobile-code style in which a component that has the know-how sends code to a remote site that has the resources and data, where it executes and returns results.
nodes.problem: How to bring computation to remote data or special resources instead of shipping bulk data to the computation; the receiving site must safely execute foreign code and account for its resource use.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Remote Procedure Invocation
nodes.what: Applications integrate by exposing procedures/services that other applications invoke synchronously over the network to exchange data and trigger behavior.
nodes.problem: Integration needs behavior sharing and encapsulation, not just data sharing; synchronous invocation buys encapsulated interfaces at the cost of tight temporal coupling and distributed-failure fragility. The design realm's remote-procedure-call element is the invocation mechanism; this entry is the system-integration style built on it.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Repository (Shared Data) Style
nodes.what: A central data structure represents the system state while a collection of independent components operate on it, coordinating only through the shared store.
nodes.problem: How to let many computations cooperate on a large, evolving body of data without direct coupling; the choice of who triggers whom (transactions vs. store state) splits the style into database and blackboard variants.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)
nodes.borderline: Same NAME as the design-realm 'repository' (Fowler data-access pattern) - different mechanism, both kept per the same-name-two-realms rule; id suffixed.

nodes.name: REST (Representational State Transfer)
nodes.what: A hybrid network-based style constraining client-server interaction to be stateless, cacheable, layered, and mediated by a uniform interface over resources identified by URIs and manipulated via exchanged representations, optionally extended by code-on-demand.
nodes.problem: How to make an Internet-scale hypermedia system evolvable, scalable, and visible to intermediaries; the constraints trade per-interaction efficiency (self-descriptive messages, statelessness) for anarchic scalability and independent deployment of components.
nodes.named_in: Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures - Fielding (2000)

nodes.name: RTOS-Based Architecture
nodes.what: A whole-system structure in which the application is decomposed into prioritized, preemptively scheduled RTOS tasks communicating through kernel objects (queues, semaphores, events), with response times set by priority rather than loop position.
nodes.problem: When response requirements differ by orders of magnitude across activities, cooperative loops cannot bound latency for the urgent ones; a preemptive kernel decouples each activity's worst-case response from the rest of the system.
nodes.named_in: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)

nodes.name: Rule-Based System
nodes.what: An interpreter specialization in which a rule engine (inference/interpretation engine) selects and fires condition-action rules from a knowledge base against working memory.
nodes.problem: How to keep volatile domain logic out of code so domain experts can evolve behavior as rules; control flow becomes emergent from rule selection rather than explicit.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

nodes.name: SEDA (Staged Event-Driven Architecture)
nodes.what: Service structured as a network of event-driven stages connected by explicit queues, each stage with its own thread pool and admission control.
nodes.problem: Well-conditioned behavior under massive load: per-stage queues give backpressure points and prevent overcommit that thread-per-request designs suffer.
nodes.named_in: SEDA: An Architecture for Well-Conditioned, Scalable Internet Services - Welsh, Culler & Brewer (SOSP 2001)

nodes.name: Sense-Compute-Control
nodes.what: An embedded-systems organization structured as a repeating loop of sensor reading, computation over the sensed values plus internal state, and actuator commands controlling the environment.
nodes.problem: How to structure reactive embedded software whose primary job is continuous interaction with physical hardware; keeps timing and I/O concerns explicit at the top level rather than buried in a call hierarchy.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

nodes.name: Service-Based Architecture
nodes.what: Small number of coarse-grained, separately deployed domain services sharing a single database, typically fronted by one UI.
nodes.problem: Pragmatic middle ground between monolith and microservices: partial independent deployability without distributed-data complexity.
nodes.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

nodes.name: Service-Oriented Architecture
nodes.what: Enterprise organized as coarse-grained reusable business/enterprise services coordinated through a mediating integration layer (often an ESB/orchestrator).
nodes.problem: Enterprise-wide reuse of business functions across applications; centralizes integration and workflow at the cost of coupling to the mediator.
nodes.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

nodes.name: Shared Database
nodes.what: Multiple applications integrate by reading and writing the same database schema, making one store the single point of data agreement.
nodes.problem: Applications need consistent, immediately visible shared data; a common schema buys freshness and one source of truth at the cost of schema-coupling every application together and contention on the shared store. Distinct from Blackboard: an integration data store, not opportunistic problem-solving control.
nodes.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

nodes.name: Shared-Nothing Architecture
nodes.what: Nodes own disjoint partitions of data and memory and coordinate only by messages; no shared disk or shared memory.
nodes.problem: Horizontal scalability without contention on shared resources; each node scales independently, at the price of cross-partition coordination.
nodes.named_in: The Case for Shared Nothing - Stonebraker (1986)

nodes.name: Space-Based Architecture
nodes.what: Processing units with replicated in-memory data grids, synchronized asynchronously to persistent storage, so the database is out of the request path.
nodes.problem: Extreme/variable concurrency where the database is the bottleneck; achieves elastic scale by removing the central data store from the hot path.
nodes.named_in: Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Richards & Ford (2020)

nodes.name: State Transition System (Architectural Organization)
nodes.what: A whole reactive system is organized as a set of states plus named transitions that move the system between them, making the state machine the top-level structure rather than an internal mechanism.
nodes.problem: How to give reactive/real-time systems an analyzable top-level structure whose behavior can be enumerated and verified; differs from an in-component FSM by governing system organization, not one module's logic.
nodes.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)
nodes.borderline: Names the same idea as the design-realm finite state machine at a different altitude; kept per same-name-two-realms rule as the system-level organization, prime Phase 3b bridge target for the design-realm FSM cluster.

nodes.name: Streaming Dataflow Architecture
nodes.what: Structures data processing as a long-running dataflow graph over unbounded streams with windowing, watermarks and triggers.
nodes.problem: Unbounded, out-of-order data cannot be handled by batch topologies; the streaming model trades off correctness, latency and cost explicitly.
nodes.named_in: The Dataflow Model - Akidau et al. (2015)

nodes.name: Subsumption Architecture
nodes.what: Layers of behavior-producing modules run concurrently, with higher layers subsuming (suppressing/overriding) the outputs of lower ones instead of a central planner.
nodes.problem: Robot control needs robust real-time reaction without a monolithic sense-plan-act pipeline; layered competence levels degrade gracefully and are incrementally buildable.
nodes.named_in: A Robust Layered Control System for a Mobile Robot - Brooks (IEEE J. Robotics and Automation, 1986)

nodes.name: Superloop Architecture
nodes.what: A whole-system structure with no operating system: one endless main loop polls and services every task in turn, optionally with interrupts as the foreground layer feeding flags/buffers to the background loop.
nodes.problem: Small systems cannot afford an RTOS's footprint and complexity; a single statically ordered loop gives minimal overhead and full determinism of structure, at the cost of coarse timing control and poor scalability.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm's super-loop is the loop mechanism itself; sources (Pont SUPER LOOP, Simon's Round-Robin in his 'Survey of Software Architectures' chapter) also treat it as the system-architecture choice against RTOS-based structure - that architecture sense is this entry.

nodes.name: Time-Triggered Architecture
nodes.what: System-level organization in which all communication and computation are driven by the progression of a fault-tolerant global time base, with statically planned activation instants known a priori at all nodes.
nodes.problem: Distributed hard real-time systems need temporal predictability, composability, and fault isolation; event-driven activation makes worst-case behavior and certification arguments hard, while a global static schedule makes temporal behavior verifiable by construction.
nodes.named_in: The Time-Triggered Architecture - Kopetz & Bauer (2003)

nodes.name: Virtual Machine (architectural style)
nodes.what: Builds the system atop an abstract machine whose instruction set is interpreted, decoupling applications from the physical platform.
nodes.problem: Portability and dynamic behavior require executing programs against a stable simulated machine rather than the real one.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)
nodes.borderline: Design realm carries bytecode-virtual-machine (the in-program engine); this is the system-organization style.

nodes.name: Zero Trust Architecture
nodes.what: A security architecture in which no implicit trust is granted by network location; every access to a resource is individually authenticated and authorized per session via policy decision/enforcement points.
nodes.problem: Perimeter-based models grant broad trust once inside the network, so a single breach yields lateral movement; moving enforcement to each resource access removes the trusted interior.
nodes.named_in: Zero Trust Architecture - Rose, Borchert, Mitchell, Connelly (NIST SP 800-207, 2020)

nodes.name: Abort
nodes.what: If an operation is determined to be unsafe, terminate it before it causes damage — the conceptually simplest way to make a system fail safely.
nodes.problem: Continuing a hazardous operation converts a detected unsafe state into an accident; stopping is often the safest available response.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Abstract Common Services
nodes.what: Where elements provide similar services, factor the similarity into a single more general/abstract service used by all, hiding the specifics of the variants.
nodes.problem: Duplicate similar services multiply both modification cost (each copy changes) and integration surface; one abstraction localizes both.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Abstract Data Sources
nodes.what: Abstract the interfaces to a program's input data so test data can be substituted easily — e.g. repointing the system from a production customer database to test databases or data files without changing functional code.
nodes.problem: Tests need controlled input data; hard-wired data sources force testing against uncontrollable production data.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Adhere to Standards
nodes.what: Conform to published interface, protocol, and data standards so that elements built independently can interoperate with less adaptation.
nodes.problem: Idiosyncratic interfaces force per-pair integration work; standardization lets the ecosystem amortize it.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Aggregate
nodes.what: Provide the ability to aggregate lower-level objects into a group so an operation applies to the whole group, e.g. selecting all slide objects and setting one font size.
nodes.problem: Repeating the same operation across many objects is tedious and error-prone for users.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Analytic Redundancy
nodes.what: Provide redundant components that are diverse not only internally but also in their inputs and outputs (e.g. computing aircraft altitude by barometric pressure, radar, and geometry), with a sophisticated blending/voting mechanism.
nodes.problem: Specification errors defeat functionally redundant components built to the same specification; independent requirement specifications and diverse input sources tolerate them, and help when some inputs are intermittently unavailable.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Audit
nodes.what: Record user and system actions and their effects so an attacker's actions can be traced and identified, supporting prosecution and improved future defenses.
nodes.problem: After a successful attack, reconstruction of what happened and by whom is impossible without a maintained record.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Authenticate Actors
nodes.what: Ensure an actor actually is who or what it claims to be, via passwords, one-time passwords, digital certificates, two-factor authentication, biometrics, or CAPTCHA challenges, possibly with periodic re-authentication.
nodes.problem: Identifiers can be claimed by anyone; proof of identity must back them before granting access.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Authorize Actors
nodes.what: Ensure an authenticated actor has the rights to access and modify data or services, via access control mechanisms assigned per actor, actor class, or role.
nodes.problem: Authenticated identity alone says nothing about what the actor may do; permissions must be checked per resource and operation.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Bound Execution Times
nodes.what: Place a limit on how much execution time is used to respond to an event — e.g. bounding iteration counts in data-dependent iterative algorithms — trading computational accuracy for bounded latency.
nodes.problem: Unbounded computations make response time unpredictable; often paired with Manage Sampling Rate, and requires assessing whether the less-accurate result is good enough.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Bound Queue Sizes
nodes.what: Control the maximum number of queued arrivals, and thereby the resources used to process them, with an explicit policy for what happens when queues overflow.
nodes.problem: Unbounded queues consume unbounded resources and hide overload; bounding them forces a deliberate overflow/loss policy, usually paired with Limit Event Response.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Cancel
nodes.what: Support user-issued cancellation: a listener not blocked by the operation being cancelled, termination of the activity, release of its resources, and notification of collaborating components so they act appropriately.
nodes.problem: Users must be able to stop an in-progress operation; naive designs block the cancel path behind the very operation to be cancelled and leak its resources.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Change Credential Settings
nodes.what: Force users to change default security settings and credentials on delivered systems, and require periodic password changes.
nodes.problem: Publicly known default credentials and stale passwords give attackers ready-made entry.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Comparison
nodes.what: Detect potentially unsafe states by comparing the outputs of redundant components and flagging divergence.
nodes.problem: A single component cannot detect its own erroneous output; comparison against redundant peers exposes it. Detection counterpart of the availability Voting tactic (which also chooses a result).
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Condition Monitoring
nodes.what: Check conditions in a process or device, or validate assumptions made during design (e.g. by computing checksums), to prevent the system from producing faulty behavior.
nodes.problem: A system can drift outside its assumed operating conditions without any single operation failing; the monitor itself must be simple enough not to introduce new faults.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Configure Behavior
nodes.what: Build components so their behavior can be configured — during build, deployment/startup, or runtime — to operate in the modes an integrating system expects.
nodes.problem: A component with a single fixed behavior fits only one integration context; configurability lets one implementation satisfy many.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Defense in Depth
nodes.what: Multiple independent security controls are layered along the path to an asset so that compromising any single control does not compromise the system.
nodes.problem: Any single control can fail or be bypassed; stacking heterogeneous barriers forces an attacker to defeat several mechanisms and buys detection time.
nodes.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006); also NIST SP 800-53 usage
nodes.borderline: Principle-flavored, admitted as the structural layering of independent controls (bridge endpoint for validation, authN/Z, and isolation design elements).

nodes.name: Defer Binding
nodes.what: Bind values and choices as late in the life cycle as cost-effective: at compile/build time (component replacement, compile-time parameterization, aspects), at deployment/startup (configuration-time binding, resource files), or at runtime (discovery, interpreted parameters, shared repositories, polymorphism).
nodes.problem: Human-mediated change is costly and error-prone; building in flexibility lets computers effect the change, trading up-front mechanism cost against per-change cost and enabling change by non-developers ('externalizing' change).
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Degradation
nodes.what: In the presence of component failures, maintain the most critical system functions while dropping or substituting less critical ones in a planned, deliberate, safe way.
nodes.problem: Individual component failures should reduce system functionality gracefully rather than cause total collapse; e.g. a navigation system falling back to dead reckoning in a tunnel.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Detect Intrusion
nodes.what: Compare network traffic or service request patterns within a system against a database of signatures or known patterns of malicious behavior (protocol, payload size, source/destination address, port).
nodes.problem: Attacks in progress must be recognized among legitimate traffic before the system can react.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Detect Message Delay
nodes.what: Detect potential man-in-the-middle attacks by checking the time taken to deliver or receive messages against normally stable delivery times, and by watching for anomalous connect/disconnect counts.
nodes.problem: An interceptor that reads or modifies messages in transit adds latency and connection churn that timing analysis can expose.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Detect Service Denial
nodes.what: Compare the pattern or signature of incoming network traffic against historical profiles of known denial-of-service attacks.
nodes.problem: Denial-of-service traffic must be distinguished from legitimate load spikes before countermeasures can be applied.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Discover
nodes.what: Match service requests to service providers at runtime through a discovery service, enabling identification and remote invocation of providers that were not bound at build time; in the energy context, requests can be annotated so providers are selected by energy characteristics.
nodes.problem: Statically bound providers cannot be swapped or selected by runtime criteria (location, version, energy cost); a discovery mechanism defers and mediates the binding.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Dynamic Classification
nodes.what: Estimate energy consumption with a dynamic model — a table lookup, a regression over past executions, or a simulation — that accounts for transient conditions such as workload.
nodes.problem: Static energy models are insufficient when consumption depends heavily on runtime conditions.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Encapsulate
nodes.what: Introduce an explicit interface to an element and hide its internals so that other elements depend only on the interface, reducing the strength of coupling and the syntactic/semantic distance to be bridged.
nodes.problem: Direct dependence on an element's internals means every internal change and every integration must confront those internals; an interface localizes the dependency.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Encrypt Data
nodes.what: Apply encryption (symmetric or asymmetric) to stored data and to communication, providing confidentiality beyond authorization controls — and the sole protection on links that have none.
nodes.problem: Data at rest and in transit can be read by parties outside the authorization perimeter; encryption makes possession without keys useless.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Escalating Restart
nodes.what: Recover by restarting components at progressively coarser granularity levels (e.g. child threads only, then unprotected memory, then all memory, then full image reload), choosing the least disruptive level that clears the fault.
nodes.problem: A full restart is maximally disruptive; matching the restart granularity to the fault minimizes the impact on service, supporting graceful degradation.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Exception Detection
nodes.what: Detect system conditions that alter the normal flow of execution, refined by the book into system exceptions, parameter fence, parameter typing, and timeout.
nodes.problem: Faults such as divide-by-zero, bus/address faults, illegal instructions, or violated timing constraints must be turned into detectable events rather than silent corruption.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Exception Handling
nodes.what: After an exception is detected, handle it using mechanisms ranging from function return codes to exception classes carrying name, origin, and cause, so the fault can be masked or repaired.
nodes.problem: Simply crashing on a detected exception is unacceptable for availability; the system needs structured information and a place to act on it.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Exception Prevention
nodes.what: Employ techniques that keep exceptions from arising at all — error-correcting codes, abstract data types such as smart pointers, and wrappers that preclude dangling pointers or semaphore access violations.
nodes.problem: Whole fault classes (resource leaks, out-of-bounds access) can be excluded by construction more cheaply than detecting and recovering from them.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Executable Assertions
nodes.what: Hand-code assertions checking that data values satisfy specified constraints — placed wherever the data is referenced or modified, expressible as method pre/postconditions or class invariants — so the program flags when and where it enters a faulty state.
nodes.problem: Faulty states can pass silently through execution; systematically placed assertions embed the test oracle in the code, increasing observability.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Failover
nodes.what: On failure of an active unit, service is switched to a redundant standby unit that assumes its role.
nodes.problem: Continuity of service across unit failures requires a designated takeover path and role reassignment.
nodes.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

nodes.name: Feature Toggle
nodes.what: Integrate a runtime 'kill switch' for new features so a deployed feature can be automatically disabled without initiating a new deployment.
nodes.problem: Even fully tested features can misbehave after deployment; controlling them without the cost and risk of redeploying requires a toggle mechanism in the architecture.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Heartbeat
nodes.what: A monitored component periodically emits a message to (or resets a watchdog timer in) a system monitor, so that the absence of the heartbeat signals failure.
nodes.problem: Failure of a component must be detected without the monitor having to actively probe it; the component itself takes the initiative to demonstrate liveness.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Identify Actors
nodes.what: Identify the source of any external input to the system — users by user IDs; other systems by access codes, IP addresses, protocols, or ports.
nodes.problem: Authentication and authorization presuppose knowing which actor an input claims to come from.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Ignore Faulty Behavior
nodes.what: Ignore messages from a particular source once they are determined to be spurious, e.g. messages from a sensor known to have failed.
nodes.problem: A faulty component can flood the system with bogus events; continuing to act on them propagates the fault.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Increase Competence Set
nodes.what: Design a component to handle more cases — states that would otherwise be faults — as part of its normal operation, e.g. waiting or returning gracefully when a resource is blocked instead of throwing.
nodes.problem: A component throws an exception when it finds itself outside the set of states it is competent to handle; enlarging that set converts faults into handled situations.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Increase Resource Usage Efficiency
nodes.what: Improve the efficiency of the algorithms used in critical areas to decrease latency and improve throughput and resource consumption.
nodes.problem: Inefficient critical-path algorithms consume resources that better algorithms would free; 'optimizing the code' is one tactic among many, not the only lever.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Increase Resources
nodes.what: Add or upgrade resources — faster processors, additional processors, more memory, faster networks — to improve performance.
nodes.problem: When demand cannot be reduced, capacity must grow; despite its cost, adding resources is often the cheapest immediate route to better performance.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Inform Actors
nodes.what: When the system detects an attack, notify the relevant set of actors — operators, other personnel, or cooperating systems — so they can act.
nodes.problem: An ongoing attack may require human or cross-system action that the detecting system cannot take alone.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Interlock
nodes.what: Protect against failures arising from incorrect event ordering by controlling all access to protected components, including enforcing the correct sequencing of events affecting them.
nodes.problem: Some hazards arise not from wrong values but from right actions in the wrong order; an interlock makes illegal orderings impossible.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Introduce Concurrency
nodes.what: Process requests in parallel — different event streams on different threads, or additional threads for different activity sets — to reduce blocked time, then choose a scheduling policy via Schedule Resources.
nodes.problem: Serialized processing leaves requests blocked behind one another even when independent; concurrency reclaims that waiting time.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Limit Access
nodes.what: Restrict access to computing resources by limiting the number of access points and/or the types of traffic allowed through them — e.g. a demilitarized zone between internet and intranet bounded by a pair of firewalls.
nodes.problem: Every access point and permitted traffic type enlarges the attack surface; minimizing both contains exposure.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Limit Event Response
nodes.what: Process events only up to a set maximum rate, queueing or deliberately dropping events that arrive faster, triggered by queue size, processor utilization, or SLA violation.
nodes.problem: Bursts beyond processing capacity force a policy choice: guarantee no loss (size queues for the worst case) or drop events (and decide whether to log or notify).
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Limit Exposure
nodes.what: Minimize the damage a successful attack can do by reducing the amount of data or services reachable through any single access point — a passive defense that compartmentalizes value.
nodes.problem: If one breached access point yields everything, every breach is catastrophic; spreading assets bounds per-attack loss.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Limit Nondeterminism
nodes.what: Find and, where possible, eliminate sources of behavioral nondeterminism such as unconstrained parallelism; where unavoidable (e.g. multithreaded response to unpredictable events), manage it with tactics like record/playback.
nodes.problem: Nondeterministic systems are pernicious to test because failures do not reproduce; determinism restores repeatability.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Limit Structural Complexity
nodes.what: Keep the structure simple enough to test: avoid or resolve cyclic dependencies, isolate and encapsulate environmental dependencies, reduce inter-component coupling, constrain inheritance depth/fan-out and polymorphism, and track metrics such as response-of-class, propagation cost, and decoupling level.
nodes.problem: Large operational state spaces make recreating an exact state — and thus reproducing failures — hard; high cohesion, loose coupling, and separation of concerns shrink the state space.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Localize State Storage
nodes.what: Store system/subsystem/component state in a single place — conveniently a state machine object tracking and reporting the current state — so tests can start the system in any desired state, at whatever granularity testing needs.
nodes.problem: Hidden or scattered state makes starting a test from an arbitrary known state difficult or impossible.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Maintain Multiple Copies of Computations
nodes.what: Run multiple replicas of a computation (replicated services in a microservice architecture, replicated web servers in a pool) with a load balancer assigning new work among them.
nodes.problem: Funneling all service requests through a single instance creates contention; replicas spread the load.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Maintain Multiple Copies of Data
nodes.what: Keep copies of data — replication (separate identical copies to reduce contention) or caching (copies, possibly subsets, on storage with different access speeds, possibly predictively prefetched) — accepting the burden of keeping copies consistent.
nodes.problem: Simultaneous access to one copy of data creates contention, and distant/slow storage adds latency; copies trade consistency-maintenance work for reduced contention and faster access.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Maintain System Model
nodes.what: The system maintains an explicit model of itself to determine expected system behavior and give users appropriate feedback — the progress bar predicting time to completion is the canonical manifestation.
nodes.problem: Users need feedback about what the system is doing and how long it will take; producing it requires the system to model its own behavior.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Maintain Task Model
nodes.what: Maintain a model of the task the user is performing so the system can infer context and assist — e.g. predictive type-ahead in search engines, spell correction in mail clients.
nodes.problem: System-initiated help requires knowing what the user is trying to do; without a task model the system cannot anticipate.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Maintain User Model
nodes.what: Maintain an explicit model of a user or user class — their knowledge of the system, expected response-time behavior, error patterns — updated dynamically or offline; user-interface customization is a special case where users edit the model directly.
nodes.problem: One-size-fits-all interaction ignores what individual users know and need; encapsulating the model makes tailoring and modification easy.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Manage Event Arrival
nodes.what: Control the arrival rate of events from external systems, canonically by setting a service level agreement that fixes the maximum event rate the system will support, constraining both system and clients.
nodes.problem: Demand beyond the sustainable arrival rate degrades everyone's response time; capping arrivals makes load explicit and pushes overflow to additional instances.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Manage Resources (Integrability)
nodes.what: Interpose an explicit resource manager that mediates access to shared computing resources (memory, threads, hardware devices) so independently developed components can share them safely.
nodes.problem: Components that each assume exclusive resource ownership conflict when integrated; a mediator arbitrates. (Named 'Manage Resources' in bck's integrability chapter; not to be confused with the performance category of the same name.)
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Manage Sampling Rate
nodes.what: Reduce (possibly dynamically) the frequency at which environmental input is sampled — sensor data rates, video frames per second — trading fidelity for predictable latency.
nodes.problem: When the system cannot keep up with the incoming data stream, lower-fidelity but stable processing may beat unstable latency; common in signal-processing systems.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Manage Service Interactions
nodes.what: Allow multiple versions of system services to be deployed and executed simultaneously, with client requests routed to any version, coordinating inter-service interactions to proactively avoid version incompatibilities.
nodes.problem: Simultaneously running old and new versions avoids fully duplicating resources during upgrade but introduces version-compatibility hazards that must be managed.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Masking
nodes.what: Mask a fault by comparing the results of several redundant components and using a voting procedure when they differ, so the faulty result never propagates; requires a simple, highly reliable voter.
nodes.problem: Some systems must keep producing correct outputs through component faults, not merely detect them; masking hides the fault behind redundancy.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Metering
nodes.what: Collect data about the energy consumption of computing resources in near real time via a sensor infrastructure — from data-center meters down to metered rack PDUs, ASICs, or battery management systems.
nodes.problem: Energy cannot be managed without being measured; different granularities of measurement need different instrumentation.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Monitor
nodes.what: A dedicated component monitors the health of other parts of the system (processors, processes, I/O, memory) and coordinates the other fault-detection tactics.
nodes.problem: Faults must be observed by some part of the system before any repair can begin; a system needs a designated observer to detect failures or congestion, e.g. denial-of-service conditions.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Non-Stop Forwarding
nodes.what: Split functionality into a control/management plane and a data plane so that when the control plane fails, the data plane keeps forwarding along known routes while routing information is rebuilt and validated.
nodes.problem: In router-like systems, supervisory failure should not stop the ongoing data-moving work; the concept originates in router design.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Nonrepudiation
nodes.what: Guarantee that the sender of a message cannot later deny sending it and the receiver cannot deny receiving it, via some combination of digital signatures and trusted third-party certification.
nodes.problem: Transactions between mutually distrustful parties need binding evidence of send and receipt.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Orchestrate
nodes.what: Introduce a control mechanism (e.g. an orchestration engine or workflow controller) that coordinates, sequences, and invokes otherwise independent services so they work together.
nodes.problem: Independently developed services have no shared control flow; centralizing coordination keeps the integration logic out of the services themselves.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Package Dependencies
nodes.what: Package an element together with its dependencies (libraries, OS version, utility containers) — via containers, pods, or virtual machines — so they deploy together and dependency versions stay consistent from development to production.
nodes.problem: An element that behaves correctly in development can fail in production when the surrounding dependency versions differ.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Parameter Fence
nodes.what: Place a known data pattern immediately after any variable-length parameters of an object so that overwrites of that memory can be detected at runtime.
nodes.problem: Buffer overruns into memory allocated for variable-length parameters are otherwise silent until they corrupt unrelated state.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
nodes.borderline: Reads as an implementation-level guard mechanism (kin to design-realm canaries/guard bytes), but bck names it explicitly as an availability sub-tactic; kept per over-inclusion rule.

nodes.name: Parameter Typing
nodes.what: Use a base class defining functions to add, find, and iterate over type-length-value (TLV) message parameters so that sender and receiver agree on content types and disagreements are detected.
nodes.problem: Untyped message payloads let sender and receiver silently disagree about the meaning of bytes on the wire.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)
nodes.borderline: Implementation-flavored like parameter fence, but named as an availability sub-tactic in bck; kept per over-inclusion rule.

nodes.name: Pause/Resume
nodes.what: Let users pause and later resume long-running operations (e.g. large downloads), temporarily freeing resources for reallocation to other tasks.
nodes.problem: Long-running operations monopolize resources and user attention; suspension without loss of progress restores control to the user.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Ping/Echo
nodes.what: Nodes exchange asynchronous request/response message pairs to determine reachability and round-trip delay, with a time threshold before the pinged component is declared failed.
nodes.problem: A monitor must determine whether a remote component is alive and reachable over a network path, and how long the path takes.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Predictive Model
