nodes.what: Combine a model with monitoring to predict, from operational metrics (session establishment rates, threshold crossings, process-state and queue-length statistics), that a fault or unsafe condition is approaching, and take corrective action early.
nodes.problem: Waiting for faults to occur before reacting is too late for high-availability and safety-critical operation; early warning enables preemptive correction.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Prioritize Events
nodes.what: Impose a priority scheme ordering events by importance of servicing them, so that under resource pressure low-priority events may be ignored at minimal cost.
nodes.problem: Not all events are equally important (a fire alarm vs. a room-temperature notice); treating them uniformly wastes resources on the unimportant under load.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
nodes.what: A queue is placed between producers and a service so bursts are absorbed by the queue and the service consumes at its sustainable rate.
nodes.problem: Intermittent heavy load overwhelms downstream services provisioned for average demand; the buffer converts bursts into throughput-bounded work.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Queue-Based Load Leveling - Azure Architecture Center (living)

nodes.name: Reconfiguration
nodes.what: Recover from failure by reassigning responsibilities — remapping the logical architecture onto the (possibly limited) resources or components still functioning — while preserving as much functionality as possible.
nodes.problem: After failures the remaining resources differ from the planned deployment; the system must keep operating on what is left, possibly combined with degradation.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Record/Playback
nodes.what: Record information as it crosses interfaces and use the recorded state to 'play the system back', recreating the fault-inducing state as input to further tests.
nodes.problem: The state that causes a failure is often hard to recreate manually; capturing it at interfaces makes failures reproducible, including in nondeterministic systems.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Redistribute Responsibilities
nodes.what: Move similar responsibilities scattered across several modules into one module (existing or new), guided by change scenarios showing which responsibilities move together.
nodes.problem: When one likely change touches many modules, or a module contains parts untouched by any scenario, responsibilities are misallocated and change cost multiplies.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Reduce Computational Overhead
nodes.what: Reduce the work spent per event by removing costly indirection (while ideally preserving encapsulation through code optimization or proxy-established direct communication), co-locating communicating components (same processor, same runtime, same rack), and periodically cleaning inefficient-grown resources such as hash tables and virtual memory maps.
nodes.problem: Intermediaries and separation of concerns — valuable for modifiability — add per-event processing and communication cost; this is the classic modifiability/performance trade-off.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Reduce Usage
nodes.what: Reduce energy use by device-level actions (lower refresh rate, dim display), removing or deactivating unneeded resources (spin down disks, power off CPUs/servers, reduce clock rate), consolidating VMs onto fewer physical servers, or offloading computation to the cloud.
nodes.problem: Resources kept powered beyond demand waste energy; usage must track need.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Redundant Spare
nodes.what: Configure one or more spare components that can step in and take over when an active component fails; hot/warm/cold variants differ in how current the spare's state is at takeover.
nodes.problem: A failed active component must be replaced quickly to keep the service available; the trade-off is between resource cost of keeping spares synchronized and recovery time.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Removal from Service
nodes.what: Temporarily place a system component out of service and reset it to scrub latent faults (memory leaks, fragmentation, soft errors) before they accumulate into failures.
nodes.problem: Latent faults accumulate during long operation; proactive resets prevent them from ever affecting service.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Repair State
nodes.what: Repair an erroneous state — effectively enlarging the set of states the component handles competently — and continue execution, e.g. lane-keeping assist steering a drifting vehicle back between the lane lines.
nodes.problem: Aborting or degrading is not always acceptable; some erroneous states can be actively corrected in place, though this is unsuited to recovering from unanticipated faults.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Restrict Communication Paths
nodes.what: Restrict the set of elements with which a given element can communicate, so the number of potential interaction points that must be understood and integrated stays small.
nodes.problem: Unrestricted many-to-many communication makes the integration surface of each element grow with the system; deliberate path restriction contains it.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Restrict Dependencies
nodes.what: Restrict which modules a given module may interact with or depend on, in practice via interface visibility and authorization; seen in layered architectures (a layer may use only lower layers) and wrappers (outsiders see only the wrapper).
nodes.problem: Unconstrained dependency graphs let changes ripple arbitrarily; restricting the allowed edges bounds the ripple. Sibling of the integrability tactic Restrict Communication Paths, kept separate as bck names both.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Restrict Login
nodes.what: Limit access from a computer after repeated failed login attempts to an account, typically for a bounded period, sometimes doubling the lockout after each further failure.
nodes.problem: Repeated failed logins signal credential-guessing attacks, but legitimate users also mistype; time-bounded lockouts balance the two.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Retry
nodes.what: Assume the fault that caused a failure is transient and retry the operation, with a limit on the number of attempts before declaring a permanent failure.
nodes.problem: In networks and server farms transient failures are expected and common; treating every failure as permanent wastes the chance of cheap recovery.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Revoke Access
nodes.what: When an attack is believed to be underway, severely limit access to sensitive resources — even for normally legitimate users — until the threat is removed.
nodes.problem: During an active compromise, normal access rights become an attack vector; temporary revocation trades usability for containment.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Rollback (Deployment)
nodes.what: Revert a defective or disappointing deployment to its prior state, tracking or being able to reverse the coordinated updates to multiple services and their data, ideally fully automatically.
nodes.problem: A deployment may involve many coordinated service and data updates; discovering a defect after release requires undoing all of them safely. Distinct mechanism from the availability Rollback tactic, which reverts runtime state to a checkpoint.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Rollback
nodes.what: On detecting a failure, revert the system to a previously saved known-good state (the rollback line), captured as checkpoints, and resume execution from there.
nodes.problem: A failure can leave state corrupted; recovery requires a consistent earlier state to return to, often combined with transactions and redundant spares.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Sanity Checking
nodes.what: Check the validity or reasonableness of a component's specific operations or outputs, typically at interfaces, based on knowledge of the internal design, system state, or the nature of the information.
nodes.problem: A component can produce syntactically valid but semantically implausible results; examining specific information flows catches such faults early.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Scale Rollouts
nodes.what: Deploy a new version of a service gradually to controlled subsets of the user population rather than to everyone at once, monitoring effects and rolling back if needed; blue/green deployment and rolling upgrade are pattern realizations.
nodes.problem: Deploying a defective service to all users maximizes damage; incremental exposure requires an architectural mechanism outside the service that routes each user's requests to the new or old version.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Schedule Resources
nodes.what: When resources (processors, buffers, networks) are contended, choose and apply a scheduling policy — priority assignment plus dispatching, e.g. FIFO, fixed-priority (semantic importance, deadline-monotonic, rate-monotonic), dynamic-priority (round-robin, EDF, least-slack-first), or static/cyclic-executive scheduling — matched to each resource's usage characteristics; in the energy realm, schedule work onto the most energy-efficient resources under task constraints.
nodes.problem: Contention forces choices among competing criteria — optimal use, importance, latency, throughput, starvation-freedom — and the chosen policy determines which are met.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Script Deployment Commands
nodes.what: Capture the many precisely ordered, coordinated deployment steps as scripts that are treated like code — documented, reviewed, tested, version-controlled — and executed by a script engine.
nodes.problem: Complex manual deployments are slow and error-prone; automation removes human error and makes deployments repeatable.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Self-Test
nodes.what: A component or subsystem runs procedures to test itself for correct operation, initiated by itself or invoked periodically by the system monitor.
nodes.problem: Latent faults in a component may not manifest during normal operation until they matter; proactive self-exercise surfaces them early.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Separate Entities
nodes.what: Limit the scope of an attack by separating entities — physical separation onto different servers/networks, virtual machines, air gaps, and keeping sensitive data apart from non-sensitive data.
nodes.problem: Co-located entities share fate under attack; separation prevents access to one from becoming access to all.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Shadow
nodes.what: Run a previously failed or freshly upgraded component in shadow mode for a predefined period, monitoring its behavior and letting it repopulate state before restoring it to an active role.
nodes.problem: Reintroducing a repaired component directly into active service risks reintroducing the fault; its correctness must be demonstrated first.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Software Upgrade
nodes.what: Upgrade executable code images in service, without affecting the running service, via function patches, class patches, or hitless in-service software upgrade built on redundant spares.
nodes.problem: Deploying fixes and features to systems that must not stop requires replacing code while it runs.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Specialized Interfaces
nodes.what: Provide dedicated test interfaces — set/get methods for important variables, report methods returning full object state, reset methods forcing a given internal state, verbose/logging/instrumentation switches — clearly separated from functional interfaces so they can be removed.
nodes.problem: Testers need to control and capture component state beyond normal inputs and outputs; but shipping code different from tested code is problematic in performance- and safety-critical systems.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Split Module
nodes.what: Refactor a module whose responsibilities are not cohesive into several modules that are each individually cohesive — not an arbitrary bisection, but a principled separation of responsibilities.
nodes.problem: When one module carries unrelated responsibilities, changes to any of them cost as much as changing all; splitting reduces the average cost of future change.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: State Resynchronization
nodes.what: Restore and verify state consistency between active and standby components, either naturally under active redundancy (with periodic comparison via checksums or message digests) or by periodic state transfer/checkpointing under passive redundancy.
nodes.problem: A reintroduced or standby component must have state consistent with the active one before it can safely take over.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Static Classification
nodes.what: Estimate energy consumption by cataloging the computing resources used and their known static energy characteristics (from benchmarks or manufacturer specifications), e.g. energy per disk read.
nodes.problem: Real-time energy data collection is sometimes impossible (e.g. on external cloud services); reference models substitute for measurement.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Substitution
aka: hardware substitution for software safety functions
nodes.what: Replace potentially hazardous software design features with protection mechanisms — typically hardware devices such as watchdogs, monitors, and interlocks — that provide and control their own resources.
nodes.problem: Software versions of protection mechanisms can be starved of resources by the very failures they guard against; substitution pays off when the protected function is relatively simple.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Tailor Interface
nodes.what: Add capabilities to or hide capabilities of an interface without changing the underlying implementation — e.g. adding buffering, data transformation, or masking functions (adapter/decorator-like mechanisms at the architectural boundary).
nodes.problem: Independently developed components rarely present exactly the interfaces their integrators need; adapting at the interface avoids modifying either side.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Throttling (service admission control)
nodes.what: A service enforces consumption limits per tenant/client and degrades or rejects excess requests to protect its SLA under load.
nodes.problem: Autoscaling has limits and lag; explicit admission control keeps the system functional when demand exceeds capacity.
nodes.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns: Throttling - Azure Architecture Center (living)
nodes.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: the design realm carries throttle/rate-limiter mechanisms (token bucket, sliding window); this is the system-boundary policy structure.

nodes.name: Timeout
nodes.what: A component raises an exception when it detects that it or another component has failed to meet its timing constraints, e.g. when a response takes longer than a set bound.
nodes.problem: Hung or slow components would otherwise block their clients indefinitely; violated time constraints must become detectable events.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Timestamp
nodes.what: Assign the state of a local clock (or a sequence number) to events immediately after they occur so that incorrect event ordering can be detected.
nodes.problem: In distributed message-passing systems, events may arrive or be processed out of order and local clocks may be inconsistent across processors.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Transactions
nodes.what: Use transaction semantics (ACID properties, most commonly implemented via two-phase commit) to bundle state updates exchanged between distributed components so they are atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable.
nodes.problem: Race conditions from concurrent updates to the same data, and partial failures mid-update, would otherwise leave inconsistent state.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Undo
nodes.what: Maintain sufficient information about earlier system state — snapshots/checkpoints or sets of reversible operations, with detailed change records where operations are not invertible — to restore it on user request, in single- or multi-level variants.
nodes.problem: Users make mistakes; recovery requires the system to have planned for state restoration, since some operations (mass replace, or anything with external effects) cannot be reversed naively or at all.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Use an Intermediary
nodes.what: Break a dependency between elements by interposing an intermediary (broker, publish-subscribe bus, name server, etc.) that manages the interaction on their behalf.
nodes.problem: Direct dependencies between many elements multiply coupling and integration effort; an intermediary centralizes and standardizes the interaction, at some performance cost.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Validate Input
nodes.what: Sanitize and check input as it is received — filtering, canonicalization, and cleansing, typically via a security framework or validation classes — as an early line of defense.
nodes.problem: Uninspected input is the vector for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and kin; validation at the boundary stops malicious payloads before they reach interpreters.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Verify Message Integrity
nodes.what: Use checksums or hash values to verify the integrity of messages, resource files, deployment files, and configuration files, maintaining the redundant verification information separately.
nodes.problem: Tampered or corrupted messages and artifacts must be detectable; even small changes must produce large, visible differences in the verification value.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

nodes.name: Voting
nodes.what: Compare computational results from multiple sources that should produce the same result and decide which to use when they differ, using simple, heavily reviewed voting logic.
nodes.problem: A single component's output cannot be trusted in the presence of hardware or software faults; multiple evaluable sources plus a highly reliable voter allow faulty results to be outvoted.
nodes.named_in: Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. — Bass, Clements & Kazman (2021)

edges.note: Bundling related values into one aggregate passed as a unit is the object-scale form of the encapsulate tactic.
A bulk get/set applies one operation to a whole set of elements - the Aggregate usability tactic at API scale.
Fusing a common call sequence into one interface method executed as a single unit gives it transaction-like atomicity.
Lazy first-call construction defers when the object is bound/created to runtime.
Externally supplied dependencies are the assembly mechanism component architectures rely on to wire replaceable components.
An external assembler binds concrete collaborators at deployment/startup rather than in the component's code.
Runtime-checked pre/postconditions and invariants are hand-coded executable assertions on data validity.
An internal DSL is a little language whose constructs are evaluated by host-language machinery - the interpreter style at library scale.
Internal iteration applies a client operation to each element without exposing the collection's representation.
Separating a usage contract into an interface type is the encapsulate tactic: clients depend only on the interface, not internals.
Explicit provided-interface types are the precondition for components with declared provided/required interfaces.
Chained expressions translated into a normal command-query API build an internal-DSL expression evaluated by the host.
An expression builder is the concrete construct that provides the fluent interface over a command-query API.
Multiple role-specific interfaces reached via a root interface (QueryInterface) is the component-interface mechanism of COM-style components.
A fixed facade whose backend is chosen per target at build/link time binds the implementation at compile/link (component replacement).
A fluent interface builds configuration/computation as an internal DSL read and executed by the host language.
A mode/flag parameter selecting among behaviors is runtime behavior configuration of a single routine.
Variadic option functions are the Go mechanism for configuring a component's behavior at construction.
The implementable HAL interface set is the design-scale realization of the architectural HAL layer (same concept, two realms).
Re-declaring the widgets from application state every frame makes the view a pure function of state re-derived each cycle.
IMGUI (rebuild each frame) and retained mode (persistent scene model) are the two opposing GUI API styles.
A separate interface exposing a component's capability/configuration metadata is the meta-level self-representation of the Reflection pattern.
Container-invoked lifecycle methods (init/activate/passivate/destroy) are the mechanism by which a container manages hosted components.
Named chained setters on a parameter object configure a call's behavior by named argument rather than position.
The C++ named-parameter idiom realizes a fluent interface for argument passing.
Returning data through caller-supplied pointers is a parameter-passing convention of the procedure-call connector.
A plugin linked at configuration time is the extension mechanism that plug-in/microkernel architectures are built from.
Selecting behavior per deployment via configuration binds the implementation late (deployment-time).
Mapping a specification to a concrete product class at runtime defers the binding of type to run time.
A persistent retained scene graph/widget tree is a central data structure that client code and the renderer operate on.
A locator resolving a concrete provider at runtime is the in-process realization of a service registry.

edges.cite: Fowler, 'Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern' (contrasts Service Locator vs DI)
edges.note: Two competing ways to obtain a dependency; Fowler explicitly weighs them against each other.
Making the only constructor validate/normalize is an abstract-data-type discipline that keeps invalid values (and their exceptions) from arising.
A named static creator hides the concrete class and instantiation choice behind a stable creation interface.
Cohesive type-safe classes over low-level non-portable system APIs introduce an interface hiding the OS internals.
Creating a whole product family behind an interface defers the choice of concrete family to configuration/runtime.
An opaque per-client session object held by the server encapsulates that client's server-side session state.
The whole point of Acyclic Visitor is to break the dependency cycle between element and visitor hierarchies.
A Visitor variant using a degenerate base visitor to remove the cyclic dependency.
An Adapter converting one class's interface to what clients expect is the object-scale adaptor connector.
Decoupling abstraction from implementation hides the implementation hierarchy behind the abstraction's interface.
Separating construction from representation encapsulates a complex build process behind a stable director/builder interface.
A self-maintaining hierarchy of cooperating elements propagating changes up and down mirrors the PAC agent hierarchy.
Passing a request along a chain of candidate handlers is the object realization of a staged processing chain.
Reifying a request as an object with execute/unexecute is the mechanism that maintains reversible-operation information for undo.
A command processor that logs and stores command objects supplies the checkpoint/history that undo/redo depends on.
The command processor schedules, executes, logs and stores reified Command objects.
Splitting an entity's state/behavior into per-domain components composed at runtime is component-based structuring at object scale.
Part-whole trees treated uniformly are the recursive containment structure applied to objects.
A collector threaded through methods, each writing its partial result, is a shared structure accumulating partial solutions.
CRTP resolves polymorphic calls at compile time, removing the virtual-dispatch indirection - a per-event overhead reduction.
Wrapping an object to add responsibilities without changing its class adds capability to the same interface.
Forwarding requests to a helper is the object-composition mechanism underpinning object-oriented organization (composition over inheritance).
A stateless domain-layer operation defined by what it does is a first-class element of the DDD domain model.
Dispatching on two runtime types is a dynamic-dispatch mechanism of the object-oriented style.
Visitor is realized by a pair of single dispatches (double dispatch).
A shared-base handle/body split hides the letter (body) implementation behind the envelope handle.
Envelope-Letter is a handle/body variant where handle and bodies share a common base class.
Asking an object for an extension implementing a given interface adds capabilities without changing the object's class.
Wrapping unrelated concrete classes in a parallel adapter hierarchy adapts them to one uniform polymorphic interface.
A unified higher-level interface hiding a subsystem is the encapsulate tactic applied to a subsystem.
Deferring which class to instantiate to subclasses binds the concrete type late.
Sharing intrinsic state across many fine-grained objects improves memory-usage efficiency.
Looking up a handler in a function-pointer table binds the invoked behavior late, replacing hard-coded branch chains.
An overridable extension-point method defers the concrete behavior to a subclass/client (late binding of a step).
Template Method calls hook methods at its designed variation points.
Registered interceptors invoked automatically at framework dispatch points are implicitly invoked handlers on internal events.
A class-per-grammar-rule interpret operation over an AST is the object realization of the interpreter style.
Sequential access without exposing the aggregate's representation is the encapsulate tactic for traversal.
A common supertype holding behavior shared by all types in a layer is a structuring aid for the Layers pattern.
An object mediating between two subsystems that stay ignorant of each other is an interposed intermediary breaking the dependency.
An empty tagging interface is static metadata about a class, queried (via type checks/reflection) to drive behavior.
Encapsulating how colleagues interact so they refer only to the mediator interposes an intermediary that breaks their direct dependencies.
Capturing and externalizing state to restore later is the snapshot/checkpoint mechanism undo relies on.
A reusable behavior slice composed into many classes factors a shared capability into one general unit.
All instances sharing static state make the class a single shared data store that many holders operate on.
Monostate (shared static state, free construction) and Singleton (single instance) are alternative ways to get global-shared behavior.
A map of exactly-one-instance-per-key is a keyed registry of instances.
Multiton generalizes Singleton to one instance per key.
A non-virtual public interface delegating to private virtual hooks fixes the public contract while hiding the variable implementation.
NVI is a disciplined form of Template Method with non-virtual public methods and private virtual hooks.
A do-nothing stand-in makes 'no object' a normally handled case rather than a null-check fault.
Null Object is the 'absent' specialization of Special Case.
Encapsulation/inheritance/polymorphism via struct embedding and function-pointer tables organizes plain C as ADT instances.
Distributing request handling recursively over a polymorphic structure is recursive containment applied to behavior.
Object Recursion typically walks a Composite structure, each node handling its part and delegating the rest.
A one-to-many change-notification dependency is the object-scale realization of publish-subscribe (mission calibration anchor).
Notifying registered dependents on state change is the mechanism implicit-invocation/event-based systems depend on.
Per-class function-pointer vtables plus self pointers realize dynamic-dispatch objects in C.
The explicit-vtable technique is one concrete way of doing object orientation in C.
Storing a method name and dispatching on it reflectively uses run-time self-representation of methods.
Assembling behavior from orthogonal policy template parameters binds each aspect at compile time (build-time selection).
Policy-Based Design is the compile-time, template-parameter counterpart of runtime Strategy.
Moving state into a separate data object exposed read-only tightens encapsulation of a class's data.
Creating objects by cloning a prototypical instance defers what gets created to a runtime-configured exemplar.
A surrogate with the same interface interposed to control access to a subject is an interposed intermediary.
A well-known object other objects use to find common services is the in-process realization of a service registry.
Attaching/detaching role objects at runtime adds and hides capabilities per client context without changing the core class.
Defining an interface in a separate package so clients depend only on it restricts inter-module dependencies.
A helper class providing one common behavior to a group of unrelated classes factors that shared service into one place.
A single shared instance providing a global access point is a central shared datum many components operate on.
A subclass giving defined behavior for particular cases handles states that would otherwise be faults as normal operation.
Encapsulating a business rule as a combinable predicate object evaluated against candidates is a small rule engine.

Recursive divide-and-conquer split vs a manager farming identical subtasks to interchangeable workers.

unbridged.why: Pure C++ translation-unit static-initialization-order idiom (Schwarz counter); no specific architecture element governs cross-TU init ordering - bridged laterally to construct-on-first-use instead.

Pure numerical-accuracy micro-technique; no architecture element (style, tactic, pattern) addresses silent floating-point precision loss - nearest tactic (exception-prevention) concerns fault classes, not rounding error.
C++ container idiom operating wholly below architectural altitude; after a real attempt the only candidate was the generic efficiency tactic, which would be a catch-all edge
FP navigation idiom over immutable structures; composes with persistent-data-structure within-realm but no specific architecture element depends on or constrains it

Preprocessor single-source code-generation idiom keeping parallel artifacts (enums/strings/tables) consistent; a coding-level DRY mechanism no specific architecture element deploys, depends on, or constrains.

Compiler object-layout micro-optimization internal to C++ class composition; below architectural granularity - no specific architecture element depends on or constrains it (kept a within-realm composes-with edge only).
